items.explanation: Persistent acid injury makes the lower oesophagus swap its native squamous lining for a tougher glandular (columnar) one. Replacement of one mature cell type by another is metaplasia, here Barrett's oesophagus, which carries a risk of adenocarcinoma.
Age-related prostatic enlargement is hormonally driven and comes from more cells, not bigger ones, so the process is hyperplasia (benign prostatic hyperplasia).
Skeletal muscle that is not used loses protein and its fibres shrink, so the limb wastes. This reduction in cell and organ size is disuse atrophy, and it reverses with rehabilitation.

Venous stasis during long immobility plus the prothrombotic effect of oestrogen favour clot formation inside a flowing deep vein (Virchow's triad). That is thrombosis, presenting as a deep vein thrombosis of the calf.

Atypical cells with loss of orderly maturation that stay above the basement membrane define dysplasia. Involvement of the full epithelial thickness is graded CIN 3, the precursor of invasive cervical cancer.
Working against a raised afterload makes cardiac myocytes enlarge rather than divide, so the ventricular wall thickens. An increase in cell size driven by workload is hypertrophy.

Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells that secrete antibody. Their abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus push the nucleus to one side and give the pale perinuclear zone and cartwheel chromatin.
Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells. They carry antigen to lymph nodes and supply the co-stimulatory signals that a naive T cell needs before it can be activated.
CD3 is part of the T-cell receptor complex on every T cell, and CD4 marks the helper subset, which recognises peptide held by MHC class II molecules.
Macrophages are monocyte-derived tissue phagocytes. Their lysosomes hold digestive enzymes, lysozyme among them, which break down ingested microbes.
CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells read peptide displayed by MHC class I, which all nucleated cells carry, and kill virus-infected or abnormal cells.
Natural killer cells are CD56-positive innate lymphocytes. They destroy infected or malignant cells that have lost normal MHC class I expression, with no prior sensitisation needed.
An epitope, or antigenic determinant, is the small region of an antigen that actually makes contact with the antibody's combining site.
Papain splits an immunoglobulin into two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment. Each Fab carries the variable domains of one heavy and one light chain, which together form the antigen-binding site.
IgE attaches to high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils. When allergen cross-links the bound IgE, the cells degranulate, which is the basis of type I hypersensitivity.
A hapten is too small to provoke an immune response by itself. It becomes immunogenic only after coupling to a larger carrier protein, as penicillin does when it binds host proteins.
The human major histocompatibility complex is the HLA region on the short arm of chromosome 6. Its highly polymorphic class I and II molecules are the main targets in graft rejection.

Superantigens such as staphylococcal toxic shock toxin bridge MHC class II and the T-cell receptor beta chain outside the peptide groove. They therefore switch on huge numbers of T cells without any antigen processing.
Transfection means deliberately introducing foreign DNA or RNA into eukaryotic cells, for example by lipofection or electroporation. Transformation is the equivalent term for bacteria.
Hybridisation is complementary base pairing between a labelled probe and its target DNA or RNA. It underlies Southern and northern blots, FISH and microarrays.

Western blotting runs proteins through SDS-PAGE to separate them by size, transfers them to a membrane and detects them with specific antibodies. Southern blots detect DNA and northern blots detect RNA.
PCR uses two primers, a heat-stable polymerase and repeated cycles of heating and cooling to copy a defined DNA segment exponentially from a tiny amount of template.

Linkage analysis follows how often a disease travels with polymorphic markers through a family. Loci that sit close together rarely separate at meiotic recombination, so a marker that co-segregates places the gene nearby.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis provokes granulomas with central caseous necrosis, ringed by epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells.
Helicobacter pylori sets up a persistent infection with a lymphocyte- and plasma-cell-rich infiltrate, often with lymphoid follicles. That is chronic, frequently active, gastritis.
Rheumatic pericarditis lays down a fibrin-rich exudate over the serosal surfaces, giving the classic 'bread and butter' appearance of fibrinous inflammation.
Sarcoidosis forms tight, well-formed granulomas without central caseation, which separates it histologically from tuberculosis.
Pyogenic bacteria in the subarachnoid space draw in masses of neutrophils and produce a purulent exudate. That is acute suppurative inflammation.
Helminths such as hookworm drive a Th2 response in which IL-5 recruits eosinophils, so the tissue reaction is eosinophil-rich.
C3b coats microbes and is recognised by complement receptor 1 on phagocytes, which greatly speeds ingestion. It is the main opsonin of the complement system.
Histamine is stored ready-made in mast-cell granules. Once released, it contracts venular endothelial cells and causes the immediate rise in vascular permeability.
The NADPH oxidase respiratory burst in phagocytes produces superoxide, which is converted to hydrogen peroxide and hypochlorous acid to kill ingested bacteria.
ICAM-1 belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily. On activated endothelium it binds leucocyte integrins such as LFA-1 and mediates firm adhesion before emigration.
IL-1, like TNF, is a pleiotropic cytokine. It upregulates endothelial adhesion molecules and acts on the hypothalamus to reset the temperature set-point, causing fever.
Lysozyme hydrolyses the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls, especially Gram-positive ones. It is an oxygen-independent killing mechanism.
Entamoeba histolytica invades the colonic mucosa and undermines it, leaving flask-shaped ulcers. Trophozoites that contain ingested red cells are diagnostic of invasive amoebiasis.
Toxoplasma gondii crossing the placenta damages the developing brain and retina. It is the classic cause of hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and scattered intracranial calcification.

Pneumocystis jirovecii attacks hosts with impaired cell-mediated immunity. It fills the alveoli with foamy exudate, its cysts stain with silver (Grocott) stains, and high-dose co-trimoxazole is the treatment.

Schistosoma haematobium lays eggs in the bladder wall. The granulomatous reaction causes haematuria and fibrosis, and chronic infection predisposes to squamous-cell bladder cancer, especially in the Nile valley.
Plasmodium falciparum, acquired in sub-Saharan Africa, causes rigors and hepatosplenomegaly and can become severe within hours. Parasitised red cells on thick and thin films confirm the diagnosis.
Candida is the commonest cause of oesophagitis in AIDS and counts as an AIDS-defining illness. It forms white mucosal plaques made of yeasts and pseudohyphae.
Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF of a young adult with a petechial rash mean meningococcal disease. Give parenteral benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone without delay.
Escherichia coli, a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus, causes most community-acquired urinary tract infections. A count of 10^5 organisms/ml or more confirms significant bacteriuria.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics in frail inpatients allow Clostridioides difficile to overgrow. Its toxins cause pseudomembranous colitis with yellow-white plaques, and finding the cytotoxin confirms it.

Alpha-haemolytic Gram-positive diplococci whose colonies have a sunken centre are Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is the commonest cause of lobar pneumonia, and alcohol misuse and poor living conditions increase the risk.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase-positive and form golden colonies identify Staphylococcus aureus, the leading cause of surgical wound infection.
Campylobacter jejuni, usually from undercooked poultry, is a curved, motile, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod and a leading cause of bacterial enteritis.
Low-risk human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 cause anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata). Types 16 and 18 are the oncogenic ones.
Epstein-Barr virus enters B cells through CD21 and causes glandular fever. The blood shows atypical lymphocytes and the heterophile (Monospot) test is positive.
Parainfluenza virus is the main cause of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) in young children, giving a barking cough and inspiratory stridor.
Enteroviruses, particularly Coxsackie and echoviruses, are the commonest cause of aseptic (viral) meningitis.
Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe, dehydrating gastroenteritis in infants and young children, although vaccination has greatly reduced it.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a rare, fatal, late complication of measles. A defective virus persists in the brain and causes progressive neurological decline years after the original infection.
In plasma-cell neoplasms the amyloid fibrils are built from monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains, which is AL amyloid.
Amyloid-beta peptide, cut from amyloid precursor protein, forms the extracellular plaques and vascular deposits of Alzheimer's disease.
Long-standing inflammation makes the liver produce serum amyloid A protein, which deposits as AA (reactive) amyloid, typically in the kidney.
In type 2 diabetes, amylin (islet amyloid polypeptide), which is co-secreted with insulin, deposits within the pancreatic islets.
Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, and the calcitonin they secrete forms amyloid in the tumour stroma.
The bladder is lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium), whose surface umbrella cells flatten out as the bladder fills.
The ectocervix, like the vagina, is covered by non-keratinising stratified squamous epithelium. It meets the columnar endocervical lining at the transformation zone.
The trachea carries respiratory epithelium: pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells mixed with goblet cells, which together form the mucociliary escalator.
Serous membranes such as the pericardium are lined by mesothelium, a single layer of flattened cells, which is simple squamous epithelium.
The epidermis is keratinising stratified squamous epithelium. Its surface layer of keratin provides a tough, waterproof barrier.
Ultraviolet radiation, especially intense intermittent exposure with sunburn, damages melanocyte DNA. It is the main environmental cause of cutaneous melanoma.
Tobacco smoke contains polycyclic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines. Squamous-cell and small-cell lung cancers have the strongest link to smoking.
Aromatic amines such as beta-naphthylamine, used in the dye and rubber industries, are concentrated in urine and cause urothelial (transitional-cell) carcinoma.
Aflatoxin B1 comes from Aspergillus flavus growing on badly stored grain and nuts. It induces TP53 mutations and hepatocellular carcinoma, and it acts synergistically with hepatitis B.
Nitrates in smoked, salted and pickled foods are converted to N-nitroso compounds, which promote intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma.
Radiation exposure of the thyroid in childhood, for example from external beam treatment or Chernobyl fallout, is the best-established cause of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
High-risk HPV types, chiefly 16 and 18, cause cervical squamous carcinoma. Their viral oncoproteins disable the p53 and retinoblastoma tumour-suppressor pathways.
Chronic H. pylori gastritis stimulates B cells in newly acquired mucosal lymphoid tissue and can give rise to gastric MALT lymphoma. Early lesions may regress after eradication therapy.
Human herpesvirus 8 (KSHV) is present in every form of Kaposi's sarcoma, which is most common in untreated HIV infection.
Chronic hepatitis B integrates into hepatocyte DNA and drives continuous inflammation and regeneration. It is the leading cause of hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide, even without cirrhosis.
Endemic (African) Burkitt lymphoma is almost always EBV-positive, with malaria as a co-factor, and carries the t(8;14) MYC translocation.
Follicular lymphoma carries t(14;18), which moves BCL2 next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus. Excess anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 lets the neoplastic B cells avoid normal cell death.
Germline BRCA1 mutations, inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, impair DNA double-strand break repair and give a high lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
Chronic myeloid leukaemia is defined by the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22). It creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase that imatinib targets.
Retinoblastoma develops when both copies of the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene on 13q are lost. This is Knudson's two-hit model, and familial cases inherit the first hit.
Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by a germline APC mutation. Loss of the second allele releases beta-catenin signalling, and hundreds of colorectal adenomas follow.
Keratin production is the hallmark of squamous differentiation. Squamous-cell lung cancer is typically central (hilar) and is strongly linked to smoking.
A lipoma is a benign tumour of mature fat cells: soft, mobile, encapsulated and yellow on cut section.
Osteosarcoma peaks in adolescence around the knee. Malignant osteoid and lifting of the periosteum (Codman triangle, sunburst pattern) are characteristic.
Painless haematuria with a bladder mass in an older adult is most often urothelial (transitional-cell) carcinoma. Smoking and aromatic amines are the key risk factors.
A small pedunculated colorectal polyp is usually a benign tubular adenoma. Its malignant potential rises with size, villous architecture and grade of dysplasia.
Signet-ring cells, in which mucin pushes the nucleus to the edge, mark diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma.
Langhans giant cells are fused macrophages with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe around the periphery, typical of tuberculous granulomas. Do not confuse them with Langerhans cells of the skin.
Schwann cells form myelin around peripheral nerve axons. Oligodendrocytes do the same job in the central nervous system.
Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules and nurture developing sperm. They also form the blood-testis barrier and secrete inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone.
Reed-Sternberg cells are large, often binucleate 'owl-eye' cells of B-cell origin (CD15/CD30 positive). They are required for the diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma.
Kupffer cells are resident macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids. They clear particles, bacteria and old red cells from portal blood.
Thiamine deficiency in alcohol misuse causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, neuropathy and wet beriberi. Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose.
Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells removes intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed in the terminal ileum. The result is pernicious anaemia with megaloblastic change.
Fat malabsorption stops uptake of the fat-soluble vitamins. Without vitamin K, factors II, VII, IX and X are not carboxylated, so the prothrombin time lengthens and bleeding follows.
A diet with no fresh fruit or vegetables leads to scurvy. Faulty collagen hydroxylation causes bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs and easy bruising.

Too little vitamin D, from limited sunlight, pigmented skin and a diet free of dairy or fortified foods, impairs mineralisation of growing bone. In children this is rickets, with bowed legs and chest deformity.
Germline mutations in mismatch-repair genes (MLH1, MSH2 and others) cause Lynch syndrome (HNPCC). It brings early colorectal, endometrial, ovarian and other cancers.
Oncogenic HPV 16 drives anal squamous-cell carcinoma, and drug-induced immunosuppression after transplant (or HIV) multiplies the risk.
Long-standing coeliac disease carries a risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma of the small bowel. Strict gluten avoidance probably lowers that risk.
Chronic H. pylori infection progresses through atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma (the Correa sequence).
A gastrinoma keeps gastrin levels high, which drives enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia and gastric carcinoid tumours, particularly in MEN1.
Prostate cancer typically spreads to the axial skeleton and forms sclerotic (osteoblastic) rather than lytic deposits. The PSA is usually very high.
Small-cell lung cancer spreads early, often to the adrenals, and can secrete ectopic ACTH, giving Cushingoid features with hypokalaemia.
A hard left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node, Troisier's sign) signals spread of an abdominal cancer, classically gastric, via the thoracic duct.
A metastatic nodule at the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) reflects peritoneal spread of an abdominal cancer, most often gastric. Upper GI bleeding points to the stomach as the primary.
An ocular prosthesis suggests earlier enucleation for uveal melanoma. That tumour characteristically metastasises to the liver, sometimes many years later.

where.title: Pathological conditions of the female genital tract

items.explanation: Most cervical cancers are squamous-cell carcinomas that arise from HPV-driven intraepithelial neoplasia at the transformation zone.
A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) contains well-differentiated tissue from all three germ layers, such as skin, hair, sebum, teeth and bone. It is benign and common in young women.
Endometriosis is functioning endometrium outside the uterus. Cyclical bleeding causes pain, adhesions and subfertility, and ovarian deposits become 'chocolate' cysts.
Unopposed oestrogen, from obesity or nulliparity, promotes endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endometrium. It classically presents with postmenopausal bleeding.
Fibroids are leiomyomas, benign smooth-muscle tumours of the myometrium with a whorled white cut surface. They cause heavy periods, pain and pressure symptoms.
Septic emboli from infective endocarditis can seed the brain and form an abscess. On imaging it is a ring-enhancing lesion, with focal signs that progress.
In older people, even minor head trauma can tear bridging veins. Blood then collects slowly in the subdural space and causes headache and fluctuating confusion days to weeks later.
A diffusely infiltrating, GFAP-positive glial tumour with mass effect is a high-grade astrocytoma (glioblastoma), the commonest primary malignant brain tumour in adults.
A wedge-shaped low-density area confined to one arterial territory is an infarct. Hypertension and smoking predispose to atherothromboembolic stroke.
Primary CNS lymphoma in advanced HIV is an EBV-driven, high-grade B-cell lymphoma. It is often multifocal and deep or periventricular.
Sjogren's syndrome causes keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Hypromellose is an artificial tear that lubricates the dry ocular surface.
Topical timolol, a beta-blocker, lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous production and is a standard treatment for open-angle glaucoma. Check first for asthma.
Conjunctivitis that recurs every summer is allergic. Antazoline is a topical antihistamine that relieves the itch and redness.
Tropicamide is a short-acting antimuscarinic mydriatic that wears off within a few hours. That makes it the usual choice for dilating the pupil to examine the fundus.
Fluorescein stains areas where corneal epithelium is missing, so abrasions and ulcers glow green under cobalt-blue light.
A branching dendritic ulcer seen with fluorescein is pathognomonic of herpes simplex keratitis. Treat with a topical antiviral and avoid topical steroids.
Gritty, red eyes with purulent discharge that crusts the lashes and spreads among close contacts indicate bacterial conjunctivitis.
Acute angle closure raises intraocular pressure abruptly. It causes a painful red eye, haloes, blurred vision and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and it is an ophthalmic emergency.
A pterygium is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva onto the cornea. It is linked to chronic ultraviolet and dust exposure in hot, sunny climates.
Anterior uveitis is strongly associated with HLA-B27 conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis. It causes pain, photophobia, circumcorneal redness, a small pupil and sometimes a hypopyon.
Water makes impacted cerumen swell until it occludes the canal, so swimming or bathing can bring on sudden conductive deafness and fullness.
Otitis externa is inflammation of the external canal skin. Pain is worse on moving the tragus or jaw, and the canal is swollen, tender and discharging.
A nasopharyngeal tumour can block the Eustachian tube and cause a one-sided middle-ear effusion with conductive loss. A unilateral effusion in an adult always needs the nasopharynx examined.
Cholesteatoma is keratinising squamous epithelium trapped in the attic. It causes foul chronic discharge, progressive conductive loss and erosion of the surrounding bone.

Otosclerosis fixes the stapes footplate, causing progressive conductive deafness in young adults, often with a family history. Hearing paradoxically seems better in background noise (paracusis of Willis).

A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at the cerebellopontine angle causes slowly progressive one-sided sensorineural deafness. Loss of the corneal reflex shows that it is compressing the trigeminal nerve.

where.title: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal air sinuses

items.explanation: The frontal sinus lies within the frontal bone, directly behind the brow ridges.
The floor of the maxillary sinus sits over the roots of the upper molars, so dental infection can spread into the sinus.
The ethmoid air cells sit between the orbits. Their paper-thin lateral wall (lamina papyracea) forms the medial orbital wall, which is why ethmoiditis can spread to cause orbital cellulitis.
The sphenoid sinus lies immediately below the pituitary fossa, which is the basis of the transsphenoidal approach to the pituitary.
The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath the inferior concha. The concha therefore lies on the medial side of the duct.
A one-sided, foul, bloodstained nasal discharge in a young child is a retained foreign body until proven otherwise.
Anaemia out of proportion to blood loss, with leucocytosis and circulating blasts, means acute leukaemia. Marrow failure causes thrombocytopenia and mucosal bleeding.
A mechanical heart valve needs lifelong anticoagulation, and over-anticoagulation with warfarin often shows itself as nosebleeds.
A pyogenic granuloma is a friable, vascular red lesion that bleeds on contact. It often appears on the nasal septum and is more common in pregnancy.
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu), an autosomal dominant disorder, produces fragile mucosal and skin telangiectasias that cause recurrent heavy nosebleeds.
The cricoid cartilage, at the level of C6, is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway.
Each vocal ligament runs from the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage angle in front to the vocal process of the arytenoid behind.
The piriform fossa lies on each side of the laryngeal inlet, and its medial wall is formed by the epiglottis and the aryepiglottic fold.
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid, which tenses the cords. The nerve is at risk when the superior thyroid vessels are ligated.
The quadrangular membrane runs from the side of the epiglottis forward to the arytenoid cartilage behind, and its free lower edge forms the vestibular fold.
Chronic voice overuse produces symmetrical nodules at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of both cords. These are singer's nodules.
Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, caused by HPV types 6 and 11, produces wart-like laryngeal growths in children that cause hoarseness.
A fixed cord lying near the midline means recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. The left nerve loops into the chest, so a bronchial carcinoma at the left hilum can involve it.
A white (leukoplakic) lesion on the vocal cord of a heavy smoker is glottic carcinoma until biopsy shows otherwise. Cord tumours cause hoarseness early.
Inhaled corticosteroids predispose to oropharyngeal and laryngeal candidiasis. Using a spacer and rinsing the mouth afterwards reduce the risk.
Juvenile laryngeal papillomas keep recurring after excision and can grow large enough to narrow the airway and cause stridor.
A bilateral mandibular fracture removes the forward support of the tongue, which falls back and obstructs the airway when the patient lies supine.
Rapid onset of high fever, toxicity, drooling and stridor in a child suggests acute epiglottitis. Keep the child upright and calm and secure the airway in theatre.
Progressive hoarseness followed by inspiratory stridor in a smoker suggests an obstructing laryngeal carcinoma, which can be mistaken for COPD.
Injury to both recurrent laryngeal nerves during thyroid surgery leaves both cords near the midline, causing stridor and respiratory distress.
Recurrent stridor that began with choking while eating points to an inhaled foreign body still lodged in the airway.
The middle constrictor arises from the stylohyoid ligament and from the greater and lesser horns of the hyoid bone.
Palatopharyngeus lies beneath the palatopharyngeal arch, the posterior pillar of the fauces.
The thyropharyngeal part of the inferior constrictor arises from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, and the cricopharyngeal part arises from the cricoid.
Stylopharyngeus is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The others are supplied through the vagal pharyngeal plexus.
The superior constrictor and buccinator share an attachment to the pterygomandibular raphe.
At the root of the neck the internal jugular vein descends in front of the first part of the subclavian artery before joining the subclavian vein.
The hypoglossal nerve curves forward across the lateral side of the internal and external carotid arteries, just above the carotid bifurcation.
The common carotid artery divides into internal and external branches at about the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3/C4).
The facial artery can be felt pulsating where it crosses the lower border of the mandible, just in front of masseter.
The external jugular vein runs downward across the surface of sternocleidomastoid under platysma, which is why it is visible on the side of the neck.
A midline cyst that rises when the tongue is protruded is a thyroglossal cyst, a remnant of the thyroid's descent that is tethered to the hyoid.
A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) bulges through Killian's dehiscence. Retained food causes regurgitation, halitosis, aspiration cough and a soft, compressible lump.
Painless, firm nodal enlargement with B symptoms and itching suggests lymphoma, especially Hodgkin. The diagnosis needs an excision biopsy.
A branchial cyst is a smooth, fluctuant swelling that bulges from beneath the anterior border of the upper third of sternocleidomastoid, usually in young adults.
A hard anterior-triangle node in an older adult with voice change suggests metastatic squamous carcinoma from the upper aerodigestive tract, such as the larynx.

where.title: Tumours of the head and neck

items.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is the commonest parotid tumour. It is benign and slow-growing, with mixed epithelial and myxoid or chondroid tissue, and it can recur if the capsule is breached.
Oral cancer in smokers and drinkers is nearly always squamous-cell carcinoma, often arising in leukoplakia. Keratinisation confirms squamous differentiation.
A benign Schwann-cell tumour of the vestibular nerve at the cerebellopontine angle is an acoustic neuroma. It causes one-sided tinnitus and sensorineural hearing loss.
Undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma is EBV-associated and especially common in southern Chinese people. It presents with nasal blockage, one-sided middle-ear effusion and neck nodes.
Ameloblastoma is a locally aggressive odontogenic epithelial tumour, usually in the posterior mandible, that looks lytic and often multilocular on X-ray.
The glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensation from the posterior tongue and pharynx, so it forms the sensory (afferent) limb of the gag reflex. The vagus supplies the motor response.
Whistling depends on orbicularis oris and buccinator. Both are muscles of facial expression, supplied by the facial nerve.
An effective cough needs laryngeal sensation and tight closure of the vocal cords. Both are supplied by vagal branches, the superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves.
The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, which turns the eye down and out (depression in adduction) and intorts it.
Bending the head down to look underneath something relies on sternocleidomastoid flexing the neck, and that muscle is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve.

Fasciculus gracilis carries proprioception, vibration and fine touch from the same side of the lower body to the nucleus gracilis. Second-order fibres from there cross as internal arcuate fibres and form the medial lemniscus.
Most corticospinal fibres (about 85-90%) cross in the pyramidal decussation of the lower medulla and then descend as the lateral corticospinal tract.
Pain and temperature fibres cross within a segment or two and rise in the anterolateral (spinothalamic) system. Of the tracts offered, the ventral spinothalamic tract is the one in this system.
The dorsal spinocerebellar tract starts in Clarke's column (the thoracic nucleus). It carries same-side unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum through the inferior peduncle.
Lissauer's (dorsolateral) tract is the thin zone between the dorsal root entry zone and the dorsal horn. Incoming pain fibres run up or down a segment or two there before they synapse.
Transient one-eyed loss of vision, like a shade coming down, is amaurosis fugax: a retinal TIA, usually from carotid emboli. Investigate with carotid Doppler imaging.
Bilateral occipital infarction causes cortical blindness with normal pupil reactions and fundi. The patient may deny being blind (Anton's syndrome).
A pituitary macroadenoma presses on the optic chiasm from below and damages the crossing nasal fibres, giving a bitemporal hemianopia.
A left sixth-nerve palsy paralyses the left lateral rectus, so horizontal double vision is worst on looking to the left.
Optic neuritis in demyelinating disease typically produces a central scotoma, with pain on eye movement and loss of colour vision.
New vessels on or near the disc mark proliferative diabetic retinopathy, driven by retinal ischaemia. It needs urgent laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF treatment.
Complete ptosis with a 'down and out' eye and a fixed dilated pupil is a third-nerve palsy that involves the pupil. Painful onset suggests compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
Cataract (opacity of the lens) slowly reduces acuity and dims the red reflex, and it blocks the view of the fundus.
Retrobulbar neuritis inflames the optic nerve behind the globe, so the disc looks normal in the acute phase. Delayed visual evoked responses confirm demyelination.
Pale discs mean optic atrophy. In heavy drinkers, nutritional (tobacco-alcohol) optic neuropathy is a recognised cause.
Small, irregular pupils that constrict to accommodation but not to light are Argyll Robertson pupils. Diabetes is a recognised non-syphilitic cause.
An apical (Pancoast) lung tumour invades the cervical sympathetic chain and the T1 root, causing Horner's syndrome (miosis, ptosis, enophthalmos) with wasting of the small hand muscles.
A Holmes-Adie pupil is a dilated, tonic pupil that reacts slowly to light and accommodation. It is typical in young women and may come with reduced tendon reflexes.
Coma with pinpoint pupils that improves with naloxone indicates opioid overdose.
A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) dilates when the light swings onto it, because the damaged optic nerve carries a weaker light signal.
A one-sided facial weakness that includes the forehead is a lower motor neurone lesion of the facial nerve itself, as in Bell's palsy, rather than a central lesion.
Brief, shooting facial pains set off by touching a trigger area are trigeminal neuralgia, usually in the maxillary or mandibular division.

Accepted answers: C, D and I. Bulbar palsy in motor neurone disease affects the lower cranial nerves (glossopharyngeal, vagus and hypoglossal), causing dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, an absent gag reflex and tongue involvement.
Raised intracranial pressure, here likely from metastatic breast cancer, stretches the long intracranial course of the abducens nerve. The result is a false-localising sixth-nerve palsy.

Accepted answers: B, G and J. A cerebellopontine angle mass compresses the facial, trigeminal and vestibulocochlear nerves together, causing facial weakness, loss of the corneal reflex and sensorineural deafness.
Neurofibromatosis type 2 produces vestibular schwannomas at the cerebellopontine angle, which compress cranial nerves V to VIII.
Parotid swelling, uveitis, fever and facial palsy together form Heerfordt's syndrome (uveoparotid fever), a manifestation of sarcoidosis.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome is reactivation of varicella-zoster in the geniculate ganglion. It causes a lower motor neurone facial palsy with ear pain and vesicles in the external canal.
Optic neuritis together with a brainstem lesion of the facial nucleus suggests multiple sclerosis with a plaque of demyelination in the pons.
When several separate nerves (ulnar, common peroneal, facial) are damaged one after another, the pattern is mononeuritis multiplex, a recognised complication of diabetes.
Eyes opening to pain (E2), incomprehensible sounds (V2) and withdrawal from pain (M4) add up to GCS 8, the threshold at which the airway should be secured.
A lucid interval followed by sudden deterioration after a blow to the temporoparietal region is typical of an extradural haematoma from middle meningeal artery bleeding.
Eyes opening to pain (E2), confused speech (V4) and localising to pain (M5) give a GCS of 11.
Bilateral periorbital bruising, a subconjunctival haemorrhage with no posterior limit and blood in the ear canal are signs of a basal skull fracture.

Repeated acceleration-deceleration blows can tear bridging veins and cause an acute subdural haematoma. Rapid loss of consciousness with a unilateral fixed dilated pupil and lateralising signs reflects mass effect and herniation.
A sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache with neck stiffness and xanthochromic CSF confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Berry aneurysms occur more often in people with adult polycystic kidney disease, and cocaine and exertion cause sharp surges in blood pressure. Together they point to aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Fluctuating drowsiness and confusion days to weeks after a minor fall in a frail older person is typical of chronic subdural haematoma.
Hemiparesis worse in the arm, with expressive dysphasia, localises to the dominant middle cerebral territory. Hypertension is the main cause of primary intracerebral haemorrhage.
Weakness worse in the leg, with frontal-lobe disinhibition and personality change, localises to the anterior cerebral artery territory.
Idiopathic (benign) intracranial hypertension typically affects obese young women. It causes morning headache, brief visual obscurations and papilloedema, with no mass on imaging.
Degenerative cervical spondylosis can refer pain from the neck up to the occiput and temples (cervicogenic headache).
Fever, headache and vomiting with a petechial rash point to meningococcal meningitis. Give antibiotics at once.
Cluster headache causes nightly attacks of severe one-sided pain around the eye, with tearing and a red eye on that side, each lasting under about an hour. Patients pace about rather than lie still.

Giant-cell arteritis causes a new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and a very high ESR. Skip lesions mean a negative biopsy does not exclude it, so start steroids promptly to protect vision.
Occipital headache with neck and shoulder stiffness and a normal ESR in an older person points to cervical spondylosis rather than giant-cell arteritis or polymyalgia.
Headache that is worse on waking and on coughing, with blurred vision and nausea, suggests raised intracranial pressure from a space-occupying lesion, likely a breast cancer metastasis.
A prodrome followed by a one-sided throbbing headache with visual flashes and vomiting is migraine with aura.
Severe, short, one-sided headaches that recur at the same time every day for weeks follow the clockwork pattern of cluster headache.
Headache with papilloedema in a young woman on the combined pill suggests cerebral venous (sagittal) sinus thrombosis. Contrast imaging may show the 'empty delta' sign.
Infective endocarditis sends septic emboli that weaken the walls of cerebral arteries and form mycotic aneurysms. These can cause embolic or haemorrhagic stroke.
Pancytopenia, renal failure, hypercalcaemia and a very high ESR suggest myeloma. The paraprotein raises blood viscosity and can cause stroke.
Adult polycystic kidney disease is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms. Rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage, worsened by the accompanying hypertension.

Recurrent miscarriage and venous thrombosis suggest antiphospholipid syndrome, which also causes arterial thrombosis and stroke in young adults. Check lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies.
ST elevation that persists months after an anterior infarct suggests a left ventricular aneurysm. Mural thrombus forms in it and can embolise to the brain.
Disinhibition, personality change, urinary incontinence and expressive dysphasia all localise to the dominant frontal lobe.
Dyspraxia, inattention and constructional difficulty, such as failing to draw a clock face, are parietal-lobe signs.
Receptive (Wernicke's) dysphasia with jargon, a hemianopia and hemiparesis point to a dominant temporoparietal lesion.
Cortical blindness with denial of the deficit (Anton's syndrome) comes from bilateral occipital cortex infarction.
Nystagmus, dysdiadochokinesia and past-pointing on one side indicate a cerebellar lesion on that same side.
Accepted answers: B and C. Being unable to name objects whose use is known (anomia), with word-finding pauses but good comprehension, is a mild expressive dysphasia from a dominant frontal lesion.
Accepted answers: C and I. Producing no speech and failing simple commands means global aphasia, a combination of expressive and receptive dysphasia from a large dominant-hemisphere infarct.
A tumour in the chest can involve the recurrent laryngeal nerve, giving a weak, hoarse voice while language itself is normal.
Accepted answers: C and G. Speech made up of meaningless jargon, with comprehension partly kept, reflects a dominant-hemisphere language disorder with expressive dysphasia.

Accepted answers: E and H. Motor neurone disease weakens the tongue and pharynx (bulbar palsy). Lingual and guttural sounds such as 'L' and 'K' suffer, giving glossal and pharyngeal dysarthria while language is preserved.
Alcohol excess causes a length-dependent sensory neuropathy through direct toxicity and poor nutrition. Macrocytosis with normal vitamin levels and signs of chronic liver disease support it.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. It also damages the peripheral nerves and the dorsal columns (subacute combined degeneration).
Visual blurring plus sensory loss in a young woman, with a normal metabolic screen, suggests central demyelination such as multiple sclerosis.
HIV itself causes a painful distal sensory polyneuropathy, especially at advanced stages. Kaposi's sarcoma and CMV retinitis show this patient has AIDS.
A loin mass with haematuria and weight loss suggests renal cell carcinoma. Cancers can cause a paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy.
An expanding red rash after a tick-exposure holiday in North America suggests Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi). It can cause a polyradiculoneuropathy that responds to antibiotics.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy) causes distal wasting, giving 'inverted champagne bottle' legs, plus pes cavus and areflexia.
Pancytopenia, renal failure, hypercalcaemia and a high ESR mean myeloma. Paraprotein and amyloid deposition can cause a mixed sensorimotor neuropathy.
Wet beriberi, from thiamine deficiency, combines high-output heart failure and oedema with a painful sensorimotor neuropathy.
Diabetic amyotrophy (lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy) causes painful, asymmetric weakness and wasting of the thigh muscles in type 2 diabetes.
Ascending weakness with lost reflexes after an infection is Guillain-Barre syndrome, an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. Monitor vital capacity closely.
Combining a thiazide-like diuretic (metolazone) with a loop diuretic causes heavy potassium loss, and hypokalaemia produces generalised muscle weakness.
Dense hemiplegia on the opposite side with dysphasia, hemianopia and sensory inattention indicates a large dominant middle cerebral artery infarct.

Myeloma deposits in vertebrae can compress the cord, giving upper motor neurone leg weakness, a sensory level and bladder retention. This emergency needs steroids, urgent MRI and radiotherapy or surgery.
Fatigable weakness affecting the eyes, chewing and swallowing, with acetylcholine-receptor antibodies, is myasthenia gravis.
An asymmetric resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia that respond well to levodopa indicate idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
Prochlorperazine, a phenothiazine dopamine antagonist often prescribed for dizziness, causes drug-induced parkinsonism that resolves once it is stopped.
Progressive supranuclear palsy combines parkinsonism with early falls, loss of vertical gaze, dysarthria and frontal slowing.
Multiple system atrophy combines parkinsonism with autonomic failure (postural hypotension) and cerebellar ataxia.
In a young person, Kayser-Fleischer rings, liver disease and low caeruloplasmin with a movement disorder indicate Wilson's disease, a disorder of copper accumulation.
Acute vertigo, vomiting and ataxia in a hypertensive person, with a low-attenuation lesion in the cerebellum on CT, indicates cerebellar infarction.
Chronic alcohol excess causes cerebellar (mainly vermis) degeneration with gait ataxia, and liver stigmata support the cause.
Friedreich's ataxia, an autosomal recessive GAA-repeat disorder, causes ataxia, pes cavus, loss of proprioception and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which explains the ECG changes.
Hypothyroidism can cause a reversible cerebellar syndrome, together with coarse facies, a hoarse voice and slow-relaxing reflexes.
Diplopia from internuclear ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and bulbar symptoms in a young adult indicate demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis.
In HIV, a ring-enhancing lesion that responds to pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine is a toxoplasma abscess. It provokes seizures by irritating the cortex locally.
Thiazides and SSRIs both cause hyponatraemia, particularly in older people. A sodium level well below 120 mmol/l causes cerebral oedema, confusion and seizures.
Phenytoin, often given after neurosurgery, has a narrow therapeutic range. Toxicity causes nystagmus, ataxia and even seizures, and it also produces folate-related macrocytosis and low calcium.

Book discrepancy: the printed key gives C (cerebral metastases), but the book's own discussion describes herpes simplex encephalitis. Of the options, G (meningitis) best matches this meningoencephalitis. Start IV aciclovir urgently.
Damage to the parathyroids during thyroidectomy causes acute hypocalcaemia. Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs show neuromuscular irritability, which can progress to seizures.
Focal motor jerking that spreads up a limb (a Jacksonian march) with no loss of awareness is a simple partial (focal aware) seizure.
Impaired awareness with automatisms such as lip-smacking, after a rising epigastric aura, is a complex partial seizure, usually from the temporal lobe.
Brief absences with instant recovery and 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG in a child are typical absence seizures.
Sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening then clonic jerking, cyanosis, incontinence and post-ictal drowsiness define a generalised tonic-clonic seizure.
A focal onset, here an aura of fear with altered awareness, that goes on to a generalised convulsion is a partial seizure with secondary generalisation.
Removing or bruising the parathyroids at total thyroidectomy causes hypocalcaemia within a day or two, and it can trigger seizures.
Fever, hypotension and a stiff neck after intracranial surgery point to postoperative bacterial meningitis. Adequate phenytoin cover makes a drug cause less likely.
A recently started thiazide in a very old, dehydrated patient often causes hyponatraemia, a common metabolic cause of seizures.
Staphylococcal endocarditis after a skin infection (aortic murmurs, splinter haemorrhages, Roth spots) can throw septic emboli to the brain and form a cerebral abscess.
Weeks of vomiting (the pelvic mass suggests pregnancy with hyperemesis) deplete magnesium. Severe hypomagnesaemia increases neuromuscular excitability and causes seizures.
Early-morning waking, poor intake, withdrawal, worthlessness and a wish to die indicate a severe depressive episode with a high suicide risk.
Little need for sleep, reckless spending, pressured speech, flight of ideas and grandiose delusions are features of mania.
Months of free-floating worry about everything, with autonomic symptoms, poor sleep and poor concentration, is generalised anxiety disorder.
Fear and avoidance of leaving home or going to public places is agoraphobia, a phobic anxiety disorder.
Hearing voices that command or comment, persecutory delusions and social withdrawal in a young adult, with drug use excluded, suggest schizophrenia.
Tricyclics such as amitriptyline have antimuscarinic effects (constipation, blurred vision, tachycardia) and alpha-blocking effects that cause postural hypotension and falls.
Lithium toxicity causes a coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and confusion. Lithium also causes hypothyroidism, as the raised TSH here shows.
Clomethiazole, used in alcohol withdrawal, often causes nasal congestion, sneezing and conjunctival irritation as well as sedation.
SSRIs such as fluoxetine can cause SIADH and marked hyponatraemia, especially in older people, which presents as confusion.
Thioridazine markedly prolongs the QT interval and can trigger torsade de pointes, which is why its use is now severely restricted.
Hyperglycaemia, heavy ketonuria and a metabolic acidosis with low bicarbonate define diabetic ketoacidosis, which is often triggered by infection.
Squamous lung cancer can secrete PTH-related peptide. Calcium above about 3 mmol/l causes confusion, dehydration and drowsiness.
An infective COPD exacerbation with type 2 respiratory failure (high PaCO2, acidaemia) causes CO2 narcosis, with confusion and agitation.
A crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over one hemisphere with mass effect is a subdural haematoma, a classic cause of confusion and falls in older people.
Fever, confusion, seizures and temporal-lobe changes that improve with aciclovir indicate herpes simplex encephalitis.
Stepwise cognitive decline in someone with vascular risk factors and previous TIAs or strokes is typical of vascular (multi-infarct) dementia.
Gradually worsening memory, word-finding difficulty and getting lost, with normal investigations, fit Alzheimer's disease.
Gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline with enlarged ventricles indicate normal-pressure hydrocephalus, which may improve with shunting.
Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of cognitive decline. A hoarse voice, macrocytosis and hyponatraemia are supporting clues, so check TSH in every dementia work-up.
Early, prominent personality change and disinhibition with relatively spared memory suggest frontotemporal dementia (Pick's disease).
Pericardiocentesis is done by the subxiphoid route: the needle enters at the left costoxiphoid angle and is aimed towards the left shoulder, avoiding the pleura and coronary vessels.
Normally the apex beat is felt in the fifth left interspace, in line with the middle of the clavicle. Displacement suggests cardiac enlargement or mediastinal shift.
The aortic area for auscultation is the second right intercostal space beside the sternum.
Tricuspid sounds are heard best low on the sternal border at about the fourth intercostal space. In this book's option list, that is the right sternal border level with the fourth space.
The pulmonary valve itself sits behind the left third costosternal junction. Its sounds are heard best a little higher, in the second left intercostal space.
The left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus, while the right coronary arises from the anterior sinus.
The coronary sinus collects most of the heart's venous blood and empties into the right atrium next to the opening of the inferior vena cava.
The right coronary artery runs in the right part of the atrioventricular (coronary) groove on the front of the heart.
The AV nodal branch arises at the crux of the heart, where the right coronary gives off the posterior interventricular artery. That is why inferior infarcts often cause heart block.
The anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery runs down to the apex and supplies it, along with the anterior septum.
Sharp central chest pain that eases on sitting forward and worsens lying flat or coughing is characteristic of acute, often viral, pericarditis.
Crushing central pain with sweating and a slow pulse suggests acute myocardial infarction, often inferior with AV-node ischaemia. Get an urgent ECG and arrange reperfusion.
Sudden tearing pain that goes through to the back, with unequal arm pressures in a hypertensive patient, indicates thoracic aortic dissection.
Rest pain that is worse than usual and does not respond to nitrates, with a normal troponin, is unstable angina rather than infarction.
Pleuritic pain after pregnancy loss with a swollen, tender leg, in a patient with lupus and possible antiphospholipid antibodies, indicates DVT complicated by pulmonary embolism.
A slow-rising pulse, a heaving but undisplaced apex and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids indicate aortic stenosis.
Previous infarcts, orthopnoea, a displaced apex, a gallop rhythm, basal crackles and an ejection fraction of 20% indicate left ventricular systolic failure.
Prominent x and y descents with an early diastolic extra sound (pericardial knock) and a raised JVP suggest constrictive pericarditis, a recognised complication of rheumatoid disease.
After cardiac surgery, hypotension, a grossly raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus progressing to PEA arrest mean cardiac tamponade.
An irregular tachycardia with weight loss, tremor and a thyroid bruit indicates atrial fibrillation caused by thyrotoxicosis, such as Graves' disease.
A slow-rising carotid pulse with exertional angina suggests aortic stenosis, which produces a crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur.
Alcoholic dilated cardiomyopathy stretches the mitral annulus and causes functional mitral regurgitation, heard as a pansystolic murmur.
A left atrial myxoma can embolise and cause TIA or stroke. As it moves into the mitral orifice it makes an early diastolic 'tumour plop'.
Endocarditis destroying the aortic valve causes aortic regurgitation: an early diastolic murmur with a collapsing pulse and visible nail-bed capillary pulsation (Quincke's sign).
A patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous 'machinery' murmur, loudest below the left clavicle.
Digoxin causes down-sloping 'reverse tick' ST depression and T-wave changes across many leads. This shows the drug's effect and does not by itself mean toxicity.
Acute pericarditis gives concave, saddle-shaped ST elevation in many leads that do not fit one coronary territory, often with PR depression.
A posterior infarct shows as a mirror image in V1-V3, with tall R waves and ST depression. Posterior leads V7-V9 show the ST elevation.
Q waves and ST elevation in II, III and aVF place the infarct on the inferior wall, usually in right coronary territory.
Q waves with ST elevation across V1-V4 indicate an anterior (anteroseptal) infarct from left anterior descending occlusion.
Early post-infarct pericarditis, in the first few days, causes positional, pleuritic pain and a friction rub from inflammation over full-thickness necrosis.
A large anterior infarct leaves an akinetic segment where mural thrombus forms. The clot can embolise and cause stroke, and anticoagulation lowers this risk.
Free-wall rupture usually happens 3-7 days after infarction, when the necrotic muscle is softest. Bleeding into the pericardium causes tamponade and sudden death.
A ventricular aneurysm is a thin, scarred segment that bulges outwards in systole. It causes persistent ST elevation, heart failure, thrombus and arrhythmias.
Dressler's syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks to months after infarction, with fever, a raised ESR and pericardial effusion. It responds to anti-inflammatory treatment.

Papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation, with a new pansystolic murmur and pulmonary oedema. Ventricular septal rupture is the main alternative and needs echocardiography to separate.
Wide-QRS regular tachycardia showing AV dissociation in a patient with ischaemic heart disease is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.
A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at almost exactly 150/min suggests atrial flutter: the atria beat at about 300/min with 2:1 conduction.
An irregularly irregular, fast pulse in an older person is atrial fibrillation, the most common sustained arrhythmia.
A regular rate near 30/min during an inferior infarct suggests complete heart block from AV-nodal ischaemia, which is often temporary.
Occasional non-conducted P waves with a constant PR interval and broad QRS is Mobitz type II block. It carries a high risk of progressing to complete block, so pacing is indicated.
IV verapamil given to someone already on a beta-blocker adds negative inotropy and AV blockade and can cause asystole. Never combine them intravenously.
Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node. It commonly causes transient chest tightness, flushing and breathlessness, and it can provoke bronchospasm in asthma.
Long-term amiodarone can cause pulmonary fibrosis, as well as thyroid, liver, skin, nerve and corneal toxicity, so monitoring is needed.
Sotalol has class III activity that prolongs the QT interval, which predisposes to torsade de pointes.
Lipid-soluble beta-blockers such as propranolol cross into the brain and cause vivid dreams, nightmares and disturbed sleep.
Gross septal thickening, an ejection systolic murmur and a family history of sudden young death indicate hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, an autosomal dominant sarcomere disorder.
A tapping apex, atrial fibrillation and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur indicate mitral stenosis, usually rheumatic.
Papillary muscle rupture after an inferior infarct causes sudden severe mitral regurgitation, with a loud new pansystolic murmur and acute pulmonary oedema.
A collapsing pulse, displaced apex and soft early diastolic murmur heard best beside the left sternum indicate aortic regurgitation. Severe hypertension can dilate the aortic root and cause it.
P waves dissociated from a slow, broad escape rhythm mean complete heart block. An AV-nodal blocker such as verapamil can bring it on when the conducting system is already diseased.
A sharp rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor suggests bilateral atheromatous renal artery stenosis, where glomerular filtration depends on angiotensin II.
Hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis, suppressed renin and an adrenal nodule indicates primary hyperaldosteronism from an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's syndrome).
Hypertension in a young man with delayed femoral pulses and an ejection murmur indicate coarctation of the aorta.

A systemic illness with blood and protein in the urine, raised inflammatory markers and a positive ANCA suggests necrotising vasculitis. In this book's options that is polyarteritis nodosa, and its renal involvement drives the hypertension.

Paroxysms of palpitations, headache and sweating with repeatedly raised urinary catecholamines indicate a phaeochromocytoma. Normal adrenal imaging suggests an extra-adrenal tumour (paraganglioma), so use functional imaging such as MIBG.
Beta-blockers, even relatively cardioselective ones such as atenolol, can block bronchial beta-2 receptors and trigger bronchospasm in asthma.
Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine can cause gum hyperplasia, as well as flushing, headache and ankle oedema.
ACE inhibitors such as enalapril stop the breakdown of bradykinin, which causes a persistent dry cough in up to about one in ten patients. Switch to an angiotensin-receptor blocker.
Minoxidil, a powerful arteriolar vasodilator, causes excess hair growth (it is used topically for baldness), fluid retention and reflex tachycardia.
Hydralazine is a classic cause of drug-induced lupus, especially in slow acetylators. Antihistone antibodies are typical, and it settles after the drug is stopped.
A right-sided colonic cancer bleeds slowly and invisibly, so a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia here is iron deficiency from chronic blood loss.
Coeliac disease impairs folate absorption in the proximal small bowel, causing macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils.
Pancytopenia with almost no reticulocytes and an empty, fatty marrow defines aplastic anaemia.
Alcohol raises the MCV directly and through liver disease, without megaloblastic marrow change. This is a non-megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia.
Chronic inflammation raises hepcidin, which traps iron in macrophages and blunts erythropoiesis. The result is the normocytic anaemia of chronic disease, a key differential of iron deficiency.
Spherocytes, a high reticulocyte count, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and a positive direct antiglobulin test in SLE indicate warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
Itch with antimitochondrial antibodies suggests primary biliary cholangitis. Liver disease changes the lipids in red-cell membranes and raises the MCV.
Infection can trigger acute haemolysis (for example in G6PD deficiency or sickle disease). The marrow then releases large, immature reticulocytes, which raise the MCV.
Hypothyroidism, suggested by dry skin, slow-relaxing reflexes and a hoarse voice, is a common non-megaloblastic cause of macrocytosis.
Bone pain, a very high ESR, Bence Jones proteinuria and pancytopenia indicate myeloma, which is a recognised cause of macrocytosis.
A very high lymphocyte count with lymphadenopathy in an older man is CLL. It often causes warm autoimmune haemolysis and immune thrombocytopenia.
Bone pain, hypoxia and severe anaemia in a young Jamaican patient suggest a sickle-cell crisis with acute chest syndrome.
Methyldopa, still used for hypertension in pregnancy, can induce warm red-cell autoantibodies with a positive Coombs test and haemolysis.
Hereditary spherocytosis gives Coombs-negative haemolysis with splenomegaly and increased osmotic fragility, caused by defects in membrane proteins such as spectrin or ankyrin.
In beta-thalassaemia major, the marrow expands to compensate. This produces frontal bossing, a 'hair-on-end' skull X-ray and hepatosplenomegaly in a child of Mediterranean origin.
Phenothiazine antipsychotics such as chlorpromazine can suppress the marrow and present with fever from infection and with bleeding.
Intramuscular gold for rheumatoid arthritis can cause marrow aplasia or agranulocytosis, which may first appear as a severe infection such as pharyngitis.
Phenytoin, often started as seizure prophylaxis after brain surgery, is a recognised cause of aplastic anaemia that presents with bleeding.
Propylthiouracil, used when carbimazole is not tolerated, can cause agranulocytosis or aplasia. Any sore throat on a thionamide needs an urgent blood count.
Sulphonylureas such as tolbutamide are a rare cause of marrow aplasia, which can present as an overwhelming infection.
Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background, with B symptoms and node pain after alcohol, indicate Hodgkin lymphoma.
Lytic bone lesions, hypercalcaemia, a paraprotein and an excess of abnormal marrow plasma cells define plasma-cell myeloma.
Massive splenomegaly and a very high white count with myeloid precursors, plus the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22), indicate chronic myeloid leukaemia.
A jaw mass in an African child caused by an EBV-associated B-cell lymphoma carrying t(8;14) is endemic Burkitt lymphoma, an extremely fast-growing tumour.
Marrow failure with myeloblasts making up 20% or more of blood or marrow cells indicates acute myeloid leukaemia.
Small, mature B lymphocytes that co-express CD5, with widespread lymphadenopathy in an older adult, define B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
ABO-incompatible blood causes intravascular haemolysis within minutes: fever, loin and chest pain, shock and haemoglobinuria. Stop the transfusion immediately.

Frail patients with renal impairment who have had large volumes develop transfusion-associated circulatory overload, with a raised JVP, crackles and hypoxia. Transfuse slowly, with diuretic cover if needed.
Febrile non-haemolytic reactions come from recipient antibodies to donor white cells, raised by earlier pregnancies or transfusions, or from cytokines in stored blood.
Regular transfusion in thalassaemia overloads the body with iron. Deposits in endocrine glands and heart cause growth failure, delayed puberty and cardiomyopathy, so chelation is needed.
High fever and shock soon after a unit starts, with compatibility confirmed, suggests bacterial contamination of the product causing septic shock.

where.title: Vascular anatomy of the head and neck

items.explanation: The left renal vein crosses in front of the abdominal aorta, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, on its way to the IVC. (The book's theme title says head and neck, but the items test thoracoabdominal vessels.)
The left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus in front of the descending thoracic aorta, so the aorta is its posterior relation.
The coeliac trunk is surrounded by the coeliac plexus and ganglia, which receive the greater splanchnic nerves.
The superior mesenteric artery emerges behind the neck of the pancreas and then runs down in front of the uncinate process and the third part of the duodenum.
The right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein. Compression of the vein here is the basis of May-Thurner syndrome.

where.title: Venous anatomy of the lower limb

items.explanation: At the ankle the great saphenous vein lies just in front of the medial malleolus, which is the classic site for a venous cutdown.
At the knee the great saphenous vein runs subcutaneously, posteromedial to the joint, about a hand's breadth behind the patella.
The saphenofemoral junction lies in the femoral triangle, medial to the femoral artery, roughly 3 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
The small saphenous vein starts behind the lateral malleolus and climbs the back of the calf to reach the popliteal fossa.
In the popliteal fossa the popliteal vein lies between the tibial nerve, which is superficial, and the popliteal artery, which is deepest.

Tearing pain between the shoulder blades that spreads down the back, with an absent leg pulse, in a young woman whose family history suggests Marfan syndrome, points to aortic dissection compromising the iliac flow.
A femoral puncture can leave a false aneurysm, an expanding pulsatile groin swelling. Thrombosis or embolism from it can make the leg acutely ischaemic.
Years of claudication followed by sudden worsening, with critical ischaemia (dependent rubor, pallor and venous guttering on elevation), is acute-on-chronic ischaemia from thrombosis on atheroma.
Popliteal aneurysms are often bilateral. Thrombosis causes acute ischaemia below the knee while the femoral pulses remain normal.
A sudden pale, pulseless, painful limb with normal pulses on the other side suggests an arterial embolus. Malignancy also raises the risk of thrombosis.
A tender, red cord along a superficial forearm vein with no deep involvement is superficial thrombophlebitis, an important differential of DVT.
Swelling of the face and arm with plethora on bending forward in a smoker suggests superior vena cava obstruction, most often from bronchial carcinoma.
A recurrent medial gaiter ulcer with oedema follows damage to venous valves after DVT. This is the post-thrombotic (post-phlebitic) syndrome.
Pleuritic pain and blood-streaked sputum about a week after major abdominal surgery, with a normal chest X-ray, suggest pulmonary embolism.
The puerperium is strongly prothrombotic, so acute one-sided swelling of the whole leg with deep tenderness indicates an iliofemoral DVT.
Sudden calf pain during an explosive movement in an unfit middle-aged player suggests a tear of the soleus or gastrocnemius fibres.
A white, tensely swollen leg after immobility following a heart attack suggests extensive iliofemoral venous thrombosis (phlegmasia alba dolens).
Persistent night pain in an adolescent's femur with no injury raises suspicion of a bone tumour, such as osteosarcoma or osteoid osteoma. X-ray it promptly.
A twisting injury followed by effusion, catching and inability to straighten the knee fully indicates a torn meniscus (cartilage).
Sudden locking from a loose fragment, with irregularity of the medial femoral condyle on X-ray in a young man, indicates osteochondritis dissecans.

where.title: Pain and swelling in the lower limb

items.explanation: Painless leg swelling with a pelvic malignancy such as cervical cancer comes from blocked lymphatics. That is secondary lymphoedema.
A tender, swollen calf with ankle oedema after long-haul travel indicates deep vein thrombosis.
Slowly progressive, painless swelling with a family history and no secondary cause suggests primary lymphoedema.
Night rest pain relieved by hanging the leg down, with an ABPI of 0.3 and dependent rubor, indicates critical limb ischaemia from atherosclerosis.
Bilateral calf pain on walking that is slow to settle with rest, with normal pulses and ABPI, suggests neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis.
Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) in someone from West Africa causes progressive lymphoedema, and eosinophilia is a helpful clue.
Painless pitting swelling of one leg in an adolescent girl, with normal investigations, suggests primary lymphoedema (praecox).
An earlier lesion removed from the sole, with enlarged inguinal and iliac nodes, suggests metastatic malignancy (such as acral melanoma) blocking the lymphatics.
Leg swelling soon after pelvic surgery indicates deep vein thrombosis.
Oedema with a very low albumin but normal liver tests suggests heavy protein loss from nephrotic syndrome.
An ulcer over the medial malleolus with lipodermatosclerosis and varicose eczema, with a normal ankle-brachial ratio, is venous.
A deep, punched-out ulcer over a bony prominence with an ankle-brachial ratio below 0.5 is arterial.
Peripheral neuropathy (here alcoholic) with ulcers at pressure points and normal ankle pressures means neuropathic ulceration.
Pyoderma gangrenosum, a neutrophilic skin disorder linked to inflammatory bowel disease, causes rapidly enlarging ulcers with violaceous, undermined edges.
Sickle-cell disease causes painful ulcers around the ankle and shin from microvascular occlusion and chronic haemolysis.
Oddly shaped, straight-edged ulcers in unusual sites that never heal despite treatment, in a cheerful patient, suggest self-inflicted (artefactual) ulceration.
A painless, punched-out ulcer under a metatarsal head with a rim of callus in a diabetic patient is neuropathic.
A long-standing ulcer that develops a raised, bleeding edge has probably undergone malignant change to squamous carcinoma (Marjolin's ulcer). Biopsy the edge.
Raynaud's phenomenon with tapering fingers and fingertip ulcers indicates systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), which can also cause painful leg ulcers.
A complicated tibial fracture often leads to DVT and venous valve damage. Years later the result is venous ulceration in the gaiter area.

where.title: Surface markings of the lung and pleura

items.explanation: Posteriorly, the parietal pleura dips to the level of the 12th rib beside the vertebral column.
In the mid-axillary line the lower edge of the parietal pleura lies at the 10th rib, two ribs below the lung edge at the 8th.
In the mid-clavicular line the pleural reflection reaches the 8th rib, while the lung edge reaches only the 6th.
The cardiac notch of the left lung starts at the level of the 4th costal cartilage.
The two pleural sacs come together behind the sternum at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage (the sternal angle).
The trachea divides at about the T4/T5 level, so the body of the fifth thoracic vertebra lies directly behind the carina.
The superior vena cava, with the phrenic nerve, lies in front of the root of the right lung.
The aortic arch hooks over the root of the left lung.
The left ventricle presses into the mediastinal surface of the left lung and forms its deep cardiac impression.
The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung to drain into the superior vena cava.
A tender swelling of a costal cartilage beside the sternum, with normal inflammatory markers and no trauma, is Tietze's syndrome, a benign costochondritis.
An apical lung cancer that invades the sympathetic chain causes Horner's syndrome (ptosis) and constant chest-wall pain. This is a Pancoast tumour.
Sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness in a smoker on the combined pill, with a swollen leg, points to DVT with pulmonary embolism.
Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness with reduced breath sounds in a tall young athlete suggests a primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Erythema nodosum together with palpitations (cardiac involvement) and vague chest pain suggests sarcoidosis.
In a young adult, headache, malaise, dry cough and patchy bilateral shadowing that looks worse than the chest examination suggest atypical pneumonia from Mycoplasma.
Malignancy, here probably colorectal, makes the blood prothrombotic. Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness with a normal chest examination therefore suggest pulmonary embolism.
Wheeze that fades as asthma worsens means very little air is moving: a silent chest is a life-threatening feature.
Lupus pernio and polyuria (from hypercalcaemia or diabetes insipidus) with exertional breathlessness point to sarcoidosis.
Progressive breathlessness, finger clubbing and fine late-inspiratory crackles at both bases indicate idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, plus ptosis and diplopia, is Lambert-Eaton syndrome, a paraneoplastic disorder of small-cell lung cancer.
Staphylococcus aureus infection in cystic fibrosis can cause necrotising pneumonia and lung abscess, with fever, rigors and haemoptysis.
Cancer predisposes to venous thromboembolism. A wedge-shaped peripheral opacity with pleuritic pain and haemoptysis is pulmonary infarction from an embolus.
Months of productive cough and weight loss with patchy consolidation and scarring at both apices suggest pulmonary tuberculosis.
Lung haemorrhage with rapidly progressive renal failure and anti-GBM antibodies is anti-GBM (Goodpasture's) disease. MPO-ANCA can coexist ('double-positive' disease).
Aspirated material tends to enter the right lower lobe because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical. The resulting consolidation gives bronchial breathing at the right base.
A large pneumothorax with absent lung markings abolishes breath sounds over the whole of that hemithorax.
A tumour that partly narrows one bronchus produces a fixed, single-pitched (monophonic) wheeze.
Pulmonary fibrosis causes fine, late-inspiratory 'Velcro' crackles at both lung bases.
Blood in the left pleural space from a lacerated internal mammary artery (haemothorax) collects at the base, so breath sounds are absent there.
Accepted answers: A, E, I and J. A large left pneumothorax reduces breath sounds, vocal fremitus and expansion on that side, and the mediastinum can shift so the trachea moves to the right.
Accepted answers: A, E, G, H and J. A massive right effusion is stony dull, silent and without fremitus, expands poorly, and pushes the trachea to the opposite (left) side.
Accepted answers: B, C and F. Consolidated lung conducts sound well, giving bronchial breathing, coarse crackles and a dull percussion note.
Accepted answers: A, E, F, H and J. Left upper lobe collapse reduces breath sounds, fremitus and expansion, is dull to percussion, and pulls the trachea towards the collapsed (left) side.
Accepted answers: B, D, F, I and J. Right apical fibrosis gives dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles over the scarred lobe, with reduced expansion and the trachea pulled to the right.
Chronic cough and weight loss after a long stay in a high-prevalence region suggest tuberculosis. A negative culture at 5 days means nothing, because mycobacteria take weeks to grow.
Lobulated pleural thickening with an effusion in a former electrician (likely asbestos exposure) suggests malignant mesothelioma.
IV drug use with a tricuspid regurgitant murmur that increases on inspiration and a pulsatile liver indicates right-sided infective endocarditis, which can cause clubbing.

Haemoptysis and weight loss with symptoms of hypercalcaemia (polyuria, constipation, abdominal pain) suggest squamous-cell lung carcinoma secreting PTH-related peptide. Pleural plaques show earlier asbestos exposure.
Cyanosis with fine late-inspiratory crackles at both bases indicates cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), a frequent cause of clubbing.
Bilateral pneumonia that does not respond to treatment in someone at risk of HIV raises the possibility of Pneumocystis. Bronchoscopy with lavage gives samples for silver staining or PCR.
Vertebral collapse with disc-space loss (Pott's disease) and a large effusion suggest tuberculosis. Pleural biopsy with aspiration has the best yield, showing granulomas and allowing culture.
Erythema nodosum with anterior uveitis suggests sarcoidosis, so the sensible first test is a chest X-ray to look for enlarged hilar nodes on both sides.
Night-time and post-exercise cough suggest asthma. A peak-flow diary shows the variable airflow obstruction that confirms it.
Spirometry (FEV1) objectively measures airflow limitation and is the standard way to track response to treatment in COPD.
Pulmonary embolism causes type 1 respiratory failure. Hypoxaemia drives hyperventilation, so the PaCO2 falls and the pH rises slightly.
An infective COPD exacerbation causes acute-on-chronic type 2 failure. The PaCO2 is high and the pH low, and a raised bicarbonate shows chronic renal compensation that cannot keep up acutely.
Anxious over-breathing blows off CO2 and gives a respiratory alkalosis with normal oxygenation. The alkalosis lowers ionised calcium and causes tingling, and rebreathing corrects it.
Profuse, prolonged diarrhoea loses bicarbonate and causes a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, partly compensated by a low PaCO2.
Diabetic ketoacidosis is a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a very negative base excess. Deep Kussmaul breathing drives the PaCO2 down in compensation.
Positive-pressure ventilation can turn a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax: hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, distended neck veins and shock need immediate decompression.
A penetrating chest wound with hypotension, distended neck veins and equal breath sounds on both sides indicates cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad).
Shock with dullness and absent breath sounds on the wounded side indicates a massive haemothorax, which needs a chest drain and fluid replacement, and often surgery.
Hyper-resonance and reduced air entry on one side, with stable pulse and blood pressure, mean a simple pneumothorax.
Several adjacent rib fractures followed by worsening hypoxia hours later, with normal percussion, suggest a flail segment with underlying pulmonary contusion.
Pertussis toxin causes a striking absolute lymphocytosis, a classic laboratory finding in whooping cough.
Non-caseating granulomas in a transbronchial biopsy are the histological hallmark of sarcoidosis.
Neutrophils with Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci in sputum indicate pneumococcal pneumonia.
Mucoid strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa are the characteristic chronic colonisers of cystic fibrosis airways.
Thickening of the alveolar walls by dense fibrous tissue is the pathology of fibrosing alveolitis (usual interstitial pneumonia).
Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, over weeks, on Lowenstein-Jensen medium and forms rough, dry, buff colonies.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a motile Gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose. It is oxidase-positive and makes pigments that colour its colonies.
Streptococcus pneumoniae forms alpha-haemolytic colonies with a sunken centre ('draughtsman') and is optochin-sensitive.
Legionella pneumophila needs buffered charcoal yeast extract agar to grow. It is a thin Gram-negative rod that stains poorly on routine Gram films.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall, so it barely stains with Gram stain and resists beta-lactams. It forms tiny 'fried-egg' colonies on special media.
A testicular germ-cell tumour in a young man spreads through the blood to the lungs as cannon-ball metastases, sometimes with liver deposits and an effusion.
Asbestos exposure from pipe lagging, with calcified pleural plaques, pleural thickening and a one-sided effusion, indicates malignant mesothelioma.
A smoker with a hilar mass, an effusion and hypercalcaemia (PTH-related peptide) most likely has squamous-cell carcinoma of the bronchus.
Acid-fast bacilli in sputum and pleural fluid confirm a tuberculous pleural effusion.
A lobar pneumonia with an adjacent basal effusion and Gram-positive diplococci is pneumococcal pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion.
An ascending post-infective neuropathy (Guillain-Barre) can weaken the breathing muscles and cause hypoventilation with a rising PaCO2. Monitor forced vital capacity.
In an exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, a high PaCO2 with raised bicarbonate (chronic compensation) and acidaemia means acute-on-chronic type 2 failure.
Pleuritic pain and a rub with hypoxaemia, a low PaCO2 and alkalosis indicate pulmonary embolism, which causes type 1 failure through ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Confusion, dry cough and hyponatraemia with hypoxaemia and an unremarkable chest X-ray fit an atypical (Mycoplasma) pneumonia causing type 1 failure.
Clubbing with fine basal crackles indicates fibrosing alveolitis. It impairs gas diffusion and gives type 1 failure with a low-normal PaCO2.
Inhaled corticosteroids such as beclometasone cause oral candidiasis. Using a spacer and rinsing the mouth after each dose reduce the risk.
High-dose inhaled or nebulised salbutamol stimulates beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle, causing a fine tremor, as well as tachycardia and hypokalaemia.
