Inhaled antimuscarinics such as ipratropium can precipitate urinary retention in men with prostatic enlargement and can worsen angle-closure glaucoma.
Years of oral prednisolone cause osteoporosis, with fragility fractures such as wrist and vertebral crush fractures. Give bone protection.
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index. Toxicity causes tachyarrhythmias, including ventricular ones, as well as seizures and vomiting, and many drugs raise its level.
A tuberculous pericardial effusion can cause tamponade: Kussmaul's sign, an impalpable apex, faint heart sounds and small QRS complexes.
Enlarged tuberculous nodes or endobronchial disease can block a bronchus and collapse the lobe beyond. Left lower lobe collapse gives a double left heart border.
Lupus vulgaris is chronic tuberculosis of the skin: reddish-brown plaques that show 'apple-jelly' nodules when pressed with a glass slide.
In HIV, tuberculosis can form a brain tuberculoma or abscess that appears as a ring-enhancing lesion and causes seizures.
Tuberculous meningitis in a young child causes fever, drowsiness, seizures and raised intracranial pressure. Early empirical anti-TB treatment saves lives.
Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, used in drug-resistant regimens, can cause tendinopathy and tendon rupture, especially of the Achilles tendon.
Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine and causes peripheral neuropathy, so pyridoxine is given as prophylaxis.
Rifampicin strongly induces liver enzymes and speeds oestrogen metabolism, so the oral contraceptive can fail. Advise a different method.
Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, with reduced acuity and red-green colour blindness. Test vision before and during treatment.
Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside that damages the vestibular and cochlear hair cells (ototoxicity) and the kidneys.
Anterior uveitis, with acutely painful red eyes that respond to topical steroids, is a common eye manifestation of sarcoidosis.
Lupus pernio is a violaceous infiltration of the nose and cheeks that goes with chronic, fibrotic pulmonary sarcoidosis.
Granulomas in the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk can cause cranial diabetes insipidus: dilute polyuria that corrects with desmopressin.
Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (Lofgren's syndrome) is acute sarcoidosis, which usually resolves.
Cardiac sarcoid granulomas can infiltrate the conducting system and cause complete heart block, with bradycardia, cannon waves and a risk of sudden death.
Small-cell carcinoma can secrete ectopic ACTH, causing Cushingoid features with marked hypokalaemia.
An anterior mediastinal mass with Reed-Sternberg cells and B symptoms in a young woman indicates Hodgkin lymphoma, usually of the nodular sclerosis type.
Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer in never-smokers. It tends to arise peripherally (so bronchoscopy is normal) and often presents with metastases.
Years of dockyard asbestos exposure followed by diffuse pleural thickening, breathlessness and weight loss indicate malignant mesothelioma.
Keratinised malignant cells in sputum mean squamous carcinoma, and an apical tumour of this type can cause Horner's syndrome.
An anterior mediastinal tumour of thymic epithelial cells mixed with lymphocytes is a thymoma, which is strongly associated with myasthenia gravis.
Morning headache, a tight collar and blackouts caused by venous congestion indicate superior vena cava obstruction.
Back pain with severe hypercalcaemia, dehydration and confusion points to bony metastases releasing calcium from bone.
Hyponatraemia with low plasma osmolality in a patient who is not dehydrated suggests SIADH, classically from small-cell lung cancer.
An apical tumour invading the lower brachial plexus (T1) and the sympathetic chain causes wasting of the small hand muscles and Horner's syndrome. This is a Pancoast tumour.
Proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, with ptosis and diplopia, is Lambert-Eaton syndrome, caused by antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.
47,XXY Klinefelter's syndrome causes a tall eunuchoid build, small testes, gynaecomastia and infertility, sometimes with learning difficulty.
45,X Turner's syndrome causes short stature, a webbed neck, a broad shield chest and streak ovaries. Coarctation and hearing problems are associated.
Trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome) causes epicanthic folds and single palmar creases. Endocardial cushion defects and VSDs are its common heart lesions.
Trisomy 18 (Edwards' syndrome) causes rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, low-set ears and clenched, overlapping fingers. Most babies die in infancy.
Trisomy 13 (Patau's syndrome) causes cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, eye defects and midline brain malformations.
Familial hypercholesterolaemia, from LDL-receptor mutations, causes very high LDL levels and premature coronary disease in several family members.
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11 mutation) combines dark freckling around the lips with hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps.
Acute intermittent porphyria causes attacks of abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric upset and hypertension, triggered by alcohol, fasting and certain drugs.
Tuberous sclerosis causes facial angiofibromas, periungual fibromas, shagreen patches and epilepsy.
Marfan's syndrome (fibrillin-1) causes tall stature, long fingers, a high-arched palate and chest deformity. Dilatation of the aortic root leads to aortic regurgitation.
Gaucher's disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency), most common in Ashkenazi Jews, causes hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias and lipid-laden storage cells.
Cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutations) causes thick secretions, bronchiectasis, chronic Pseudomonas infection and clubbing from childhood.
A sickle crisis with severe pain, hypoxia and lung crackles in a young Afro-Caribbean man is acute chest syndrome, a medical emergency.
Hereditary haemochromatosis (usually HFE) causes iron overload with a very high ferritin, liver fibrosis and cirrhosis. It is treated by venesection.
21-hydroxylase deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) causes a neonatal salt-wasting crisis and virilisation, such as clitoromegaly in girls. It responds to hydrocortisone and fluids.
Large volumes of dilute urine with high plasma osmolality that do not correct with desmopressin indicate nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, most often from X-linked V2-receptor mutations.
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections in boys.
G6PD deficiency, common in men of Middle-Eastern origin, makes red cells vulnerable to oxidant drugs such as some antimalarials. Exposure triggers acute haemolysis.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin) causes proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers' sign and a very high creatine kinase in young boys.
A prolonged APTT with normal INR and very low factor VIII, with haemarthrosis in a boy, means haemophilia A.
Infants usually begin to chew lumpy solid food at around 9 months.
Steady head control, lifting the head when prone, is expected by about 3 months.
Most children walk unaided by 12-15 months, and not walking by 18 months is the usual limit that prompts assessment.
First meaningful words usually appear at about 12 months.
Building a tower of about six cubes is typical at around 24 months.
A competent adult who physically cannot sign can still give valid consent by speaking. Record the verbal consent clearly, with a witness.
Going beyond what was agreed, such as removing the uterus during a diagnostic laparoscopy when it was not an emergency, is touching without consent. In law that is battery.
Not warning a patient of a material risk that a reasonable person would want to know about can be negligent, even if a consent form was signed.
When parents refuse life-saving blood for a child, the court can be asked to authorise treatment, for example by making the child a ward of court.
A competent 16-year-old can consent to his own treatment, and written consent should be obtained before an operation.
Major facial injury with bleeding into the mouth, respiratory distress and a GCS of 8 threatens the airway, which always comes first.
Shock from an unstable pelvic fracture is a circulation problem. Large-bore IV access and fluid and blood resuscitation, with pelvic stabilisation, take priority.
Absent breath sounds on one side with shock suggests a haemopneumothorax. It is a breathing problem that needs a chest drain before circulation measures.
Hypotension and tachycardia must be corrected before neurological assessment, because poor perfusion worsens secondary brain injury.
Even with a possible cord injury, tachycardia with hypotension suggests bleeding. Circulation comes before imaging and neurosurgical review.
A firm, round lump tethered to the skin of the scalp, with episodes of infection, is a sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst.
A keratoacanthoma grows over a few weeks into a dome with a central keratin-filled crater and may regress on its own. Excise it to exclude squamous carcinoma.
Lipomas are soft, lobulated, mobile subcutaneous lumps and may be multiple.
An external angular dermoid is a congenital inclusion cyst along an embryonic fusion line at the outer end of the eyebrow, lying deep to the skin.
Seborrhoeic keratoses (basal-cell papillomas) are greasy, brown, 'stuck-on' raised plaques that are very common in older people.
The UK breast screening programme, which grew out of the Forrest report, invites women in the target age range for mammography every three years.
Every new breast lump gets triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (mammography or ultrasound) and tissue sampling (FNA or core biopsy).
Barrett's oesophagus is kept under endoscopic surveillance with systematic quadrantic biopsies. How often depends on whether there is metaplasia alone or low- or high-grade dysplasia.
The Amsterdam criteria pick out families likely to have hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, based on several affected relatives across generations, one diagnosed young.
Familial adenomatous polyposis is autosomal dominant. Affected relatives have regular colonoscopy and then prophylactic colectomy, often with an ileo-anal pouch.
Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease whom the test correctly calls negative.
The positive predictive value is the proportion of positive results that are true positives.
Predictive values depend heavily on how common the disease is in the tested population (prevalence). Sensitivity and specificity do not.
The positive likelihood ratio, sensitivity divided by (1 - specificity), shows how much a positive result raises the odds of disease.
Someone free of the disease who tests negative is a true negative.
Acute cellular rejection usually appears in the first weeks to months after transplant. It causes fever, a tender, swollen graft and rising creatinine with no obstruction.
High-dose steroid immunosuppression predisposes to opportunistic infection, notably CMV, which causes colitis, retinitis and leucopenia.
After allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, donor T cells can attack the recipient's skin, gut and liver. That is graft-versus-host disease.
Long-term calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppression such as ciclosporin predisposes to EBV-driven post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, which presents like lymphoma.
Chronic rejection causes slow loss of graft function with hypertension, proteinuria and intimal vascular thickening, months to years after transplantation.
Accepted answers: H and I. Lobar collapse shows as a dense opacity with volume loss, such as a raised horizontal fissure or a double left heart border.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is the classic radiographic sign of sarcoidosis, with lymphoma and tuberculosis as the main differentials.
Accepted answers: D and J. A visible pleural edge with no lung markings beyond it means pneumothorax, and mediastinal shift away from that side suggests tension.
Accepted answers: E and F. A malignant lesion may be a solitary mass (a primary carcinoma) or multiple round 'cannon-ball' metastases.
Right middle lobe consolidation blurs the right heart border (the silhouette sign) while the right hemidiaphragm stays clear.
Upper-zone fibrosis with volume loss and raised hila is typical of old tuberculosis. Sarcoidosis, radiation and ankylosing spondylitis are other causes.
An upper-zone cavity suggests reactivated tuberculosis. Squamous carcinoma and staphylococcal or Klebsiella abscess are the differentials.
In infants the normal thymus can project from the mediastinum as a triangular 'sail' shadow.
An enlarged left atrium from mitral valve disease straightens the left heart border ('mitralisation') and can splay the carina.
Accepted answers: D, F and H. Cardiomegaly means a cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 on a PA film, whether from chamber dilatation, valve disease or pericardial fluid.
Perihilar 'bat's wing' shadowing, with upper-lobe venous diversion, septal lines and effusions, indicates alveolar pulmonary oedema.
Thickened, dilated bronchial walls appear as tramlines and ring shadows, which are the radiographic signs of bronchiectasis.
A large or retrosternal goitre shows as a superior mediastinal mass that pushes the trachea sideways.
A large pericardial effusion makes the cardiac outline globular, like a water bottle, with clear lung fields.
Bronchiectasis shows tramline and ring shadows from thick-walled, dilated airways, often in the lower zones.
Heart failure shows cardiomegaly, upper-lobe venous diversion, interstitial and alveolar oedema and pleural effusions.
A thoracic aortic aneurysm widens the mediastinal contour along the course of the aorta.
A pericardial effusion enlarges the heart shadow into a globular shape with clear lungs, and echocardiography confirms it.
The 'sail sign' in an infant represents a normal or enlarged thymus.
Mitral valve disease enlarges the left atrium, which straightens the left heart border and may give a double right heart contour.

where.title: CT head scans I – clinical scenarios

items.explanation: A patient with breast cancer and signs of raised intracranial pressure most likely has a cerebral metastasis, which appears as a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema after contrast.
Atrial fibrillation predisposes to cardioembolic stroke. A large right-hemisphere infarct appears as a low-density area in the middle cerebral territory.
Thrombolysis combined with heparin and antiplatelet drugs carries a real risk of intracerebral bleeding, which shows as a high-density (white) area on non-contrast CT.
Gradual deterioration days after a fall suggests a subdural haematoma, a crescent-shaped collection over the hemisphere, which a rebleed can suddenly enlarge.
A meningioma is an extra-axial, well-defined, evenly enhancing mass attached to the dura and is often found incidentally.

where.title: CT head scans II – radiological diagnosis

items.explanation: An established infarct appears as a low-attenuation area that follows an arterial territory.
Accepted answers: A, B and I. Fresh blood is hyperdense (white) on CT, whether in brain tissue, the subarachnoid space or the ventricles.
Vasogenic oedema spreads as low-density, finger-like areas through the white matter around tumours and abscesses, such as the ring-enhancing lesion.
A rim of contrast enhancement around a central low-density core is typical of abscess, metastasis or high-grade glioma.
Accepted answers: D, F, I and J. Any large mass, such as a haematoma or a tumour with oedema, can push midline structures across.
Accepted answers: B, F and I. Raised intracranial pressure shows as effaced sulci, compressed ventricles or hydrocephalus, for example after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

where.title: CT head scans III – intracerebral abnormalities

items.explanation: A subdural haematoma is a crescent-shaped collection that follows the inner skull surface and can cross suture lines.
Accepted answers: A and I. An intracerebral haemorrhage is a hyperdense collection within the brain tissue.
An extradural haematoma is a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection limited by the sutures, usually from middle meningeal artery bleeding.
Accepted answers: A and C. A right-hemisphere stroke can be haemorrhagic (A) or ischaemic (C, the right-sided infarct).
A meningioma is a well-defined, extra-axial, evenly enhancing mass with a broad base on the dura.
Submucosal mucus-secreting (Brunner's) glands are a hallmark of the duodenum, concentrated in its first and second parts. Their alkaline mucus helps neutralise acid arriving from the stomach.
The pylorus sits on the transpyloric plane at about L1, just to the right of the midline. Its thickened circular muscle forms the pyloric sphincter.
The sigmoid mesocolon has an inverted-V root whose apex lies over the left ureter where it crosses the pelvic brim, a useful landmark when mobilising the sigmoid.
The ascending colon is fixed retroperitoneally on iliacus and quadratus lumborum and sits in front of the lower pole of the right kidney.
Jejunal mucosa carries tall, dense villi and prominent circular folds that maximise absorptive surface; the large bowel has no villi at all.

This is digoxin toxicity. The new thiazide has caused hypokalaemia, and age-related renal impairment slows digoxin clearance. Toxicity shows as nausea, vomiting, confusion and slow AF. Check a digoxin level and correct the potassium.

Abrupt, vomiting-dominant food poisoning within hours of eating suggests a toxin already formed in the food. Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin is the classic cause, and the illness settles within a day or so with fluids.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically appears at 2-8 weeks: non-bilious projectile vomiting, an olive-like mass on a test feed and hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis. Treat with fluid and electrolyte correction, then pyloromyotomy.
Peritonitis leaves adhesions, the commonest cause of small-bowel obstruction. Colicky central pain eased by bilious vomiting, with distension and dehydration, places the block in the small intestine.
Fever, right iliac fossa guarding and a neutrophilia indicate acute appendicitis. Here vomiting is a symptom of an acute surgical abdomen rather than a primary gut infection.
Major burns and critical illness cause mucosal ischaemia, producing multiple acute stress erosions (Curling's ulcers) within days. Acid-suppression prophylaxis is used in high-risk ICU patients.
Recurrent ulceration that breaks through high-dose acid suppression, together with a pancreatic mass, points to a gastrin-secreting tumour. Confirm with a raised fasting gastrin and screen for MEN1.

Macrocytosis and a high INR suggest alcohol-related liver disease with poor synthetic function. Large fresh haematemesis in this setting is variceal until proven otherwise: give terlipressin and antibiotics, then band urgently.
Months of early satiety, anorexia and weight loss with a microcytic anaemia are alarm features of gastric cancer. Slow oozing from the tumour gives coffee-ground vomitus.

Forceful retching after binge drinking can split the mucosa at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Blood appears only after repeated vomiting, the patient is stable and most tears stop bleeding without intervention.
A new change in bowel habit after 50, with tenesmus, mucus and pellet-like stools, is a red flag for a distal colorectal tumour. Arrange urgent colonoscopy.
Antipsychotics such as clozapine have antimuscarinic effects that slow colonic transit. A dry mouth is the clue to an anticholinergic, drug-induced cause.

After hip surgery, bed rest, poor intake and an unfamiliar routine commonly cause faecal loading. With no sinister features, this is simple constipation; treat with laxatives, enemas and early mobilisation.
Lifelong, very infrequent defecation with no urge, in a young woman without alarm features, fits chronic idiopathic (slow-transit) constipation.

A smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss probably has a squamous lung cancer secreting PTH-related peptide. The resulting hypercalcaemia causes constipation and abdominal pain and can upset bladder function.
Acute febrile watery diarrhoea with cramps after travel, following a flu-like prodrome, fits bacterial enterocolitis, e.g. Campylobacter or enterotoxigenic E. coli. Rehydration is the priority.
Right-sided colon cancers seldom obstruct. They bleed silently, presenting with iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss and altered bowel habit in older adults.
Frequent bloody, mucoid stools with anaemia, high inflammatory markers and left-sided tenderness indicate a severe flare of ulcerative colitis by Truelove-Witts criteria. Admit for IV steroids.
Years of alternating bowel habit with bloating and pain relieved by defecation, normal blood tests and a normal sigmoidoscopy meet Rome criteria for irritable bowel syndrome.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics, especially cephalosporins, in a frail inpatient predispose to Clostridioides difficile colitis. Send stool for toxin, isolate the patient and stop unnecessary antibiotics.
Tremor, tachycardia, warm peripheries, onycholysis and oligomenorrhoea with weight loss indicate thyrotoxicosis. Vitiligo suggests an autoimmune cause such as Graves' disease.
Weeks of thirst and weight loss in a teenager with a random glucose over 11.1 mmol/l is type 1 diabetes. Insulin deficiency drives fat and protein breakdown.
Macrocytosis, low platelets, AST above ALT, hyponatraemia, low urea and hepatomegaly are the footprint of heavy alcohol use, here after emotional upheaval.
Ascites, hepatomegaly, a pleural effusion and multiple lung opacities point to widespread metastatic malignancy, a classic cause of cachexia and anorexia.
Negative stool tests exclude infection. Mouth ulcers with colitis, anaemia and weight loss favour Crohn's disease; crypt abscesses can occur in either form of IBD.
Fever with rigors, upper abdominal pain and jaundice (Charcot's triad) plus hypotension indicate ascending cholangitis. It needs IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage, usually by ERCP.
Right iliac fossa pain with nausea, vomiting and a neutrophilia in a young man, with clear urine, is classic acute appendicitis.
Epigastric pain boring through to the back with persistent retching in a heavy drinker suggests acute alcoholic pancreatitis. Confirm with lipase or amylase and score the severity.

An older patient with long-standing left-sided symptoms now has localised left iliac fossa peritonism and a raised white count, so diverticulitis is likely. Inflammation next to the bladder can cause microscopic haematuria.
Severe loin-to-groin colic with restlessness and haematuria is ureteric colic. Many stones are missed on plain films, so a non-contrast CT KUB is the test of choice.

An inferior myocardial infarction can present as epigastric pain and nausea, especially in the very elderly. Sweating, breathlessness and raised cardiac enzymes with a normal abdomen point to the heart.
Previous peritonitis and surgery leave adhesions. Colicky central pain, vomiting and distension with a recent normal bowel action indicate small-bowel obstruction.

A hypertensive older man with sudden epigastric-to-back pain, shock and weak femoral pulses has a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm. Take him straight to theatre; do not delay for imaging if unstable.
Absolute constipation with no flatus, marked distension and a tympanic but non-tender abdomen in an older woman indicate large-bowel obstruction, often from cancer or volvulus.
Sudden severe epigastric pain progressing to a rigid, silent abdomen, with the patient lying still, is generalised peritonitis from a perforated peptic ulcer. An erect chest film shows free gas.
Repeated pancreatitis in a drinker followed by an ill-defined, tender epigastric mass with fullness and nausea suggests a pancreatic pseudocyst. These walled collections form weeks after an attack.
Progressive obstructive jaundice with back pain, weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law) indicates carcinoma of the pancreatic head. The palpable mass is the distended gallbladder.
A hard, irregular liver causing jaundice, together with a left iliac fossa mass and a year of altered bowel habit, suggests sigmoid carcinoma with hepatic metastases.
Haematemesis from varices, jaundice, confusion and ascites with an enlarged liver are features of decompensated cirrhosis with portal hypertension.
A very tender right upper quadrant mass that moves with breathing, with fever but no jaundice, reflects an inflamed, distended gallbladder from gallstone disease (acute cholecystitis or empyema).
Dysphagia that progresses from solids to liquids, with major weight loss and low albumin, is oesophageal carcinoma until proven otherwise. Request urgent endoscopy with biopsy.

A wasted, fasciculating tongue, absent jaw jerk, facial weakness and drooling are lower motor neurone bulbar signs, e.g. in motor neurone disease. Pseudobulbar palsy gives a spastic tongue and brisk jaw jerk.
Equal difficulty with solids and liquids, regurgitation, a dilated oesophagus with a smooth distal taper and failure of sphincter relaxation on manometry define achalasia.
Steroids and ciclosporin after transplantation predispose to oesophageal candidiasis, which causes painful swallowing and diffuse plaques or ulceration. Treat with systemic fluconazole.
Long-standing heartburn, abnormal pH monitoring and confluent erosive oesophagitis are complicated reflux disease. New dysphagia for solids reflects a peptic stricture.
Signet-ring cells infiltrating a thickened, rigid stomach wall without a discrete mass are diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma, which gives the 'leather bottle' (linitis plastica) appearance.
NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that protect the mucosa. Many superficial, bleeding defects scattered through the stomach are acute erosive gastritis.

Sheets of atypical lymphocytes invading the gastric glands (lymphoepithelial lesions) indicate a marginal-zone MALT lymphoma. It is strongly linked to H. pylori, and early disease may regress after eradication.
Kaposi's sarcoma is an HHV-8-driven, AIDS-defining tumour. Violaceous plaques made of spindle cells around slit-like vascular channels can involve the gut as well as the skin.
H. pylori produces chronic antral gastritis with plasma cells and lymphocytes; neutrophils mark it as 'active'. Treat with eradication therapy.
A sharply punched-out antral ulcer whose base shows only debris and granulation tissue, with no neoplasia in adjacent mucosa, is a benign chronic peptic ulcer that has bled.
A bleeding ulcer in the first part of the duodenum needing endoscopic therapy, with a positive urease (CLO) test, is an H. pylori-related duodenal ulcer. Eradicate once haemostasis is achieved.

Chronic reflux can replace the squamous lining of the lower oesophagus with columnar, intestinal-type epithelium. This is Barrett's oesophagus, a premalignant change that needs endoscopic surveillance.
A succussion splash, persistent vomiting and hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis in chronic ulcer disease indicate pyloric stenosis, i.e. gastric outlet obstruction from scarring.
Long-standing acid injury heals by fibrosis, forming a benign peptic stricture that blocks solids. Biopsy at endoscopy is still needed to exclude cancer.
Multiple ulcers in unusual places, including the oesophagus, with a markedly raised serum gastrin indicate a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).
Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analogue that protects against NSAID ulcers, commonly causes diarrhoea and can stimulate uterine bleeding or contractions. It is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Cimetidine has anti-androgenic effects and inhibits cytochrome P450. Prolonged use can cause gynaecomastia, which is rare with other H2 antagonists or PPIs.
Aluminium-containing antacids are constipating, whereas magnesium salts loosen the stool. Heavy aluminium hydroxide use explains the new constipation.
Large amounts of calcium carbonate can cause milk-alkali syndrome. The blood gas shows a metabolic alkalosis (high pH and bicarbonate) with a normal PaCO2.
Bismuth, part of quadruple rescue therapy for H. pylori, harmlessly turns the tongue and stools black and can cause nausea. Warn patients beforehand so they are not alarmed.

Apical calcification and hilar nodes show past TB. Malabsorption with a normal upper endoscopy and duodenal biopsy suggests ileocaecal tuberculosis, which affects the terminal ileum rather than the proximal small bowel.

Strongly positive anti-endomysial and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies with mouth ulcers, macrocytosis and weight loss indicate coeliac disease. Confirm on duodenal biopsy, then start a gluten-free diet.
A Polya (Billroth II) gastrectomy leaves a blind afferent loop where bacteria multiply. A positive breath test and a response to antibiotics confirm small-bowel bacterial overgrowth.
Malabsorption after a long stay in the tropics, with partial villous atrophy, no identifiable pathogen and recovery on folate, B12 and tetracycline, is tropical sprue.
Alcohol excess with steatorrhoea, hyperglycaemia and calcification across the upper abdomen indicates chronic pancreatitis with exocrine and endocrine failure.

Prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics in a frail elderly inpatient, followed by offensive diarrhoea, suggests C. difficile infection. Test stool for toxin and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
Reheated rice is the classic source of Bacillus cereus, a spore-forming Gram-positive rod. Its preformed toxin causes vomiting and/or watery diarrhoea within hours.
Giardia, classically acquired in St Petersburg, causes watery diarrhoea, bloating and sulphurous belching. Cysts or trophozoites in stool confirm it, and metronidazole treats it.
Profuse 'rice-water' stools after work in an endemic area, with a motile, comma-shaped Gram-negative rod, is cholera. Aggressive oral or IV rehydration saves lives.
In advanced HIV, Cryptosporidium (seen as acid-fast oocysts in stool) causes severe, persistent watery diarrhoea. Restoring immunity with antiretroviral therapy is central to control.
Continuous inflammation spreading proximally from the rectum, confined to the mucosa, with crypt abscesses and distorted crypt architecture, is ulcerative colitis.
Aortic aneurysm repair can sacrifice the inferior mesenteric artery. The splenic flexure, a watershed zone, is the classic site of ischaemic colitis.
Skip lesions with linear ulcers and non-caseating granulomas in a child whose growth is faltering are characteristic of Crohn's colitis.
C. difficile toxins after antibiotic exposure produce pseudomembranous colitis: raised yellow plaques of fibrin, mucus and inflammatory cells on the mucosa.
Chronic watery diarrhoea with a normal-looking colon but a thickened subepithelial collagen band on biopsy is collagenous (microscopic) colitis. Always biopsy normal mucosa in chronic diarrhoea.
Acute bloody diarrhoea with a positive Campylobacter culture and only acute inflammation on biopsy is an infective colitis. Chronic architectural distortion would suggest IBD instead.
Cholestatic liver tests with beaded bile ducts on cholangiography in ulcerative colitis indicate primary sclerosing cholangitis. It raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer.
After ileal resection, unabsorbed fat binds calcium in the gut, leaving dietary oxalate free to be absorbed. The result is calcium oxalate stones, here complicated by an infected, obstructed kidney.
A red eye with blurred vision and photophobia during active colitis is anterior uveitis, which needs same-day ophthalmology review. Episcleritis is milder and does not affect vision.
An enlarging, undermined ulcer on the shin during a colitis flare is pyoderma gangrenosum. Avoid debridement (pathergy) and treat with steroids and control of the bowel disease.
Terminal ileal Crohn's disease interrupts bile-salt recycling, so bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol and gallstones form. Here a stone in the common duct has caused cholangitis.
Months of altered bowel habit with weight loss, anaemia and dark blood, plus a normal anorectal examination, suggest a colonic carcinoma beyond the reach of the finger and proctoscope.
Frequent diarrhoea with blood mixed into the stool, microcytic anaemia, leucocytosis and a high ESR over three months in a young woman fits ulcerative colitis.
Painless red bleeding with a normal anorectal examination in a man over 50 needs colonoscopy. A colonic adenomatous polyp is a likely source and can be removed endoscopically.
Painless bright-red blood on the paper and in the pan, separate from the stool and linked to straining, is typical of haemorrhoids.
Acute bloody diarrhoea with cramps, a raised white count and recent travel to Africa suggests an infective colitis (e.g. Shigella, Campylobacter or amoebiasis). Send stool for culture and microscopy.
Piles that prolapse on defecation and must be pushed back are third-degree haemorrhoids. Bright-red blood on the paper is the usual accompanying symptom.
An irregular, raised ulcer at the anal verge with pain, bleeding and discharge in an older patient is an anal carcinoma (usually squamous) until biopsy proves otherwise.
A large mass that appears on straining, with mucus, bleeding and incontinence in an elderly woman, is a full-thickness rectal prolapse due to a weak pelvic floor and sphincter.
A puckered opening near the anus that discharges pus, in a teenager with features of ileal Crohn's disease, is an anal fistula. Delineate its course with MRI before surgery.
A sudden, exquisitely painful, tense purple lump at the anal margin is a perianal haematoma, a thrombosed external vein. It can be evacuated under local anaesthetic in the first few days.
Emergency resection of perforated sigmoid disease with an end colostomy and a closed rectal stump is a Hartmann's procedure. Continuity can be restored later.
Stricturing terminal ileal Crohn's disease causing recurrent obstruction is treated by resecting the ileocaecal segment, a limited right hemicolectomy.
Penetrating abdominal trauma with massive bleeding needs an emergency laparotomy. Long midline wounds after sepsis and ICU stays commonly develop incisional hernias.
Removing the colon and rectum with a temporary ileostomy, then building an ileal pouch joined to the anus, is restorative proctocolectomy. Frequency and urgency are expected afterwards.
A low rectal cancer requiring removal of the anal canal leaves a permanent end colostomy with no anus: abdominoperineal excision of the rectum.

A sac that leaves the abdomen lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels has come through the deep ring, so this is an indirect inguinal hernia. Inguinal hernias appear above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
The femoral canal is bordered by the lacunar ligament on its medial side and by the femoral vein laterally. A sac in this space is a femoral hernia.
The deep ring is found 1-2 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (halfway from ASIS to pubic tubercle). The mid-inguinal point is different and marks the femoral artery.
The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the canal and splits to form the superficial ring. Incising it opens the canal during hernia repair.
The internal spermatic fascia comes from transversalis fascia at the deep ring. Internal oblique gives the cremasteric layer and external oblique the external spermatic fascia.
An irreducible, tender hernia with peritonism, fever, tachycardia and red, oedematous overlying skin indicates strangulation, i.e. its blood supply is compromised. It needs emergency surgery.
A hernia through the linea semilunaris at the lateral border of rectus abdominis is a Spigelian hernia.
In a sliding hernia, part of the sac wall is formed by a viscus such as the sigmoid colon or bladder. Opening the sac carelessly can therefore enter the bowel lumen.
An irreducible hernia that is not tender and causes no obstructive or ischaemic features is incarcerated. Here it is a paraumbilical hernia.
An irreducible hernia with colicky pain, vomiting and distension but no tenderness is obstructed. It has not yet strangulated, but surgery is needed promptly.
The quadrate lobe lies between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for the ligamentum teres, i.e. medial to the gallbladder.
The porta hepatis is the hilum of the liver, where the portal vein and hepatic artery enter and the hepatic ducts leave.
The superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament surround the bare area, which contacts the diaphragm directly without peritoneum.
The posterior surface of the left lobe bears an impression for the abdominal oesophagus.
The caudate process joins the caudate lobe to the right lobe and forms the upper boundary of the epiploic foramen, the entrance to the lesser sac.
Mild jaundice with isolated bilirubin elevation and normal enzymes, brought out by an intercurrent infection, is Gilbert's syndrome: a benign defect in bilirubin conjugation.
Acute hepatitis with transaminases in the hundreds after travel, with an IgM antibody response, is hepatitis A. It spreads faeco-orally and has a short incubation.
Polycythaemia predisposes to hepatic vein thrombosis. Tender hepatomegaly, ascites and jaundice are Budd-Chiari syndrome, confirmed by Doppler ultrasound or venography.
Cholestatic jaundice with pruritus in a middle-aged woman with strongly positive antimitochondrial antibodies is primary biliary cholangitis (formerly primary biliary cirrhosis).
Painless obstructive jaundice with a dilated duct and distended gallbladder but no stones suggests a distal block from carcinoma of the pancreatic head. CT and ERCP confirm it.
A cholestatic picture, raised IgM, high cholesterol, antimitochondrial antibodies and loss of bile ducts with granulomas define primary biliary cholangitis. Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line.
Hepatitis B is the only DNA virus among the options. Viral antigen in hepatocytes with chronic inflammation and fibrosis indicates chronic HBV, which is common in sub-Saharan Africa.
Skin darkening, hepatomegaly and cirrhosis with heavy iron in hepatocytes are hereditary haemochromatosis. Also look for diabetes, arthropathy and hypogonadism, and screen relatives.
A myeloproliferative disorder with acute painful hepatomegaly, ascites and biopsy evidence of outflow congestion is hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome).
Chronic liver disease in a teenager with copper in hepatocytes and low caeruloplasmin and serum copper is Wilson's disease. Look for Kayser-Fleischer rings and start chelation.
Rifampicin can cause hepatitis or cholestasis and turns urine, tears and sweat orange-red. It also induces liver enzymes, so drug interactions are common.
Erythromycin and other macrolides are classic causes of cholestatic hepatitis, typically appearing within days to weeks of starting a course.
Amiodarone causes hepatotoxicity as well as thyroid, lung, skin and eye problems. Check liver and thyroid function before and during treatment.
The dry cough shows she is on an ACE inhibitor. Lisinopril rarely causes cholestatic jaundice, which resolves after the drug is stopped.
Azathioprine can cause a cholestatic hepatitis as well as marrow suppression. Check TPMT activity before starting, then monitor blood counts and liver tests.
Adenocarcinoma cells in ascites from a woman most often come from peritoneal spread of ovarian cancer. Check CA-125 and image the pelvis.
Granulomas point to tuberculous peritonitis, an exudative, lymphocyte-rich ascites. Confirm by peritoneal biopsy or culture.
In nephrotic syndrome, urinary protein loss lowers albumin and the liver responds by making more lipoprotein, so high cholesterol accompanies the oedema and ascites.
Acute pancreatitis can leak pancreatic juice into the peritoneum, giving ascites with a very high amylase alongside a high serum amylase.
A very high GGT reflects alcohol-induced enzyme induction, so alcoholic cirrhosis with portal hypertension (a high serum-ascites albumin gradient) is the likely cause.
Multiple ulcers extending beyond the duodenal bulb into its second and third parts suggest acid hypersecretion from a gastrinoma, usually in the pancreas or duodenum.
Gallstone pancreatitis with shock and tachypnoea is severe, haemorrhagic-necrotising disease. It needs critical-care support and ERCP if obstruction or cholangitis persists.
A pancreatic head mass with malignant glandular cells on aspiration, presenting with painless obstructive jaundice, is ductal adenocarcinoma.
Repeated alcohol-triggered attacks, pain eased by sitting forward, steatorrhoea and pancreatic calcification on the plain film indicate chronic pancreatitis.

Recurrent exercise-related dizziness, palpitations and blackouts in a young man suggest hypoglycaemia from an insulinoma. Look for Whipple's triad and inappropriately high insulin during a supervised fast.
The trigone forms where the caudal mesonephric ducts are absorbed into the back wall of the bladder. This gives it a mesodermal origin and a smooth lining.
The paramesonephric ducts fuse caudally to form the uterus (body and cervix) and upper vagina. Their unfused cranial parts become the uterine tubes.
The ovary rests in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall, overlying the origin of the internal iliac artery and the ureter.
The prostatic urethra runs through the prostate, from the bladder neck down to the pelvic floor.
The membranous urethra crosses the deep perineal pouch, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter. It is vulnerable in pelvic fractures.
The ileocolic artery crosses in front of the right ureter in the abdomen on its way to the ileocaecal region.
In the female pelvis the uterine artery passes over the ureter beside the cervix ('water under the bridge'), so the ureter is at risk during hysterectomy.
The right adrenal gland is tucked behind the bare area of the liver and the IVC, on the upper pole of the right kidney.
The second part of the duodenum curves in front of the right renal hilum and pelvis, so it is at risk in right-sided renal surgery.
The far end of the transverse colon and splenic flexure lie in front of the left kidney near its hilum. That makes the left renal pelvis the related structure.
A very high PSA with prostatism, months of back pain (bone metastases) and anaemia indicates metastatic prostate cancer. Local invasion can cause the haematuria.
Painless visible haematuria in an older smoker with past aromatic-amine exposure (rubber or dye industry) is bladder cancer until cystoscopy proves otherwise.
Bilateral ballotable flank masses with haematuria and impaired renal function are adult polycystic kidney disease. Haematuria comes from bleeding into cysts.
Haematuria, loin pain and a palpable loin mass, with anaemia and a high ESR, is the classic (if late) triad of renal cell carcinoma.
Sudden severe loin pain radiating to the groin with microscopic haematuria in a young man indicates a ureteric stone. Confirm with CT KUB.
A teenager with hypertension, loin pain, haematuria, bilateral ballotable kidneys and a relative who died young of a brain haemorrhage has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
Fever, rigors, vomiting and loin tenderness with nitrite-positive urine in a stone former indicate acute pyelonephritis. Image to exclude an obstructed, infected kidney.
Constitutional symptoms with acid-fast bacilli in early-morning urine samples confirm genitourinary tuberculosis. Routine urine culture is typically sterile.
Sterile pyuria with an obstructed system and a filling defect in the proximal ureter on IVP points to an obstructing calculus.
In the very elderly, a UTI often presents as confusion and falls. A Gram-negative rod sensitive to common oral agents is most likely E. coli, the commonest urinary pathogen.
Albumin is a negative acute-phase protein and leaks out through inflamed capillaries, so it falls quickly during severe infection. Here the source is urosepsis.
Severe hepatocellular injury with jaundice, a high INR and autoantibodies (an autoimmune overlap picture) reduces the liver's albumin synthesis.
A positive anti-endomysial antibody, low folate and macrocytosis indicate coeliac disease. The damaged mucosa malabsorbs nutrients, including protein.
PAS-positive macrophages in small-bowel biopsy are diagnostic of Whipple's disease. It causes a protein-losing enteropathy with diarrhoea, arthralgia and oedema.
A BMI of 16 from dietary restriction and compulsive exercise is protein-energy malnutrition, as in anorexia nervosa. Albumin falls once deprivation is prolonged.
Haemoptysis, lung shadowing and rapidly worsening renal failure after a respiratory infection form a pulmonary-renal syndrome. Check anti-GBM antibodies urgently (Goodpasture's disease).
Fever, tender finger-pulp nodules (Osler's) and a new murmur indicate infective endocarditis. Immune-complex glomerulonephritis is a recognised complication.
Purpura over the shins, abdominal pain and nephritis in a child, with no evidence of streptococcal infection, is Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis).
Night sweats, widespread lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and hilar nodes suggest Hodgkin lymphoma. It is classically linked to minimal-change nephropathy.
A smoker with haemoptysis, cachexia and nodes probably has bronchial carcinoma. Solid tumours can cause a paraneoplastic membranous nephropathy.
Years of analgesics for back pain explain both the bleeding peptic ulcer and the renal failure. Long-term NSAID use causes chronic interstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis.
Recurrent childhood UTIs, often due to vesicoureteric reflux, scar the kidneys. Small, shrunken kidneys with advanced renal failure are chronic pyelonephritis (reflux nephropathy).

Recurrent painful crises with severe anaemia in a man of African-Caribbean origin suggest sickle-cell disease. Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic medulla causes papillary necrosis and interstitial damage.
Very poor glycaemic control with vascular disease leads to diabetic kidney disease. Tubulointerstitial injury contributes to progression alongside the glomerular changes.
Sensorineural deafness with haematuria progressing to renal failure in a boy is Alport syndrome, a type IV collagen defect that is usually X-linked.
Penicillamine for RA commonly alters taste and can cause membranous nephropathy, producing the nephrotic syndrome a few weeks to months after starting.
Visible haematuria within days of a sore throat (synpharyngitic) suggests IgA nephropathy. Post-streptococcal disease appears one to three weeks after the infection.
Upper airway (nasal) and lung disease with renal involvement and a very high c-ANCA (PR3) indicate granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis).
Fever after West Africa with red-cell inclusions and low platelets indicates malaria. Plasmodium malariae is classically linked to an immune-complex nephrotic syndrome.
Loss of podocyte foot processes as the only biopsy abnormality is minimal-change disease. It usually responds well to corticosteroids.
Sheep-farming regions such as Wales are endemic for Echinococcus. Hydatid cysts in liver and kidney develop calcified walls visible on plain films.
Haematuria after time in Africa with a calcified bladder wall indicates Schistosoma haematobium infection, which also predisposes to squamous bladder cancer.
Apical lung calcification alongside bilateral renal calcification points to old tuberculosis that has spread to the kidneys.
High calcium with low phosphate and vague 'stones, bones, groans and moans' symptoms indicate primary hyperparathyroidism, a cause of nephrocalcinosis and stones.
Proteus splits urea, making the urine alkaline so that struvite precipitates. The stone grows into a branching staghorn calculus filling the collecting system.
Bilateral renal masses, severe hypertension, a high haematocrit and end-stage renal failure in a young adult are adult polycystic kidney disease.
Chronic inflammation from long-standing RA causes AA amyloidosis. Apple-green birefringence with Congo red confirms it, and amyloid kidneys are typically enlarged with nephrotic features.

A large renal mass with abdominal swelling, haematuria and fever in a young child is a nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour). The book's key prints G, but its explanation describes Wilms' tumour, so B is used.
Prostatic outflow obstruction backs up into both kidneys, causing palpable hydronephrotic kidneys, a palpable bladder and post-renal failure.
A large, fluid-filled lesion in an otherwise normal kidney, found incidentally, is a simple renal cyst. It is usually harmless.
Berry aneurysms are associated with polycystic kidney disease. Rupture gives a sudden severe headache, coma and raised intracranial pressure (hypertension with bradycardia, papilloedema).
Hypertension develops early in polycystic kidney disease, driven by cyst-related renin activation. AV nipping and exudates show end-organ damage.
Cysts can produce excess erythropoietin, so secondary polycythaemia can occur even with advanced renal failure.
A solid mass in a polycystic kidney with haematuria and night sweats raises concern for renal cell carcinoma, which needs cross-sectional imaging.
Infected cysts and recurrent urinary infection are common in polycystic kidneys. Here Gram-negative urosepsis has led to shock.
A large clear-cell tumour invading the adrenal and renal vein is renal cell carcinoma. Tumour thrombus in the vein is typical of this cancer.
Past exposure to dye-industry aromatic amines and a papillary trigone lesion with atypical urothelial cells indicate transitional-cell (urothelial) carcinoma.
A large malignant embryonal kidney tumour in an infant is a nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour).
Chronic schistosomal irritation causes squamous metaplasia of the urothelium, leading to keratinising squamous-cell carcinoma of the bladder.
A benign tumour of blood vessels, smooth muscle and fat in a patient with tuberous sclerosis is an angiomyolipoma. Large lesions risk haemorrhage.
Major upper GI haemorrhage with shock reduces renal perfusion (prerenal injury). Absorbed blood protein raises the urea out of proportion to creatinine.
Prostate cancer with a very high PSA and back pain has obstructed outflow, causing bilateral hydronephrosis and post-renal failure.
In bilateral renal artery stenosis, suggested here by widespread atheroma, glomerular filtration depends on angiotensin II. An ACE inhibitor removes this support and precipitates renal failure.
Lying on the floor for days causes muscle breakdown. A very high CK with hyperkalaemia indicates rhabdomyolysis, in which myoglobin injures the tubules.
A purpuric rash on the legs and buttocks, arthralgia and haematuria with a raised IgA indicate Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis (IgA vasculitis).
Anti-Ro/La antibodies with arthritis indicate Sjogren's syndrome, a recognised cause of mixed cryoglobulinaemia with vasculitic rash and glomerulonephritis.
Freshwater exposure followed by fever, myalgia, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and renal failure is leptospirosis (Weil's disease).
Rheumatic valve disease with fever, a murmur, anaemia and vasculitic lesions suggests infective endocarditis. Its chronic antigenaemia can drive cryoglobulin formation and nephritis.
Sore throat, marked lymphadenopathy and atypical lymphocytes indicate infectious mononucleosis. EBV is among the infections that can trigger cryoglobulinaemia.
An IgM paraprotein with lymphoplasmacytoid cells in the marrow and no lytic lesions is Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia. The monoclonal IgM can behave as a type I cryoglobulin.
IV amphotericin B for severe fungal infection is markedly nephrotoxic, causing tubular injury, potassium wasting and rising creatinine. Lipid formulations reduce the risk.
Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are both nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Monitor trough levels and renal function during treatment.
Intramuscular gold for RA can cause membranous nephropathy with proteinuria, oedema and declining renal function.
An ACE inhibitor started after MI in a man with vascular disease (probable renal artery stenosis) has caused renal failure and hyperkalaemia. The cough confirms the drug class.
High-dose co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV can cause interstitial nephritis and crystal nephropathy, and its trimethoprim component also raises creatinine and potassium.
A painful crisis with severe anaemia and visible haematuria in a man of African-Caribbean origin indicates sickle-cell disease with renal papillary necrosis.
Bilateral hilar nodes with lung infiltrates indicate sarcoidosis. It damages the kidney through hypercalcaemia, nephrocalcinosis and granulomatous interstitial nephritis.
A young woman with malar rash, arthritis, heavy proteinuria, oedema and severe hypertension has lupus nephritis. Renal biopsy guides immunosuppression.
Fistulating Crohn's disease can track into the urinary tract or surrounding tissues, causing infection; oxalate stones and amyloid are other renal complications. Mouth ulcers support Crohn's.
An RNA hepatitis virus in a former injecting drug user is hepatitis C. It is the classic cause of cryoglobulinaemic type I mesangiocapillary (membranoproliferative) glomerulonephritis.
Leg weakness, a sensory level and a palpable bladder in metastatic breast cancer indicate malignant spinal cord compression. Arrange urgent MRI and give dexamethasone.
Cognitive decline, gait apraxia and urinary incontinence form the triad of normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Some patients improve after CSF drainage.
Urgency and frequency with normal tests that respond to the antimuscarinic oxybutynin indicate detrusor overactivity (an unstable bladder).
Poor stream and terminal dribbling with a low PSA that improve on an alpha-blocker indicate benign prostatic hyperplasia, with overflow incontinence.
In a frail elderly woman, a urinary infection often presents atypically, with confusion, falls and new incontinence. A positive dipstick and culture support it.
Recurrent Proteus infection with a large calcified mass and a hydronephrotic kidney indicate an obstructing (staghorn) renal stone.
Spinal and rib bone pain with outflow symptoms and a palpable bladder in an older man suggests metastatic prostate carcinoma causing obstruction.
A pancreatic mass with bilateral hydroureters indicates retroperitoneal encasement of both ureters, i.e. malignant retroperitoneal fibrosis causing obstructive uropathy.
Bone pain, very high ESR, hypercalcaemia and lytic lesions indicate myeloma. Filtered light chains precipitate as casts that obstruct the tubules (cast nephropathy).
Leg weakness with a sensory level and a breast mass suggest spinal metastases compressing the cord. Loss of bladder control produces a neurogenic bladder with retention.
Gradual hesitancy, weak stream and dribbling with a smooth, enlarged prostate and a modest PSA indicate benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes a large, insensate, atonic bladder with painless chronic retention, overflow incontinence and back-pressure on the kidneys.
Bleeding from a bladder tumour forms clots that block the outflow and the catheter. Clot retention needs a three-way catheter with bladder washouts and irrigation.
After pelvic or groin surgery, pain, anaesthesia and local swelling can cause painful acute retention. The book attributes it to prostatic oedema.
Long-term urethral catheters cause urethral injury and scarring. A catheter that cannot pass beyond the first part of the urethra suggests a stricture; seek urology help.
A painless, fluctuant, transilluminating scrotal swelling that hides the testis but leaves the cord above it normal is a primary (idiopathic) hydrocele.
Sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting and a high-riding testis in a boy is torsion. Explore surgically at once without waiting for imaging.
A hard, irregular testis with raised AFP and beta-hCG in a young man indicates a non-seminomatous germ-cell tumour (teratoma). Pure seminoma does not raise AFP.
Fever, urinary symptoms and a hot, red, tender hemiscrotum indicate acute epididymo-orchitis, usually from ascending infection.
A tense, tender, non-transilluminating swelling after trauma, with the testis impalpable, indicates bleeding into the tunica vaginalis (a haematocele).
Heavy, painless periods causing anaemia with an enlarged, bulky uterus point to uterine fibroids (leiomyomas).
Endometrial tissue lying within the myometrium, with painful heavy bleeding and a tender, enlarged uterus, is adenomyosis.
Normal examination, haemoglobin and clotting with no objective excess loss after stopping the pill suggest periods that are within normal limits, i.e. physiological.
Chlamydia with pelvic pain and menorrhagia indicates pelvic inflammatory disease. Treat the patient and trace partners.
Heavy periods with iron deficiency, a prolonged bleeding time and a long APTT in a teenager suggest von Willebrand disease. Low factor VIII explains the APTT.
Post-coital bleeding with a friable, ulcerated cervix and dyskaryotic cells is cervical carcinoma until proven otherwise; arrange colposcopy and biopsy.
Deep dyspareunia, painful periods and irregular bleeding diagnosed at laparoscopy and improved by diathermy and danazol indicate endometriosis.
Irregular and intermenstrual bleeding in an older nulliparous woman with adenocarcinoma on hysteroscopic biopsy is endometrial carcinoma.
An everted, reddened cervix with contact bleeding and a normal smear is a cervical ectropion, which is benign and common in young women.
A positive pregnancy test, unilateral pain, bleeding and no intrauterine sac on ultrasound mean ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
Amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, a markedly raised prolactin and a small pituitary lesion indicate a prolactinoma. Dopamine agonists are first-line.
Obesity, hirsutism and amenorrhoea with raised LH and testosterone and low SHBG are polycystic ovary syndrome.
Severe weight loss to a BMI of 15 with amenorrhoea indicates anorexia nervosa, which suppresses hypothalamic GnRH release.
A raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone with hirsutism, short stature and menstrual disturbance indicates late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency).
Massive postpartum haemorrhage followed by failed lactation, amenorrhoea and profound fatigue indicates pituitary infarction (Sheehan's) with panhypopituitarism.
Itchy small labial lesions weeks after a new sexual contact, with a normal cervix, are genital warts caused by HPV.
Gram-negative diplococci with discharge and vulval irritation indicate gonorrhoea. Test and treat for coexisting chlamydia too.
Thin, shiny, atrophic vulval skin in an older woman, with non-atypical changes on biopsy and a response to oestrogen cream, is a vulval dystrophy.
A frothy green discharge, vulval erythema and a punctate ('strawberry') cervix with flagellated protozoa indicate Trichomonas vaginalis. Treat with metronidazole.
Budding yeasts with pseudohyphae and white plaques indicate vulvovaginal candidiasis. Her poorly controlled diabetes predisposes to it; the book also accepts diabetes mellitus (C).

where.title: Neoplasms of the female genital tract

items.explanation: A smooth-walled ovarian cyst containing sebum, hair, bone and teeth is a mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst), the commonest ovarian tumour in young women.
Postmenopausal bleeding in an obese, hypertensive, nulliparous woman with malignant glands reflects unopposed-oestrogen endometrial adenocarcinoma.
An everted, rolled-edge vulval ulcer with groin nodes and keratin pearls on biopsy is squamous-cell carcinoma of the vulva.
Multiple well-circumscribed myometrial masses with a whorled white cut surface and benign smooth-muscle histology are leiomyomas (fibroids).
A solid ovarian germ-cell tumour of large polygonal cells with prominent nucleoli and lymphocytes is a dysgerminoma, the ovarian counterpart of seminoma.

where.title: Cutaneous innervation of the upper limb

items.explanation: The axillary nerve, through its upper lateral brachial cutaneous branch, supplies skin over the lower deltoid. Test this 'regimental badge' patch after a shoulder dislocation.
The skin over the medial epicondyle is supplied by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, a branch of the medial cord.
The skin of the anatomical snuffbox is supplied by the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar skin. It leaves the nerve above the flexor retinaculum, so thenar sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
The ulnar nerve supplies the skin of the little finger, including the nail bed through its digital branches.

where.title: Nerve supply of the muscles of the upper limb

items.explanation: Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve from the posterior cord (C5-6).
Brachioradialis is supplied by the main radial nerve, above the elbow where it divides.
Supinator is supplied by the posterior interosseous (deep radial) nerve, which passes through the muscle and can be trapped there.
Flexor carpi ulnaris is one of only one and a half forearm flexors supplied by the ulnar nerve.
Flexor carpi radialis belongs to the superficial flexor group supplied by the median nerve.
Brachioradialis arises from the upper part of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.
Triceps inserts on the olecranon process of the ulna and extends the elbow.
The common extensor origin gives rise to extensor carpi radialis brevis on the front of the lateral epicondyle. Its tendon origin is implicated in tennis elbow.
Brachialis inserts into the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity, making it a pure elbow flexor.
Supinator wraps around the proximal radius and attaches to its upper lateral, anterior and posterior surfaces.
The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove on the back of the humeral shaft, so it is at risk in mid-shaft fractures (wrist drop).
The ulnar nerve lies against the back of the medial epicondyle, the 'funny bone'. It is easily compressed or injured there.
The median nerve enters the forearm between the superficial and deep heads of pronator teres, a site of entrapment.
The brachial artery ends in the cubital fossa at about the level of the radial neck, dividing into radial and ulnar arteries.
The radial artery leaves the snuffbox and enters the palm between the heads of the first interosseous muscle to form the deep palmar arch.

where.title: Cutaneous innervation of the lower limb

items.explanation: Skin over the femoral triangle, including the saphenous opening, is innervated by the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh supplies the lateral thigh, including the skin over the greater trochanter. Compression causes meralgia paraesthetica.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies the lower anterolateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot.
The sural nerve supplies the lateral border of the foot and little toe. It is a common site for nerve biopsy.
The deep peroneal nerve supplies only the first dorsal web space. Testing it helps localise peroneal nerve lesions.

where.title: Nerve supply of the muscles of the lower limb

items.explanation: Adductor longus, like the other medial thigh adductors, is supplied by the obturator nerve.
Biceps femoris is supplied by the sciatic nerve: the long head by the tibial division and the short head by the common peroneal division.
Extensor digitorum longus lies in the anterior compartment, supplied by the deep peroneal nerve.
Peroneus brevis lies in the lateral compartment, supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve, and everts the foot.
Tibialis posterior, in the deep posterior compartment, is supplied by the tibial nerve and inverts the foot.
The great saphenous vein pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening to drain into the femoral vein.
The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery.
The common peroneal nerve winds round the lateral neck of the fibula, where fractures or tight plasters can injure it and cause foot drop.
The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus, medial to the talus, where its pulse is felt.
The perforating branch of the peroneal artery passes forwards in front of the lateral malleolus to join the lateral malleolar network.

where.title: Muscle attachments of the lower limb

items.explanation: The straight head of rectus femoris arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine; sprinters can avulse it.
Adductor longus arises from the front of the body of the pubis, just below the pubic crest.
Biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula, alongside the lateral collateral ligament.
Tibialis anterior inserts on the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal.
Peroneus brevis inserts on the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal base; inversion injuries can avulse it.
Increasing forearm pain with numbness and poor capillary refill after an elbow fracture is compartment syndrome. A palpable pulse does not exclude it; urgent fasciotomy is needed.
A missed scaphoid fracture that leaves a separate fragment on later films has failed to unite (non-union), a risk because of the scaphoid's retrograde blood supply.
Knee dislocation can stretch the common peroneal nerve, giving foot drop and numbness of the dorsum of the foot despite intact pulses.
Burning pain, swelling and trophic changes months after a distal radius fracture indicate complex regional pain syndrome (Sudeck's atrophy, algodystrophy).
A comminuted fracture entering the wrist joint damages the articular surface, leading to secondary osteoarthritis years later.
A flattened shoulder contour, a bulge below the clavicle and numbness over the deltoid indicate an anterior shoulder dislocation with axillary nerve injury.
A blow to the upper arm causing wrist drop suggests a humeral shaft fracture injuring the radial nerve in the spiral groove.
Persistent wrist pain months after a fall on the outstretched hand suggests a missed scaphoid fracture. Image it, as delays risk non-union and avascular necrosis.
A swollen elbow with an absent radial pulse in a child after a fall indicates a displaced supracondylar humeral fracture compromising the brachial artery.
An elbow effusion with a fat-pad sign but no visible fracture after a fall usually hides a radial head fracture. Loss of extension is a common sequel.
Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals in an exquisitely painful big toe in a publican (alcohol) confirm acute gout.
Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray and weakly positively birefringent crystals in an elderly knee indicate calcium pyrophosphate arthritis (pseudogout).
Knee arthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis after dysentery is reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome).
A grossly deformed but relatively painless ankle in long-standing diabetes with sensory neuropathy is a Charcot (neuropathic) joint.
A hot, swollen joint days after an intra-articular injection is septic arthritis until proven otherwise; Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism. Aspirate before IV antibiotics.
Scaly plaques at the elbow and hairline with a deforming hand arthritis indicate psoriatic arthritis, which can mimic rheumatoid patterns.
Asymmetrical involvement of the distal interphalangeal joints with a painful weight-bearing knee in an older woman is osteoarthritis.
Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with arthritis in someone of Mediterranean origin is Behcet's disease, a variable-vessel vasculitis.
A cheek rash with hand and foot arthritis and anti-dsDNA antibodies indicates systemic lupus erythematosus.
Sicca symptoms with reduced tear production on Schirmer testing and anti-Ro/La positivity in established arthritis indicate secondary Sjogren's syndrome.
Foot drop and a median nerve deficit, two separate named nerves, indicate mononeuritis multiplex, usually from rheumatoid vasculitis.
Chest pain with fever, a scratchy rub and widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation is pericarditis, a recognised serosal complication of RA.
Gradual symmetrical tingling of hands and feet indicates a peripheral sensory neuropathy in RA (vasculitic, drug-related or entrapment).
Severe painful red eye with congestion of the deep scleral vessels is scleritis. Necrotising disease can thin the sclera (scleromalacia), so refer urgently.
RA with splenomegaly and neutropenia is Felty's syndrome. It predisposes to infection; thrombocytopenia explains the purpura.
A cushingoid face with easy bruising but normal platelets and clotting reflects long-term prednisolone thinning the skin and capillaries.
A low COX-2/COX-1 selectivity index marks a non-selective NSAID such as diclofenac, which damages the gastric mucosa and can cause bleeding ulcers.
Hydroxychloroquine, especially in excess, can bleach and thin the hair and cause retinal toxicity with blurred vision. Regular eye screening is advised.
D-penicillamine can induce a lupus-like syndrome and membranous glomerulonephritis, explaining the malar rash and renal failure.
Weekly intramuscular gold can cause bone-marrow aplasia. Sore throat and purpura with pancytopenia need the drug stopped immediately.
A BMI around 36 overloads the knees; obesity is a major modifiable risk factor for knee osteoarthritis.
An isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with cortical thickening and a coarse trabecular pattern is Paget's disease, which deforms bone and leads to secondary osteoarthritis.
In sickle-cell disease, vaso-occlusion causes avascular necrosis of the femoral head, and joint collapse then leads to secondary osteoarthritis.
Extreme joint laxity with recurrent dislocations suggests Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Hypermobile joints wear prematurely.
Psoriatic plaques with destructive finger arthritis and telescoping digits (arthritis mutilans) indicate psoriatic arthropathy.
A fixed thoracic kyphosis ('question mark' posture) with apical lung fibrosis is late ankylosing spondylitis.
Arthritis, painful heels (enthesitis) and conjunctivitis following chlamydial urethritis form Reiter's syndrome.
Recurrent bloody diarrhoea with peripheral arthritis that flares alongside the bowel disease is enteropathic arthritis linked to IBD.
PAS-positive macrophages in the bowel wall confirm Whipple's disease, which causes diarrhoea, weight loss, arthritis and sacroiliitis.
The book credits three features: knee arthritis (C), circinate balanitis on the glans (D) and conjunctivitis causing the gritty red eyes (E).
The classic triad is arthritis (C), conjunctivitis (E) and urethritis (J). The pigmented plantar and palmar lesions are keratoderma blennorrhagicum (F); all four are credited.
Blurred vision with photophobia and no discharge is anterior uveitis (B). The book also credits arthritis (C) and plantar fasciitis (I).
Painful heels and soles are enthesitis: Achilles' tendonitis (A) and plantar fasciitis (I), both credited.
Bloody nasal discharge, lung involvement and renal failure with a high c-ANCA (PR3) titre indicate granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).
Severe hypertension with renal microaneurysms on angiography and negative ANCA indicate a medium-vessel vasculitis: polyarteritis nodosa.
An older woman with temporal headache, scalp tenderness and an ESR over 100 has giant-cell arteritis. Start high-dose steroids immediately to protect vision.
Wheeze, marked eosinophilia and renal impairment indicate eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss). It is often p-ANCA positive rather than c-ANCA.
Palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with arthritis and raised IgA is Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis).
Acute knee arthritis with sterile fluid containing weakly positively birefringent crystals is calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout) arthropathy.
Liver disease, diabetes and bronze pigmentation indicate haemochromatosis. Iron deposition predisposes to chondrocalcinosis and a hook-like MCP arthropathy.
Widespread chondrocalcinosis with hypercalcaemia, depression and vague pains suggest primary hyperparathyroidism, a recognised cause of pyrophosphate deposition.
Chalky tophi discharging from the fingers and ear lobes indicate chronic tophaceous gout. Urate disease can coexist with cartilage calcification.
Weight gain, slowing, macrocytosis and hyponatraemia with autoimmune vitiligo suggest hypothyroidism, which is associated with chondrocalcinosis.
Hypercalcaemia, deranged liver tests, hyponatraemia and multiple large lung lesions indicate disseminated malignancy (carcinomatosis), a classic cause of a very high ESR.
Sudden fever, shock and collapse in a young woman using tampons is toxic shock syndrome, caused by staphylococcal superantigen toxin.
Bone pain, hypercalcaemia, free light chains in the urine and an IgG paraprotein indicate multiple myeloma. The paraprotein pushes the ESR very high.
Aching and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles with a raised ESR in an older woman, without headache, is polymyalgia rheumatica. It responds dramatically to low-dose steroids.
An injecting drug user in acute heart failure with a new early diastolic murmur has aortic valve endocarditis, usually from Staphylococcus aureus.
Malar rash, arthralgia, cytopenias and renal involvement indicate SLE. Anti-dsDNA is the most specific antibody and tracks disease activity.
Raynaud's, facial telangiectasia, oesophageal dysmotility and a small mouth indicate limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST), typically anticentromere-positive.
Proximal weakness, a periorbital (heliotrope) rash and a very high CK indicate dermatomyositis; anti-Jo-1 marks the antisynthetase subset. The lung lesion warrants a cancer search.
Bloody nasal discharge, lung symptoms and severe renal failure point to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which is strongly associated with c-ANCA (PR3).
Stroke and recurrent miscarriage in SLE indicate antiphospholipid syndrome. Anticardiolipin antibodies (with lupus anticoagulant) confirm it, and anticoagulation is needed.
A deforming inflammatory arthritis with dry eyes and mouth indicates secondary Sjogren's syndrome, a recognised cause of Raynaud's phenomenon.
One-sided Raynaud's in a teenager with a bruit above the clavicle suggests a cervical rib compressing the subclavian artery (thoracic outlet syndrome).
Lethargy and weight gain in a woman with autoimmune vitiligo indicate hypothyroidism, which can cause Raynaud's phenomenon.
Tight, swollen fingers and perioral tightening after long-standing Raynaud's, with anticentromere antibodies, indicate limited systemic sclerosis.
Blistering after UV exposure, arthralgia, myalgia, Raynaud's and a strongly positive ANA in a young woman point to SLE.

Uraemic encephalopathy, pericarditis, anaemia and very high creatinine indicate end-stage renal failure. Low calcium, high phosphate and raised ALP reflect renal bone disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
An isolated high alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate and a thickened, coarse pelvis is Paget's disease of bone.
Low calcium and phosphate with a high bone ALP in a woman of South Asian origin with diffuse aches indicate vitamin D-deficient osteomalacia.
A smoker with a lung mass, hypercalcaemia, low phosphate and a normal bone scan has humoral hypercalcaemia from tumour PTH-related peptide (usually squamous carcinoma).
Bone pain, anaemia, low platelets, renal failure, hypercalcaemia and a very high ESR fit multiple myeloma with marrow infiltration.
Weight loss, sweats, palpitations and fast AF with shoulder-girdle weakness indicate thyrotoxic myopathy. It improves once the patient is euthyroid.
Weakness of all limbs with bulbar dysfunction, normal CK and no sensory loss suggests motor neurone disease, which can mimic a proximal myopathy.
Bitemporal hemianopia, enlarging hands and feet, hypertension and proximal weakness indicate a growth hormone-secreting pituitary macroadenoma (acromegaly).
Weight gain, abdominal striae, hypertension, hyperglycaemia and proximal weakness are features of Cushing's syndrome. Steroid excess causes muscle catabolism.
Stigmata of chronic liver disease, macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia and a very high CK point to alcohol-induced myopathy.
Massive postpartum haemorrhage can infarct the enlarged pituitary. Failure of lactation followed by amenorrhoea, fatigue and weight gain indicates hypopituitarism (Sheehan's syndrome).
After bilateral adrenalectomy, loss of cortisol feedback lets a corticotroph adenoma grow. High ACTH darkens the skin and the tumour can invade the cavernous sinus (Nelson's syndrome).
Surgery near the hypothalamus can damage ADH-producing neurones. Sudden large volumes of dilute urine afterwards indicate cranial diabetes insipidus; treat with desmopressin.
A prolactin this high is only produced by a prolactin-secreting tumour, not by stalk compression. Chiasmal compression and hypopituitarism indicate a macroadenoma; cabergoline is first-line.
Anosmia from birth with delayed puberty and low gonadotrophins but otherwise normal pituitary function is Kallmann's syndrome: failed GnRH neurone migration.
Pigmentation, postural hypotension, weight loss, hyperkalaemia and other autoimmune diseases (pernicious anaemia, vitiligo) indicate autoimmune Addison's disease.
Rapid virilisation together with cortisol excess and suppressed ACTH implies an adrenal source secreting androgens too, which is typical of adrenal carcinoma.
High ACTH and cortisol that do not suppress even with high-dose dexamethasone, with a normal pituitary scan, indicate ectopic ACTH secretion. Pigmentation and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia follow.
Pituitary-driven Cushing's suppresses on high-dose but not low-dose dexamethasone because the adenoma partly keeps its feedback. This is Cushing's disease.
Cushingoid features with macrocytosis, hepatomegaly, normal adrenals and a normal pituitary suggest alcohol-induced pseudo-Cushing's. It resolves with abstinence.
A painless lump in the thyroid with a high fT4 and suppressed TSH is an autonomous, hyperfunctioning nodular goitre. A nuclear scan would show hot areas.
A rapidly growing hard, fixed thyroid mass in an elderly woman with stridor, cord palsy and nodes is anaplastic carcinoma, which carries a very poor prognosis.
Severe thyrotoxicosis with a diffuse goitre and a bruit in a young woman is Graves' disease. The bruit reflects increased gland vascularity.
A smooth, diffuse, euthyroid goitre arising in pregnancy reflects a higher iodine requirement; this is a simple colloid goitre.
Hypercalcaemia with raised PTH and a catecholamine-secreting adrenal mass suggest MEN2A. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is the thyroid component, so check calcitonin and RET.
Steatorrhoea and recurrent abdominal pain with new diabetes indicate chronic pancreatitis. Loss of islet cells causes secondary (type 3c) diabetes.
Carpal tunnel syndrome, larger rings, sweating, headache and galactorrhoea suggest acromegaly. Growth hormone opposes insulin and causes hyperglycaemia.
A short history of polyuria, thirst and weight loss in a teenager is type 1 diabetes. Check ketones.
Diabetes with skin bronzing, hepatomegaly, arthralgia and hypogonadism is haemochromatosis: iron damages the pancreatic islets, liver, joints and pituitary.
Weight gain, bruising, weakness, low libido and depression with diabetes indicate cortisol excess. In a previously healthy young man, a pituitary source (Cushing's disease) is most likely.
Unsteadiness only in the dark, loss of joint position sense and a painless ulcer under the metatarsal head indicate peripheral sensory neuropathy.
Painful wasting of the quadriceps with a lost knee jerk in an older person with type 2 diabetes is diabetic amyotrophy (lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy).
Weakness in median, ulnar and radial territories with intact sensation reflects several individual nerves damaged together: mononeuritis multiplex.
