Proteinuria in long-standing type 1 diabetes with hypertension and normocytic anaemia indicates diabetic nephropathy. An ACE inhibitor or ARB slows progression.
A large postural blood pressure fall causing falls on standing indicates autonomic neuropathy.
Microaneurysms, blot haemorrhages and hard exudates sparing the macula, without new vessels, are background (non-proliferative) retinopathy.
Sudden painless loss of vision with no red reflex and a hazy fundus indicates vitreous haemorrhage, usually from fragile new vessels.
New vessels plus ischaemic features (cotton-wool spots) indicate proliferative retinopathy, which needs laser or anti-VEGF treatment.
Sudden profound monocular loss with a pale retina and a cherry-red spot at the macula is central retinal artery occlusion.
A swollen disc with haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots throughout the retina ('stormy sunset') is central retinal vein occlusion.

where.title: Drug complications in patients with diabetes

items.explanation: Acarbose blocks intestinal alpha-glucosidase, so undigested carbohydrate is fermented in the colon, causing flatulence and bloating.
Non-selective beta-blockers blunt the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia and can delay recovery, reducing hypoglycaemia awareness.
Chlorpropamide causes a disulfiram-like facial flush with alcohol. It is now rarely used, partly because its long action causes hypoglycaemia.
Thiazide diuretics impair insulin release and sensitivity, so blood glucose and insulin requirements rise.
Metformin can cause lactic acidosis when sepsis or poor perfusion impairs lactate clearance. The gas shows high anion-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.
Carbimazole can cause agranulocytosis, which typically presents as a sore throat. Stop it and check a full blood count urgently.
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide reduce gallbladder contraction, so gallstones and biliary sludge form during long-term use.
Chlorpropamide enhances ADH action on the kidney, causing dilutional hyponatraemia (an SIADH-like effect).
Ovulation induction with clomifene can cause ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: enlarged cystic ovaries, ascites and abdominal pain.
Oral bisphosphonates such as alendronate irritate the oesophagus and can cause erosions and ulcers. Take with water while upright and stay upright afterwards.
Ill-defined lumpiness that enlarges and becomes tender before menstruation is fibrocystic change, a hormonally responsive benign condition.
A hard upper outer quadrant mass with axillary nodes and a spiculated, calcified mammographic lesion in an older woman is invasive ductal carcinoma.
Thick creamy nipple discharge with dilated subareolar ducts and no epithelial cells in the fluid is duct ectasia.
A mobile, well-defined solid lump with benign cytology in a young woman is a fibroadenoma (a 'breast mouse').
A hot, red, tender segment soon after childbirth with neutrophils on aspiration is acute lactational mastitis, usually from Staphylococcus aureus.
A net-like, pigmented rash on the shins comes from chronic heat exposure, e.g. sitting close to a fire or heater: erythema ab igne. It hints at a cold, possibly hypothyroid, elderly person.
Papules on the cheeks, forehead and chin with years of easy flushing, and no comedones, indicate rosacea.
A shiny, waxy, yellow-brown plaque on the shin in a diabetic patient is necrobiosis lipoidica, a diabetic skin lesion.
Night sweats, weight loss and a productive cough suggest pulmonary TB. A scaly cutaneous plaque in this context is lupus vulgaris, which is skin tuberculosis.
Very itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces with granular IgA deposits in skin are dermatitis herpetiformis, the skin form of gluten sensitivity.
Widespread blistering with oral and eye involvement after a chest infection (often Mycoplasma) or a drug is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which needs specialist supportive care.
Blisters on knees, elbows and buttocks with weight loss, diarrhoea, macrocytosis and positive endomysial antibodies indicate dermatitis herpetiformis with coeliac disease.
Blistering confined to a band from the loin round to the umbilicus follows the T10 dermatome, i.e. shingles (herpes zoster reactivation).
Tense blisters on the limbs and trunk of an elderly person, with no mucosal involvement, indicate bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal split).
Fragile, easily de-roofed blisters leaving raw erosions, with mouth and eye involvement in an unwell patient, indicate pemphigus vulgaris (intraepidermal split).
Dry, itchy, lichenified flexural eczema in a child with hay fever is atopic eczema.
Pale, slightly scaly hypopigmented patches in a child with darker skin are pityriasis alba, a mild form of eczema.
Dry, cracked 'crazy paving' eczema on the shins of an elderly inpatient is asteatotic eczema (eczema craquele) caused by skin dryness.
Raw, inflamed hands in a trainee hairdresser reflect irritant or allergic contact dermatitis from chemicals and wet work.
Discrete, coin-shaped, itchy eczema patches on the limbs are discoid (nummular) dermatitis.
Intense itching with papules and burrows in the finger webs in someone living in poor conditions is scabies. Treat contacts at the same time.
Generalised pruritus with night sweats, lymphadenopathy, weight loss and hepatosplenomegaly suggests Hodgkin lymphoma.
Scaly extensor and scalp plaques with pitted, ridged nails indicate psoriasis, which can be itchy.
Weight loss, dysphagia, an epigastric mass and Virchow's node suggest gastric cancer. Chronic blood loss causes iron deficiency, a recognised cause of generalised itch.
Starting an ACE inhibitor in a vasculopath can precipitate renal failure. Nausea, vomiting, confusion and itching are uraemic symptoms.
A smoker with haemoptysis, deep pigmentation, weakness and marked hypokalaemia has ectopic ACTH secretion, typically from small-cell lung cancer.
Patches that fail to tan, mostly on the back, and respond to an azole are pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia yeast).
Depigmented patches on the hands in a woman with autoimmune hypothyroidism (and possibly pernicious anaemia) are vitiligo.
Palmar crease pigmentation, postural hypotension, low glucose and wasting in a young woman indicate primary adrenal failure (Addison's disease).
Velvety dark thickening of the neck and axillae in an obese diabetic is acanthosis nigricans, a marker of insulin resistance.
Subacute endocarditis on a rheumatic mitral valve gives finger clubbing (A) and splinter haemorrhages (I); both are credited. Osler's nodes support the diagnosis.
Separation of the nail from its bed (onycholysis, 'Plummer's nails') is a recognised sign of thyrotoxicosis.
Chronic liver disease causes clubbing (A) and white nails (leuconychia, C) from hypoalbuminaemia; both are credited.
Thickened, curved 'ram's horn' toenails in a neglected elderly person are onychogryphosis.
Copious purulent sputum with tramlines after old TB indicates bronchiectasis, a classic cause of finger clubbing.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, raised serum ACE and hypercalcaemia indicate sarcoidosis (Lofgren-type presentation).
Night sweats, weight loss, upper-zone crackles and cervical nodes in a heavy drinker suggest tuberculosis, a well-known trigger of erythema nodosum.
Night sweats, weight loss and generalised lymphadenopathy after severe EBV infection suggest lymphoma. Hodgkin's disease is EBV-linked and can cause erythema nodosum.
Fever, sore throat and neck nodes with a positive monospot indicate infectious mononucleosis (EBV), one cause of erythema nodosum.
Lobar pneumonia with Gram-positive cocci on sputum indicates streptococcal (pneumococcal) infection. Streptococci are a common trigger of erythema nodosum.
A very high ASOT shows a recent streptococcal infection, one of the recognised triggers of erythema multiforme.
Dry cough, patchy bilateral shadowing, hyponatraemia and mildly abnormal liver tests suggest Mycoplasma pneumonia, a classic cause of erythema multiforme and SJS.
Months of bloody diarrhoea and weight loss suggest ulcerative colitis, which can be accompanied by erythema multiforme.
A malar rash, arthritis, renal failure and strongly positive anti-dsDNA indicate SLE, which can produce erythema multiforme-like lesions.
A recent cold sore on the lip followed by target-like blistering lesions is the commonest pattern of erythema multiforme: herpes simplex-triggered.
Haemoptysis, renal failure and a strongly positive c-ANCA indicate granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a recognised association of pyoderma gangrenosum.
Massive splenomegaly, leukoerythroblastic counts, Philadelphia-negative disease and a dry marrow tap indicate myelofibrosis.
An IgM paraprotein with cytopenias, a high ESR and no lytic lesions indicates Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia.
Inflammatory low back and buttock pain with sacroiliac erosions in a young man indicates ankylosing spondylitis.
Episodic bloody diarrhoea with crypt abscesses and goblet-cell depletion is ulcerative colitis, the commonest association of pyoderma gangrenosum.
A pink, well-perfused, normally breathing newborn with good saturations needs no intervention. Simply observe a mildly slow but adequate heart rate.
Neonatal bradycardia is almost always due to hypoxia. In an apnoeic, pale baby, first open the airway and give inflation breaths with bag-valve-mask ventilation before considering drugs.
This is a sinus tachycardia compensating for hypovolaemia and acidosis in DKA. Treat the cause with careful fluids and insulin, not with antiarrhythmic measures.
Pulseless ventricular tachycardia is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm. Deliver an unsynchronised shock (about 4 J/kg) promptly alongside CPR.
An infant heart rate around 230 with no response to vagal manoeuvres is supraventricular tachycardia. Rapid IV adenosine is the next step.
High-dose corticosteroids used during leukaemia induction commonly raise blood pressure, so the hypertension is iatrogenic. The soft murmur is likely innocent or flow-related.
Short stature and dysmorphism suggest Turner syndrome. A systolic murmur radiating to the back with upper-limb hypertension points to coarctation of the aorta.
Bloody diarrhoea followed by pallor, purpura, anaemia and renal impairment is haemolytic-uraemic syndrome, usually after E. coli O157 infection.
Hypertension with delayed puberty and normal catecholamines suggests a form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (e.g. 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency) causing mineralocorticoid excess.
A firm abdominal mass with pallor and hypertension in a young child suggests neuroblastoma. Catecholamine secretion raises the blood pressure.
Children with severe neurodisability are prone to aspiration pneumonia. Co-amoxiclav covers the oral anaerobes and the usual respiratory pathogens.
Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea after antibiotics is treated with oral vancomycin, which acts inside the gut lumen.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci on central lines are usually methicillin-resistant, so IV vancomycin (often with line salvage measures) is used.
Respiratory distress soon after birth in a preterm infant may be infection as well as surfactant deficiency. Start benzylpenicillin and gentamicin to cover group B streptococcus and Gram-negatives.
A mild febrile illness with pharyngitis and bilateral otitis in a well child is usually viral. Antibiotics are not needed initially.
Posterior cervical nodes in a well baby with severe seborrhoeic dermatitis of the scalp are reactive nodes draining the inflamed skin.
A painless papule followed weeks later by tender nodes draining that limb, in a household with a cat, is cat scratch disease (Bartonella henselae).
Tonsillitis, tender generalised nodes and hepatomegaly indicate infectious mononucleosis (EBV).
Weight loss, parotid swelling and persistent generalised lymphadenopathy in a child from a high-prevalence area suggest HIV infection.
Petechiae, recurrent infections and widespread painless nodes suggest marrow failure from acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Check a blood film urgently.
Golden crusting on worsening eczema with fever is impetiginised eczema, usually due to Staphylococcus aureus.
Fever in a well child with a central line and sterile peripheral cultures suggests line colonisation by coagulase-negative staphylococci.
Fever, cramps and distension followed by diarrhoea fit Salmonella enteritidis gastroenteritis.
Fever with reduced consciousness and a focal seizure but no rash, in a school-age child, makes pneumococcal meningitis likely.
Fever and respiratory distress with lobar consolidation is classic pneumococcal pneumonia.
New, increasing apnoeas with temperature instability and lethargy in an ex-preterm infant suggest sepsis, including meningitis. Do a full septic screen.
Apnoeas starting after a switch from continuous to bolus feeds suggest reflux. Larger feed volumes provoke regurgitation and reflex apnoea.
Poor feeding, apnoeas and a hyperexpanded chest in a young infant without fever fit RSV bronchiolitis.
Coughing spasms followed by apnoea or cyanosis in a young infant, with siblings who have chronic coughs, suggests pertussis.
Irritability, seizure-like movements, a shrill cry and apnoeas after perinatal asphyxia indicate seizures from hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy.
Morning vomiting with a new sixth-nerve palsy suggests raised intracranial pressure from a posterior fossa tumour. Image the brain: CT (A) or MRI (F) are both credited.
A rapidly enlarging head in an ex-preterm infant suggests hydrocephalus after intraventricular haemorrhage. Cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle is ideal.
Severe hyponatraemia in bronchiolitis on IV fluids suggests SIADH. Paired serum and urine osmolality confirms inappropriately concentrated urine.
Increasing drowsiness after head trauma needs an urgent CT head to look for an intracranial haematoma.
Prolonged focal febrile seizure with persistent drowsiness needs a CT head before any lumbar puncture, to exclude a space-occupying lesion or raised pressure.
Painless distension with a large ballotable flank mass in a toddler is typical of Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma).
Sudden pallor, shock and a rapidly enlarging spleen in a young child with sickle-cell disease is acute splenic sequestration.
A week of pain and fever then generalised peritonism with absent bowel sounds suggests a perforated appendix with peritonitis; young children often present late.
Progressive distension with no bowel action since birth in a term baby suggests Hirschsprung's disease. Confirm with rectal suction biopsy.
Abdominal and periorbital swelling in a well school-age child suggests nephrotic syndrome with ascites. Check urine protein and serum albumin.
Sudden choking cough with unilateral reduced breath sounds in a toddler suggests an inhaled foreign body. Bronchoscopy diagnoses and removes it.
Loud snoring with pauses in breathing in an obese child suggests obstructive sleep apnoea. Overnight oximetry is a useful first test.
A mild asthma exacerbation that settles promptly with a bronchodilator needs no investigation.
Recurrent pneumonia with poor weight gain in an infant raises suspicion of cystic fibrosis, so a sweat test is indicated.
Coryza with stridor only when upset and no hypoxia is mild croup, diagnosed clinically. Investigations are unnecessary.
Weight falling off months after weaning, with offensive stools and a distended abdomen but preserved length, suggests coeliac disease after gluten exposure.
Poor feeding with tachypnoea, recession and hepatomegaly at six weeks suggests heart failure, e.g. from a large left-to-right shunt.
A child falling behind in height while weight gain stays normal (becoming relatively plump) suggests growth hormone deficiency.
Proportionate poor growth of weight, length and head with developmental delay in an infant suggests hypothyroidism (or another global cause); thyroid function should be checked.
Severe chest infection, chronic diarrhoea and faltering growth in a child from a high-prevalence region suggest HIV infection.
Clinical dehydration without shock and a normal sodium is best treated with oral rehydration solution, given little and often or by nasogastric tube.
Hypernatraemic dehydration without shock is still best treated orally with rehydration solution, which corrects the sodium slowly and safely.
Ongoing watery losses with normal observations and electrolytes need oral rehydration solution to replace the losses.
Mild diarrhoea in a well-perfused child without dehydration needs no special fluids. Continue a normal diet with usual drinks.
Hypotension with tachycardia means shock. Give a rapid isotonic saline bolus first, then reassess.

where.title: Causes of abnormal cardiac auscultation findings

items.explanation: A scratchy sound in time with the heartbeat a few days after open-heart surgery is a pericardial friction rub (post-pericardiotomy inflammation).
A murmur under the left clavicle in a thriving, symptom-free infant is consistent with a small patent ductus arteriosus. Arrange echocardiography and later closure.
A neonate with respiratory distress, right-arm hypertension and a murmur radiating to the back suggests coarctation, which may become duct-dependent. Check femoral pulses.
A pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge with heart failure at six weeks, as pulmonary resistance falls, is a ventricular septal defect.
Fixed splitting of the second sound with a soft pulmonary flow murmur in a well child indicates an atrial septal defect.

where.title: Interpretation of paediatric blood gas results

items.explanation: Profound hypoxaemia despite 100% oxygen, with normal CO2 and lactate, indicates a fixed right-to-left shunt from cyanotic congenital heart disease (failed hyperoxia test).
Metabolic alkalosis with a positive base excess in a vomiting young male infant fits pyloric stenosis.
Respiratory acidosis with high CO2 and fast breathing in a young infant indicates respiratory failure, most likely from bronchiolitis.
Severe metabolic acidosis with low CO2 compensation and only modestly raised lactate in a floppy neonate suggests an inborn error of metabolism (e.g. organic acidaemia).
Low CO2 with normal base excess in a distressed, oxygen-requiring toddler is early asthma: hyperventilation before fatigue sets in.
A febrile infant holding the hip flexed and externally rotated with a neutrophilia has septic arthritis of the hip. It needs urgent aspiration and washout.
An active early adolescent with thigh or knee pain, a limp and apparent shortening has a slipped upper femoral epiphysis. Examine the hip in any child with knee pain.
Limited hip abduction with apparent shortening and an asymmetrical gait in a young child, with normal neurology, indicate developmental (congenital) dislocation of the hip.
A febrile infant with a swollen, tender thigh refusing to move the leg suggests osteomyelitis of the femur, often from haematogenous Staphylococcus aureus.
Late walking, an unsteady gait and calf pseudohypertrophy in a boy suggest Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Check creatine kinase.
An infant with tachypnoea, recession, prolonged expiration and widespread crackles and wheeze has bronchiolitis.
A hyperexpanded right chest with quiet breath sounds and the trachea pushed to the left indicates a right (tension) pneumothorax, a recognised complication of asthma.
Fine basal inspiratory crackles in a child with nephrotic syndrome suggest pulmonary oedema from fluid overload.
Reduced left-sided expansion with crackles and a central trachea after a viral illness indicates left-sided pneumonia.
Absent left breath sounds with reduced expansion and the trachea pulled towards the left suggest lobar collapse from an inhaled foreign body blocking the left main bronchus.
Image H shows destructive lytic lesions in the proximal femur and pelvis. Myeloma and metastases from lung, breast, kidney or thyroid typically cause this pattern.
Image C shows linear calcification within the knee cartilage (chondrocalcinosis). Pyrophosphate deposition is the commonest cause.
Image B shows a grossly thickened skull vault from Paget's disease, with abnormal bone remodelling.
Image D shows syndesmophytes bridging the vertebrae into a 'bamboo spine', the end stage of ankylosing spondylitis.
Image J shows atlanto-axial subluxation, a dangerous cervical complication of rheumatoid arthritis that can compress the cord.
Image G shows a dense sclerotic lesion in L5. Osteoblastic metastases from prostate (or breast) cancer are the main cause.
Image D, the bamboo spine, is the hallmark of advanced ankylosing spondylitis, an HLA-B27-associated axial arthritis.
Image F shows tophaceous gout: punched-out juxta-articular erosions with soft-tissue tophi in the hand.
Metastases can be sclerotic (image G, L5) or lytic (image H, femur and pelvis); the book credits both G and H.
Image B is Paget's disease of the skull. The pelvis, femur and spine are other common sites.
Image E shows asymmetric joint-space loss, subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes at the DIP and thumb-base joints, typical of osteoarthritis.
Image C, knee chondrocalcinosis, is the radiological sign of pyrophosphate arthropathy (pseudogout).
Limb paraesthesia and weakness in long-standing RA suggest cervical myelopathy from atlanto-axial subluxation (image J). Avoid neck manipulation at anaesthesia and get neurosurgical advice.
Weakly positive birefringent crystals with knee chondrocalcinosis (image C) confirm pyrophosphate arthropathy, which is often mistaken for gout in older men.
Bone pain with a very high ALP but normal calcium, phosphate and GGT (so not liver-derived) suggests Paget's disease (image B).
A very high PSA with back pain indicates metastatic prostate cancer, usually sclerotic (image G). The book also accepts the lytic lesions in image H.
Progressive spinal stiffness and breathlessness from chest-wall rigidity, with a family history of HLA-B27-linked disease, fit ankylosing spondylitis (image D).
Image D is a barium swallow showing a dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly to a narrow lower segment, the appearance of achalasia.
Image H, a chest film, shows a gas-filled stomach behind the heart giving a double left heart border: a large hiatus hernia.
Three images show malignancy: a contracted 'leather bottle' stomach (A), an irregular malignant gastric ulcer (E) and an apple-core colonic stricture (I). All are credited.
Image F shows dilated small-bowel loops with valvulae conniventes and multiple fluid levels, i.e. small-bowel obstruction.
Image C, a double-contrast enema, shows loss of haustra with pseudopolyps, i.e. chronic ulcerative colitis.
Image G shows numerous barium-filled outpouchings along the colon: diverticulosis.
Gas under the diaphragm (image B) is expected for a day or two after laparoscopy because of the insufflated gas. In a well patient with a soft abdomen, reassure and observe.
Weight loss, constipation, iron-deficiency anaemia and a cholestatic rise in ALP suggest colonic cancer (image I, apple-core lesion) with liver metastases.
A barium study showing diverticula (image G) gave the benign answer, and fibre plus laxatives improved her symptoms. Cancer still needs excluding with this history.
Previous abdominal surgery, colicky pain, profuse vomiting and tinkling bowel sounds indicate adhesive small-bowel obstruction (image F).
Progressive lower dysphagia needing fluids to wash food down, with regurgitation of undigested meals, fits achalasia (image D).
Image I shows a short, irregular circumferential narrowing with shouldered edges, the 'apple core' of a colonic carcinoma.
Image C shows a featureless tube without haustral folds ('lead pipe'), caused by chronic ulcerative colitis.
Image A shows a small, rigid, non-distensible stomach from diffuse tumour infiltration: linitis plastica.
Image D shows a dilated oesophagus with a smooth distal taper (bird's beak), typical of achalasia; Chagas' disease can mimic it.
Image F shows dilated small bowel (valvulae across the full width) and image J dilated large bowel (haustra); the book credits both F and J.
Image B shows free gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm, i.e. pneumoperitoneum, usually from a perforated viscus or recent surgery.
Post-prandial right upper quadrant pain with dyspepsia suggests biliary colic. Abdominal ultrasound is the first-line test for gallstones.
Sudden back pain with leg paralysis in a hypertensive smoker suggests an aortic dissection or aneurysm compromising spinal supply. A stable patient needs urgent CT angiography.
Sudden epigastric pain with generalised peritonism suggests a perforated viscus. An erect chest film looking for free gas, with abdominal films, is the next step.
Absolute constipation with gross distension suggests large-bowel obstruction. Plain abdominal and chest radiographs come first.
In a young woman with right iliac fossa pain and a past ovarian torsion, diagnostic laparoscopy can distinguish appendicitis from gynaecological causes and treat either.
Passive soiling starting after childbirth suggests obstetric injury to the anal sphincter. Endoanal ultrasound shows the defect.
New incontinence with looser, more frequent stools and mucus in an older man needs colorectal cancer excluding by colonoscopy.
Prolonged instrumental deliveries stretch the pudendal nerves. Sphincter weakness and urge incontinence then develop gradually over years.
Constant soiling in an immobile nursing-home resident usually reflects faecal impaction with overflow around the hard stool. Rectal examination confirms it.
Sudden cramps, nausea and frequent watery stools with urgency mean acute gastroenteritis has overwhelmed normal continence. It is self-limiting.
A reducible lump after straining, positioned above and medial to the pubic tubercle, is an inguinal hernia; femoral hernias sit below and lateral to it.
Painful bilateral groin nodes with dysuria and urethral discharge are reactive inguinal lymphadenopathy from a sexually transmitted infection.
A fluctuant femoral-triangle mass with hip pain on extension and constitutional symptoms suggests a tuberculous psoas abscess tracking down from the spine.
Small-bowel obstruction in an elderly woman with a small painful groin-crease swelling suggests a strangulated femoral hernia; these often go unnoticed.
A pulsatile groin mass after arterial puncture for angiography is a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm). Duplex ultrasound confirms it.
Early respiratory distress after thyroidectomy suggests upper airway obstruction, usually a neck haematoma compressing the trachea. Open the wound at the bedside if necessary.
Poor pain relief after abdominal surgery stops deep breathing and coughing. Day-1 breathlessness, low-grade fever and reduced basal breath sounds indicate basal atelectasis.
Bilateral fine crackles with breathlessness and no fever in a man with ischaemic heart disease suggest pulmonary oedema from fluid overload or a cardiac event.
Absent breath sounds at a base with reduced vocal resonance and an albumin of 20 g/l suggest a pleural effusion due to low oncotic pressure.
Severe pancreatitis followed by refractory hypoxaemia with bilateral diffuse infiltrates and no evidence of heart failure is ARDS.
Oliguria with abdominal distension, hypotension and tachycardia after aneurysm repair suggests bleeding, i.e. haemorrhagic shock.
Hypotension unresponsive to fluid challenges, pallor and 'indigestion' in a diabetic vasculopath suggest a silent MI causing cardiogenic shock.
Mildly reduced urine output in the first postoperative hours with stable observations is expected: the surgical stress response increases ADH and aldosterone.
Abrupt anuria with otherwise normal observations usually has a mechanical cause. Check for a full bladder (retention) or a blocked catheter first.
Sir James Paget described Paget's disease of the nipple and Paget's disease of bone.
John Snow pioneered ether and chloroform anaesthesia and traced cholera to the Broad Street pump, founding modern epidemiology.
Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups, making safe transfusion possible.
Theodor Billroth, working in Vienna, performed the first successful gastrectomies (Billroth I and II) and shaped formal surgical training.
William Halsted introduced rubber surgical gloves, the radical mastectomy and an inguinal hernia repair, and created the surgical residency system.
A feeding jejunostomy placed at oesophagectomy allows enteral feeding to start early, bypassing the fresh anastomosis.
Patients on peritoneal dialysis need to limit fluid, potassium and phosphate, so a low-volume, low-electrolyte diet is appropriate.
When unsafe swallowing after a stroke means feeding will be needed for more than about four weeks, a PEG tube is better tolerated than a nasogastric tube.
With under 100 cm of viable small bowel and a stoma, the gut cannot absorb enough, so parenteral (intravenous) nutrition is needed.
In severe acute pancreatitis, enteral feeding is preferred over TPN because it maintains gut integrity. Feeding beyond the duodenum by nasojejunal tube rests the pancreas.
Cord transection above the sympathetic outflow removes vasomotor tone. Hypotension with an inappropriately slow pulse despite fluids is neurogenic shock.
Penetrating chest trauma with raised neck veins, muffled heart sounds and hypotension is cardiac tamponade. This obstructive shock needs urgent decompression.
Sudden abdominal pain with hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria and weak femoral pulses suggests a ruptured aortic aneurysm causing haemorrhagic shock.
Fever, confusion, tachypnoea and hypotension with warm peripheries days after surgery indicate septic (distributive) shock.
Pelvic and open femoral fractures plus a haemothorax can lose litres of blood. Worsening tachycardia and hypotension are haemorrhage, not a drug reaction.
During the primary survey, the standard trauma films (chest, pelvis and lateral cervical spine) are the first imaging adjuncts.
With flank bruising and abdominal pain, a FAST scan at the bedside quickly looks for free intraperitoneal fluid.
A haemodynamically stable patient with free fluid should have CT to define the solid-organ injury. Many can then be managed non-operatively.
Renewed instability with known intra-abdominal blood means ongoing haemorrhage. He needs an emergency laparotomy, not more imaging.

where.title: Investigation and management of gastrointestinal disease

items.explanation: Chronic constipation without bleeding, where endoscopy failed because of faeces, can be assessed with a double-contrast barium enema; CT colonography is the modern equivalent.
An actively bleeding ulcer with a visible vessel needs endoscopic haemostasis: adrenaline injection combined with a second modality (thermal or clips).
Long-standing bright-red blood on the paper in a young, well man with a normal haemoglobin suggests a low anorectal source. Rigid proctosigmoidoscopy is the first step.
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in a man needs both upper and lower GI tract examined (bidirectional endoscopy) to find occult blood loss or cancer.
Ongoing bleeding with haemodynamic instability after negative endoscopy needs mesenteric angiography, which can locate the bleed and embolise it.

Ectopic ACTH from a lung tumour produces so much cortisol that its mineralocorticoid action drives renal potassium loss. Severe isolated hypokalaemia, with sodium, urea and creatinine near normal, is the expected pattern and explains the weakness.

Pulmonary tuberculosis is a recognised trigger of SIADH. Retained free water dilutes the sodium while potassium and renal function stay normal; volume status, thyroid, adrenal and drug causes must be excluded first.
Blood in the gut is digested and absorbed as a protein load that is converted to urea, and hypovolaemia adds a pre-renal component. Urea therefore rises far out of proportion to creatinine.

Every value is implausibly low, the signature of a sample diluted by infusion fluid drawn upstream of a drip. Repeat it from the other arm or after pausing the infusion rather than acting on the numbers.

Dual blockade with an ACE inhibitor plus an angiotensin receptor blocker suppresses aldosterone and glomerular perfusion, so potassium climbs and renal function worsens, especially in frail patients with heart failure. Either result set showing hyperkalaemia with renal impairment is accepted.
Antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel promote slow upper gastrointestinal blood loss. Chronic loss exhausts iron stores and gives a microcytic anaemia, often with a reactive rise in platelets.

Phenytoin is among the drugs (with chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, carbimazole and gold) that can cause marrow failure. A hypocellular, fatty marrow with pancytopenia and few reticulocytes defines aplastic anaemia.

Myeloma cells replace the marrow and suppress all three lineages, while the paraprotein raises the ESR and causes renal impairment and hypercalcaemia. Seek a monoclonal band, urinary light chains and lytic lesions on plain films.

In thalassaemia trait the MCV is far lower than the mild anaemia would predict and ferritin is normal, which argues against iron deficiency. Haemoglobin electrophoresis confirms it and relatives should be tested.
Mycoplasma infection induces cold-reacting IgM antibodies that bind red cells, giving a Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia; the reticulocytosis explains the raised MCV.

Heavy asbestos exposure causes a fibrosis that, unlike most pneumoconioses, favours the lung bases; pleural plaques mark the exposure. Impaired gas exchange gives hypoxaemia with a normal or low CO2 (type 1 failure).

Obesity hypoventilation (Pickwickian) syndrome combines nocturnal hypoventilation with obstructive apnoeas, so CO2 is retained and bicarbonate rises in compensation. Morning headache and daytime sleepiness follow, and non-invasive ventilation plus weight loss help.

Alveolar flooding from acute left heart failure causes hypoxaemia without CO2 retention, and poor perfusion adds a lactic metabolic acidosis. Perihilar 'bat-wing' shadowing is the classic film appearance.
An atypical pneumonia with dry cough, hyponatraemia, mild renal impairment and marked hypoxaemia suggests Legionella, and a positive urinary antigen confirms it quickly.
Clubbing, fine basal crackles and a restrictive defect fit idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive fibrosis without an identifiable cause. It causes type 1 failure until late disease.
Malignant ascites in a woman with a very high CA-125 and adenocarcinoma cells in the fluid points to ovarian cancer with peritoneal spread; CA-125 is better for monitoring than diagnosis.

A dilated, failing left ventricle after old anterior infarction has progressed to right-sided failure: high venous pressure with functional tricuspid regurgitation drives fluid into the abdomen and legs. A negative Kussmaul's sign argues against constriction.
Occupational asbestos exposure predisposes to mesothelioma of the peritoneum as well as the pleura. Diffuse peritoneal infiltration with ascites needs biopsy, and treatment is usually palliative.
Systemic symptoms, anaemia and multiple round 'cannonball' lung deposits suggest renal-cell carcinoma, which spreads through the bloodstream. Renal imaging will show the primary.

In someone from a high-prevalence population, terminal ileitis with abdominal lymphadenopathy should suggest gastrointestinal and peritoneal tuberculosis before Crohn's disease. It responds to standard antituberculous therapy.

Oestrogen-containing contraception raises clotting risk and can cause cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Raised pressure (papilloedema) with an unremarkable plain scan, and a filling defect in the sinus on contrast imaging (the delta sign), confirm it; treat with anticoagulation.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects young overweight women, causing headache and visual blurring with normal imaging. It can threaten vision, and weight loss and diuretics such as acetazolamide help.
Meningism with a CSF showing lymphocytes but normal glucose and protein fits viral meningitis. It is usually self-limiting and managed supportively once bacterial causes are excluded.

A crescent-shaped collection over the hemisphere that is the same density as brain, with midline shift, is a subacute subdural haematoma. Its mass effect can mimic a stroke and needs urgent neurosurgical referral.

New headache in an older person with shoulder girdle pain and a very high ESR indicates giant-cell arteritis with polymyalgia. Start high-dose steroids at once to protect vision, then confirm with temporal artery biopsy.

Low calcium with high alkaline phosphatase suggests osteomalacia, and hypocalcaemia makes nerves hyperexcitable: tapping the facial nerve causes facial twitching (Chvostek) and an inflated arm cuff produces carpal spasm (Trousseau). Both signs are credited.

Free aortic regurgitation creates a wide pulse pressure, which causes head nodding with each beat (de Musset), visible nail-bed pulsation (Quincke) and a to-and-fro femoral bruit on light compression (Duroziez). All three are credited.
An enlarged left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node in gastric cancer is Troisier's sign, reflecting lymphatic spread via the thoracic duct.
Haemorrhagic pancreatitis tracks blood to the periumbilical skin (Cullen) and the flanks (Grey Turner), and fat necrosis binds calcium so Trousseau's sign may appear. All three are credited.
When gentle sideways pressure makes apparently normal skin slide off, Nikolsky's sign is positive, typical of pemphigus vulgaris, where the epidermal cells lose their adhesion to each other.
Appendicitis that has been contained by omentum and adjacent bowel forms a tender, ill-defined mass, sometimes with an abscess. Many are managed first with intravenous antibiotics.

Recurrent attacks of pain and diarrhoea with weight loss over years point to terminal ileal Crohn's disease, where inflamed, matted loops form a tender mass. Medical treatment and bowel imaging come before surgery.
B symptoms with groin nodes suggest lymphoma, so a vague iliac fossa mass is most likely a nodal mass along the iliac chain. Biopsy and staging CT are needed.
A large mass arising from the pelvis, whose lower edge cannot be felt, in an older woman is ovarian cancer until proven otherwise.

Right-sided colon cancers bleed slowly and rarely obstruct early, so iron-deficiency anaemia with a hard mobile right iliac fossa mass in an older man indicates caecal carcinoma. Colonoscopy is the investigation.

Single-duct bloodstained discharge without a lump in a woman younger than the usual cancer age typically comes from an intraduct papilloma, a benign, vascular growth in a major duct. Excision of the duct is diagnostic and curative.
Duct ectasia affects women around and after the menopause: dilated subareolar ducts fill with thick secretions and periductal fibrosis pulls the nipple into a slit.
Galactorrhoea and subfertility in a young woman, with a bitemporal field defect, indicate a prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma pressing on the optic chiasm.
In an older woman, heavily bloodstained discharge from one breast must be presumed malignant and assessed by examination, imaging and biopsy.
Bilateral discharge from several ducts with long-standing breast pain fits fibrocystic change, a benign exaggeration of the normal cyclical response of breast tissue.

Renal-cell carcinoma can secrete renin, erythropoietin and PTH-related peptide, explaining hypertension, polycythaemia and hypercalcaemia, and lung metastases explain the breathlessness, even without the classic flank mass.

Facial oedema with haematuria and proteinuria about two weeks after a streptococcal throat infection indicates post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Treatment is supportive and children usually recover fully.

Painless visible haematuria with weight loss in an older man is urothelial (transitional-cell) bladder cancer until cystoscopy proves otherwise; it is far commoner than the squamous type linked with stones.
Anticoagulation after a recent pulmonary embolism explains the bleeding; check the INR. Haematuria on anticoagulants can still unmask a lesion, so further investigation may be needed.

Loin-to-groin colic in a restless patient with microscopic haematuria indicates a ureteric stone. A normal plain film does not exclude it because some stones are not radio-opaque; CT is now the usual test.
Loss of lactobacilli with anaerobic overgrowth gives a thin, grey, fishy discharge, vaginal pH above 4.5 and epithelial cells studded with bacteria (clue cells): bacterial vaginosis.
Primary genital herpes produces a flu-like prodrome followed by several painful vesicles and tender inguinal nodes, unlike the solitary painless chancre of syphilis.

Gram-negative intracellular diplococci identify Neisseria gonorrhoeae, acquired from the mother's cervix during delivery. Chlamydia also causes neonatal conjunctivitis but is not visible on Gram stain.
Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest cause of both non-specific urethritis in men and pelvic inflammatory disease in women; fever with cervical excitation fits the latter.
A motile, flagellated protozoon on wet-mount microscopy is diagnostic of Trichomonas vaginalis, which causes an offensive, often frothy discharge.
A malignant tumour made of glandular cells is by definition an adenocarcinoma, the usual type in the colon and rectum; distal tumours tend to present with bleeding and altered bowel habit.
Keratinising atypical cells on cytology and an invasive cervical mass point to squamous-cell carcinoma, which accounts for most cervical cancers.
Paget's disease of bone predisposes older adults to secondary osteosarcoma, often in the pelvis or femur, seen as a destructive lesion with patchy osteoid mineralisation.
A pleural mass decades after shipyard asbestos exposure, with both epithelial and sarcomatoid components on histology, is malignant mesothelioma.
A smooth, mobile, well-circumscribed solid lump with benign cytology in a young woman is a fibroadenoma, a benign mixed tumour of glandular and stromal tissue.

The book's key is the T4 vertebral body, which is where the plane of the sternal angle meets the spine and divides the superior from the inferior mediastinum. The xiphisternal joint itself lies at about T9, so the item appears to mean the sternal angle.
The aortic arch begins and ends at the level of the sternal angle, so it lies entirely within the superior mediastinum, arching over the left lung root.
The right phrenic nerve runs down on the lateral surface of the superior vena cava, the right atrium and the IVC to reach the diaphragm.
The oesophageal hiatus lies at about T10, in a sling of the right crus; the inferior vena cava passes at T8 and the aorta at T12.
The groove between trachea and oesophagus on the left carries the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which loops under the aortic arch as a branch of the left vagus.

where.title: Cutaneous innervation of the upper limb

items.explanation: The median nerve supplies the palmar skin of the lateral three and a half digits, and its digital branches curl round to supply their nail beds.
Brachioradialis inserts at the radial styloid, where the skin is supplied by the forearm's lateral cutaneous nerve, the sensory continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve.
The pisiform lies on the medial side of the wrist, in skin supplied by the palmar cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve.
Skin over the deltoid insertion (the regimental badge area) is supplied by the axillary nerve's upper lateral cutaneous branch, which is tested after shoulder dislocation.
The common flexor origin is the medial epicondyle, where the overlying skin is supplied by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm from the medial cord.
Productive cough, pleuritic pain and localised crackles fit lobar pneumonia; middle lobe consolidation blurs the right heart border on a frontal film.

Sudden deterioration with hypoxia and shock after chest trauma is a tension pneumothorax, seen as a hyperlucent hemithorax without lung markings and mediastinal shift away. Decompress immediately, then insert a drain.
Renal-cell carcinoma spreads through the blood and characteristically produces multiple round, well-defined lung deposits (cannonball metastases).
A lung mass in a smoker with cushingoid features and profound hypokalaemia indicates bronchial carcinoma secreting ACTH, most often small-cell.
Bulky mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes are typical of lymphoma, and prior Epstein-Barr infection is linked with Hodgkin's lymphoma. Staging CT should follow.

Exertional angina and syncope with a narrow pulse pressure and LVH indicate severe aortic stenosis. Its systolic ejection murmur may follow an ejection click, and the stiff, pressure-loaded ventricle adds a fourth heart sound. All three options are credited.

A large anterior infarct leaves a failing, stiff left ventricle: rapid filling of the overloaded ventricle gives a third sound and atrial contraction into the non-compliant ventricle gives a fourth, producing a gallop. Both are credited.

A collapsing pulse and head nodding indicate severe aortic regurgitation, heard as an early diastolic murmur best heard along the left sternal border. The regurgitant jet can also impede mitral opening, producing an Austin Flint mid-diastolic rumble; both are credited.

Atrial fibrillation with a small-volume pulse and a tapping, undisplaced apex after rheumatic fever indicates mitral stenosis: an opening snap then a low mid-diastolic rumble at the apex. A shorter gap between S2 and the snap means tighter stenosis.

Mitral valve prolapse classically gives a mid-systolic click as the leaflets billow back, then a late systolic murmur once they leak. Non-specific T-wave changes are a recognised association; both options are credited.

Pernicious anaemia, often seen with other autoimmune conditions such as vitiligo, causes B12 deficiency with marked macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils and sometimes low white cells and platelets.
A very high count made almost entirely of mature lymphocytes, with smudge cells on the film and painless nodes in an older adult, is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
Gastric cancer, suggested by weight loss, early satiety and a Virchow's node, bleeds slowly and produces iron-deficiency anaemia with a low MCV and normal white cells.
Bone pain, recurrent infections, hypercalcaemia and a very high ESR indicate myeloma. Marrow infiltration causes pancytopenia, and excess immunoglobulin makes red cells stack into rouleaux.

Itch after bathing, plethora and splenomegaly with a raised red cell mass indicate polycythaemia vera. A high haematocrit with raised neutrophils and platelets fits this myeloproliferative disorder, usually driven by a JAK2 mutation.
Fever with signs of fluid on the side of a recently drained pneumothorax suggests infection of the pleural space. An empyema needs drainage plus antibiotics that cover staphylococci.

Dullness with reduced breath sounds, fremitus and vocal resonance indicates fluid. With weight loss and Horner's syndrome this is likely a malignant effusion from an apical lung tumour; send fluid for cytology.
Clubbing and fine basal crackles that persist after coughing indicate pulmonary fibrosis, here asbestosis, with plaques confirming the exposure.

Hyper-resonance with absent breath sounds and fremitus, but a central trachea and normal saturation, indicates a simple pneumothorax rather than tension. Aspiration is the first step if treatment is needed.
Dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal fremitus indicates consolidated lung, here an acute community-acquired pneumonia.
Violaceous skin and palatal lesions in someone with probable advanced HIV are Kaposi's sarcoma, a vascular tumour driven by HHV-8; the neurological picture suggests a second opportunistic process.
White corrugated plaques on the side of the tongue that cannot be scraped off, in a person with HIV, are oral hairy leukoplakia caused by Epstein-Barr virus; candida plaques would wipe away.
Coeliac disease commonly causes recurrent aphthous ulcers, and malabsorbed iron, folate or B12 leave a smooth, atrophic tongue. Both options are credited.
Long-standing, painless, bilateral white lacy streaks on the buccal mucosa are typical of oral lichen planus, which does not rub off.
Severe malnutrition causes vitamin C deficiency, with bleeding around hair follicles and from the gums, while coexisting B-vitamin and iron deficiency causes atrophic glossitis. Both are credited.

Weak hip abductors from painful arthritis cannot hold the pelvis level, so the opposite side drops when standing on the affected leg (Trendelenburg), and pain shortens the stance phase (antalgic gait). Both are credited.

Dupuytren's contracture and gynaecomastia suggest alcohol-related liver disease, and alcohol damages the cerebellum. Past-pointing and dysdiadochokinesia confirm cerebellar dysfunction, giving a broad-based unsteady gait.
A high-stepping, stamping gait from lost proprioception is sensory ataxia. With anaemia, think of B12 deficiency damaging peripheral nerves or the dorsal columns (subacute combined degeneration).
Resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity and an expressionless face indicate parkinsonism, with short shuffling steps that hurry forward (festination).
Long-term corticosteroids cause a proximal myopathy, so rising from a chair and holding the arms up are difficult and the pelvis rolls from side to side when walking (waddling gait).

A glandular-fever-like illness with a negative heterophile (Paul-Bunnell) test raises toxoplasmosis or CMV; specific IgM serology confirms Toxoplasma, which is usually self-limiting in healthy people.
Bilateral hilar nodes with erythema nodosum, raised serum ACE and hypercalcaemia in a young adult indicate sarcoidosis.
Widespread firm, rubbery nodes with a biopsy dominated by large abnormal B cells indicate non-Hodgkin lymphoma; most are of B-cell origin.
Sore throat, fever and tender cervical nodes with atypical mononuclear cells on the film and rising specific IgM indicate Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis.
Generalised lymphadenopathy, oral thrush, lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia in someone from a high-prevalence region indicate HIV infection. Test after consent, with a CD4 count and viral load.

Months of dyspepsia and weight loss, then vomiting with a succussion splash, indicate pyloric obstruction, likely from gastric cancer. Losing gastric juice causes hypokalaemia and pre-renal uraemia, which must be corrected first.
Fever, cramps and diarrhoea after foreign travel, following a short prodrome, suggest bacterial gastroenteritis such as Campylobacter, Salmonella or E. coli.
Colicky central pain, distension and bilious vomiting indicate small-bowel obstruction, and a tender groin lump in an elderly woman suggests an incarcerated femoral hernia as the cause.

Massive tympanitic distension with faeculent vomiting and preceding weight loss, without hernias or scars, suggests large-bowel obstruction from a colorectal cancer, with stagnant contents refluxing back into the small bowel.
Epigastric pain boring through to the back with persistent retching in a heavy drinker indicates acute pancreatitis; a raised amylase or lipase confirms it.
Progressive one-sided sensorineural deafness and tinnitus, plus loss of the corneal reflex and facial weakness, point to a cerebellopontine angle tumour, usually a vestibular schwannoma.
Glue ear, from eustachian tube dysfunction, leaves a dull, retracted drum and a flat tympanogram; in a young child the hearing loss can delay speech.

A new one-sided middle ear effusion in an adult, with neck nodes and a postnasal lesion, suggests nasopharyngeal carcinoma blocking the eustachian tube. Always examine the postnasal space in this situation.
When the ear itself is normal, earache is often referred through the trigeminal nerve from the teeth or jaw joint; an impacted wisdom tooth is the source here.
Attacks of vertigo lasting hours, with fluctuating sensorineural deafness and tinnitus that worsens beforehand, are typical of Meniere's disease, caused by endolymphatic hydrops.

where.title: Head injury and the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

items.explanation: Spontaneous eye opening, orientated speech and obeying commands score 4 + 5 + 6 = 15. A probable depressed skull fracture still needs CT despite the normal score. (The options run A to L with no D.)
Eyes opening to pain (2), confused speech (4) and localising pain (5) total 11. Collapse after a lucid interval suggests an extradural haematoma.
No eye, verbal or motor response gives the minimum score of 3, here reflecting severe diffuse brain injury.
No eye opening (1), no speech (1) and extension to pain (2) total 4, which implies very severe brain injury.
Eyes opening to voice (3), inappropriate words (3) and obeying commands (6) total 12. Panda eyes and CSF-stained nasal leak suggest a base-of-skull fracture.
Obesity, hirsutism and infrequent periods with a raised LH:FSH ratio, high-normal testosterone and low SHBG (so more free androgen) indicate polycystic ovary syndrome.
Very low body weight switches off hypothalamic GnRH release, so FSH and LH are low and periods stop; prolactin and pelvic imaging are normal.
Severe period pain and deep dyspareunia with a fixed retroverted uterus in a woman in her thirties suggest endometriosis.
Short stature, webbed neck and primary amenorrhoea with high gonadotrophins and low oestradiol indicate Turner's syndrome, in which the ovaries are only fibrous streaks.
Long-standing diabetes with vascular and neuropathic complications commonly causes erectile dysfunction, which may go unmentioned; the female partner's assessment is normal.
White oesophageal plaques with both yeasts and hyphae on biopsy indicate Candida; Aspergillus does not form yeasts. Chemotherapy predisposes to it.
Foamy alveolar exudate containing cup-shaped organisms on silver stain is diagnostic of Pneumocystis (now P. jirovecii) pneumonia in advanced HIV.
Enlarged cells with 'owl's eye' intranuclear inclusions are the hallmark of cytomegalovirus, which reactivates in advanced AIDS to cause colitis, retinitis and oesophagitis.
Warts on the hands and cervix with CIN in a transplant recipient reflect human papillomavirus, which persists and progresses faster under immunosuppression.
Profuse watery diarrhoea in HIV with tiny organisms stuck to the small-bowel surface indicates Cryptosporidium parvum, identifiable on biopsy or on a modified acid-fast stool stain.
Tamoxifen acts as a partial oestrogen agonist on the endometrium, increasing gland numbers; crowded, proliferating glands are hyperplasia.
Replacement of the ciliated columnar bronchial lining by stratified squamous epithelium in a smoker is squamous metaplasia, an adaptive change that can progress to dysplasia.
Weeks of immobility shrink skeletal muscle fibres, producing disuse atrophy.
A stroke with a necrotic area in the opposite hemisphere is most likely a cerebral infarct: tissue death from loss of blood supply.
Chronic lung disease raises pulmonary vascular resistance, so right ventricular muscle cells enlarge to meet the extra workload: hypertrophy, culminating in cor pulmonale.
Muffled heart sounds, an impalpable apex and a high JVP after a viral illness suggest a large pericardial effusion, seen as an enlarged, globular heart shadow.
Malar flush and a rumbling apical diastolic murmur after rheumatic fever indicate mitral stenosis; the enlarged left atrium straightens the left heart border.
An untreated large anterior STEMI can cause acute left ventricular failure, shown by alveolar oedema, upper-lobe venous diversion and effusions on the film.
Decades of copious purulent sputum with haemoptysis indicate bronchiectasis, seen as thickened, dilated airways (tramlines and ring shadows).
Tearing interscapular pain with unequal arm blood pressures indicates thoracic aortic dissection, often with a widened mediastinum; CT angiography confirms it.

where.title: Innervation of the muscles of the upper limb

items.explanation: Serratus anterior is supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) on the medial wall of the axilla; injury causes winging of the scapula.
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm muscles: coracobrachialis, biceps and brachialis.
Extensor carpi radialis longus, like brachioradialis, is supplied by the main radial nerve above the elbow, before the posterior interosseous branch arises.
The median nerve runs between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres and supplies it.
Flexor carpi ulnaris is supplied by the ulnar nerve, which passes between its two heads at the elbow, along with the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus.

Exertional angina with left ventricular dysfunction, managed so far with an antiplatelet and as-needed nitrate only, should next receive a cardioselective beta-blocker such as bisoprolol, which relieves angina and improves survival in heart failure.

Ischaemic ST depression with a negative troponin is unstable angina. Adding clopidogrel to aspirin (dual antiplatelet therapy) reduces further events, at the cost of more bleeding, especially in the elderly.

Refractory ischaemia despite heparin, nitrates and anti-anginals while awaiting PCI warrants a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor such as abciximab, which blocks the final common pathway of platelet aggregation.

An early anterior STEMI needs reperfusion; when thrombolysis is used, a fibrin-specific agent such as tPA is preferred here because streptokinase can worsen hypotension. Primary PCI is the modern first choice where available.

Angina persisting on a beta-blocker needs a second anti-anginal; the book chooses nicorandil, a potassium-channel opener. Current guidance would equally accept a calcium-channel blocker or long-acting nitrate, plus referral for angiography.
Inflammatory back pain radiating to the buttocks in a young man, with anterior uveitis and sacroiliac erosions, indicates ankylosing spondylitis, strongly associated with HLA-B27.
Back pain with pancytopenia, purpura and a very high ESR in an older man suggests myeloma with vertebral lytic deposits; look for a paraprotein, urinary light chains and renal impairment.
Fever with destruction of two adjacent vertebrae and the disc between them in a homeless man suggests spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease), which can form a cold abscess and compress the cord.
New back pain months after resecting a colon cancer suggests skeletal spread; colorectal deposits in bone are usually lytic.
Coarsened trabeculae with a thickened cortex in the pelvis of an older man are typical of Paget's disease, which causes bone pain with a raised alkaline phosphatase.
Acute hepatitis A, spread faeco-orally and linked with shellfish from contaminated water, gives transaminases in the thousands with a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; specific IgM confirms it.
Gilbert's syndrome reduces bilirubin conjugation, so stress or fasting, such as after surgery, produces a mild, mainly unconjugated rise with all other liver tests normal.
A very high alkaline phosphatase with a normal gamma-GT and normal transaminases comes from bone rather than liver, as in Paget's disease.
Muscle breakdown releases AST along with creatine kinase, so a high AST with a normal ALT and otherwise normal tests points to rhabdomyolysis rather than liver injury.

A pancreatic head tumour blocks the common bile duct, giving painless jaundice with conjugated bilirubin and a cholestatic pattern: very high alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT with only a modest transaminase rise.

Severe abdominal pain with tachycardia and hypertension after an alcohol binge, with essentially normal bloods including amylase, suggests acute intermittent porphyria; alcohol and many drugs trigger attacks.
Fever, a positive Murphy's sign and a cholestatic picture in an overweight woman indicate acute cholecystitis from gallstones; ultrasound confirms the stones and duct size.
Small-bowel obstruction in a very elderly woman with localised groin tenderness suggests an incarcerated femoral hernia, which is easily missed and needs urgent surgery.
In decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis with ascites, pain and encephalopathy, an ascitic white count above 250 per cubic millimetre (neutrophils) confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Pain after meals in a smoker with coronary and peripheral arterial disease, with normal endoscopy and bloods, suggests chronic mesenteric ischaemia (intestinal angina), confirmed by angiography.
Progressive confusion and a new limb weakness developing over days after a fall in an elderly person suggest a subdural haematoma; by ten days it may be the same density as brain on CT.
Confusion and diarrhoea with hyponatraemia, lymphopenia and hypoxaemia despite a near-normal film suggest an atypical pneumonia such as Legionella.
SSRIs such as paroxetine commonly cause SIADH and hyponatraemia in older people, presenting with confusion that resolves when the drug is stopped.
Adding an ACE inhibitor to diuretics, including spironolactone, can precipitate renal failure in an older patient; confusion, hiccups and muscle twitching are features of uraemia.
Chlorpropamide is a very long-acting sulphonylurea that accumulates in the elderly, causing recurrent hypoglycaemia; sweating and confusion that reverse with glucagon confirm it.
Tender red nodules over the shins are erythema nodosum, a panniculitis; the oral contraceptive pill is a recognised trigger, along with streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, TB and IBD.
Pustules that break down into an expanding necrotic ulcer on the shin are pyoderma gangrenosum; look for associated IBD, inflammatory arthritis or a haematological disorder.
Target lesions appearing after starting a drug such as trimethoprim indicate erythema multiforme; mucosal involvement suggests the more severe Stevens-Johnson spectrum.
Flaccid superficial blisters that rupture to leave raw areas, with mouth involvement, indicate pemphigus vulgaris, caused by IgG against adhesion molecules between epidermal cells.
A granulomatous skin plaque containing acid-fast bacilli in a patient with active pulmonary disease is lupus vulgaris, a form of cutaneous tuberculosis.
Severe pain on defecation with bright-red blood after childbirth is typical of an acute anal fissure, often too tender to examine; topical GTN or diltiazem usually heals it.
Weeks of bloody diarrhoea with raised inflammatory markers and anaemia in a young adult is most likely ulcerative colitis.
Recurrent painless dark-red bleeding in an elderly woman with long-standing constipation and left-sided pain fits diverticular bleeding.
An ulcer with a raised, everted irregular edge at the anal verge is anal cancer, usually squamous and linked with HPV; chemoradiotherapy is the first-line treatment.
Recurrent painless bleeding in a very elderly patient with normal endoscopy and contrast studies suggests angiodysplasia, best located by angiography during active bleeding.
A Monteggia injury is a proximal ulnar fracture with dislocation of the radial head; the Galeazzi is its mirror image, a distal radial fracture with distal radioulnar dislocation.
The Salter-Harris system classifies fractures through the growth plate in children; higher grades carry more risk of growth disturbance.
Ankle fractures of the fibula and tibial malleoli are traditionally called Pott's fractures, now graded by the Weber system.
Garden grades intracapsular femoral neck fractures: grade II is complete but undisplaced.
An intra-articular fracture-subluxation at the base of the thumb metacarpal is a Bennett's fracture, which is unstable.
A dehydrated, nil-by-mouth patient with a hot, tender parotid has acute bacterial (usually staphylococcal) parotitis caused by reduced salivary flow.
Dry eyes and mouth with salivary swelling and lymphadenopathy in a young man with a negative autoantibody screen suggest HIV-associated salivary disease rather than Sjogren's syndrome.
Pain and swelling of the submandibular gland at mealtimes indicate a stone obstructing the duct; most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland.
A painless, smooth parotid lump with normal facial nerve function in middle age is most likely a pleomorphic adenoma, the commonest salivary tumour.
Rapid growth, pain and facial palsy in a long-standing parotid lump signal malignant change; adenoid cystic carcinoma characteristically spreads along nerves.

Rupturing membranes with a high head and excess liquor lets the cord slip past the presenting part; sudden fetal bradycardia without bleeding means cord prolapse. Knee-chest positioning relieves compression until urgent delivery.
No cervical change over four hours in a first labour usually reflects weak or inco-ordinate contractions (uterine inertia), treated by augmentation.
Meconium seen after the membranes rupture moves a low-risk labour into a higher-risk category, so continuous CTG with a low threshold for fetal blood sampling is advised.
More than four or five contractions every ten minutes on oxytocin is hyperstimulation, which starves the fetus of oxygen between contractions; stopping the infusion is the first step.
Arrest in the late first stage in a multiparous woman with strong contractions is most often due to an occipito-posterior malposition; oxytocin is avoided if obstruction is possible.
Escherichia coli, a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus from bowel flora, causes most urinary tract infections, usually ascending via the urethra.
Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus and a leading cause of bacterial meningitis; the pneumococcus is the Gram-positive alternative.
Streptococcus pneumoniae, an alpha-haemolytic Gram-positive diplococcus, causes most lobar pneumonia.
Toxin-producing Clostridium difficile, an anaerobic Gram-positive spore-forming bacillus, causes pseudomembranous colitis, typically after antibiotics.

Helicobacter pylori is a curved, flagellated, urease-producing organism living in gastric mucus that causes most chronic gastritis and peptic ulcers; its urease underlies the breath and rapid biopsy tests.

Rheumatic fever scars the mitral valve, enlarging the left atrium and straightening the left heart border, and its pancarditis can cause a pericardial effusion with a globular heart. Both images are credited.
Long-standing hypertension leads to left ventricular failure and also predisposes to thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection. Both images are credited.
Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymic enlargement and thymoma in the anterior mediastinum; the book matches it to the image with the thymic 'sail' shadow.
Dressler's syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks after infarction; an accompanying effusion enlarges the cardiac outline into a globular shape.
Severe childhood respiratory infections such as measles or whooping cough damage airway walls and can lead to bronchiectasis later in life.
Iodine deficiency causes a large multinodular goitre, which can extend into the thorax and push the trachea aside.
The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve exits the middle cranial fossa via the foramen rotundum to reach the pterygopalatine fossa.
Parotid secretomotor fibres travel in the glossopharyngeal nerve via the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion, then reach the gland with the auriculotemporal nerve.
Lateral rectus, which abducts the eye, is supplied by the abducent (sixth) nerve.
Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus; the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles receive the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Taste from the front of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani, part of the facial nerve, to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the facial nerve; it keeps food between the teeth while chewing.
The mylohyoid muscles form the floor of the mouth, running from the mylohyoid line of the mandible to a midline raphe and the body of the hyoid.
Hyoglossus lies deep to the submandibular duct, lingual nerve and hypoglossal nerve, all of which run on its lateral surface.
Masseter's superficial part arises from the lower border of the zygomatic arch and inserts on the outer face of the mandibular ramus and angle.
Lateral pterygoid inserts into the articular disc and capsule of the temporomandibular joint and the neck of the mandible, pulling them forward to open the jaw.

Typical anginal pain with T-wave changes and a positive stress test but entirely normal coronary arteries suggests cardiac syndrome X (microvascular angina), a diagnosis of exclusion that is commoner in women.
Posterior infarction appears as a mirror image in V1-V3: horizontal ST depression with tall, dominant R waves. It is managed as a STEMI, and posterior leads V7-V9 reveal the ST elevation.

Sharp pain eased by sitting forward with widespread concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation outside a single coronary territory indicates acute pericarditis; a raised troponin implies myocardial involvement (myopericarditis).
Prolonged ischaemic pain with T-wave inversion but no ST elevation, plus a raised troponin, is a non-ST-elevation MI; diabetes can make the symptoms less typical.
ST elevation in II, III and aVF reflects an inferior STEMI, usually from right coronary occlusion; epigastric pain is a common presentation of inferior ischaemia.
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci on a urethral swab with an acutely swollen joint indicate disseminated gonococcal infection; the joint fluid itself is often culture-negative.
A hot knee alongside an apical pneumonia in an alcohol-dependent man suggests haematogenous tuberculous arthritis; aspirate the joint and culture for mycobacteria.
Arthritis with urethritis and conjunctivitis after chlamydial infection is reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome), which can recur with each new infection.
Weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals identify calcium pyrophosphate disease (pseudogout); allopurinol, started for presumed gout, does nothing to prevent it.
A haemarthrosis after a contact injury with a normal PT and reduced factor VIII indicates haemophilia A, an X-linked disorder; mild deficiency may only show itself after trauma.
Pain before meals with belching, a positive urea breath test and iron-deficiency anaemia points to a bleeding duodenal ulcer; eradicate H. pylori with a PPI plus two antibiotics.
Iron-deficiency anaemia with weight loss, altered bowel habit, cholestatic liver tests and multiple liver lesions indicates colorectal cancer with hepatic metastases.
Macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia, a prolonged INR and low albumin suggest alcohol-related cirrhosis with portal hypertension, so a large fresh haematemesis is most likely variceal.
Left iliac fossa pain, high fever and leucocytosis in an older woman indicate acute diverticulitis, here complicated by bacteraemia and dehydration.
Occult blood loss with normal upper and lower endoscopy and an ileal lesion on a technetium scan, which highlights ectopic gastric mucosa, indicates a Meckel's diverticulum.
Bone pain and weight loss in an elderly man suggest metastatic prostate cancer; PSA is used for diagnosis, monitoring treatment and detecting relapse.
A pigmented lesion with satellite deposits and hard inguinal nodes is metastatic melanoma; tyrosinase, an enzyme of melanin synthesis, is the melanoma-related marker in this list.
A solitary liver mass in someone with chronic hepatitis C is likely hepatocellular carcinoma, in which alpha-fetoprotein is often markedly raised.
CA 19-9 is the marker used to monitor pancreatic cancer and to detect recurrence after resection.
CA 15-3 and CA 27.29 are both mucin (MUC1) antigens used to monitor breast cancer and detect recurrence or metastasis; both are credited.
Nystagmus, dysdiadochokinesia and past-pointing on one side localise to the cerebellar hemisphere on the same side; posterior fossa strokes may be missed on CT.
A palate pulled away from one side and a tongue deviating towards it indicate vagus and hypoglossal palsies on that side, localising to the medulla and causing dysarthria and dysphagia.
A homonymous hemianopia arises from a lesion behind the optic chiasm; with no new limb signs, the opposite occipital cortex is the likely site.
Pinpoint pupils and deep coma that do not respond to naloxone suggest a pontine lesion, which may be invisible on CT and shown only by MRI.
Burning or shooting pain in the limbs on the hemiparetic side after a stroke is central post-stroke (thalamic) pain, treated with neuropathic agents such as gabapentin.

A painless genital papule or ulcer followed by tender inguinal nodes, caused by an obligate intracellular organism (Chlamydia trachomatis L serovars) and cured by doxycycline, is lymphogranuloma venereum.
A painful, ragged, friable genital ulcer with Gram-negative coccobacilli is chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; suppurating nodes may follow.
A beefy, heaped-up ulcer with an encapsulated Gram-negative bacillus (Klebsiella granulomatis) after exposure in an endemic area is donovanosis (granuloma inguinale).
Multiple painful vulval ulcers with fever and myalgia are primary genital herpes; herpesviruses have an icosahedral capsid.
A painless genital ulcer weeks after exposure, with motile spirochaetes on dark-ground microscopy, is the chancre of primary syphilis.
Sudden severe right upper quadrant pain from a stone impacting in the cystic duct, without fever, is biliary colic; mild liver test changes are common.
Recurrent discomfort after meals with belching, normal liver tests and no fever fits chronic cholecystitis; confirm stones on ultrasound and offer elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Small-bowel obstruction in an elderly woman with no hernia may be gallstone ileus: a large stone enters the gut through a cholecystoenteric fistula and lodges in the terminal ileum.
Epigastric pain radiating to the back with a very high amylase and raised LDH indicates acute pancreatitis; gallstones are a leading cause in older people.
Severe cholecystitis with a tender palpable gallbladder and marked leucocytosis suggests the obstructed gallbladder has filled with pus (empyema), needing urgent drainage or surgery.
Shock with an effusion that drains blood after a stab wound indicates a haemothorax; at about 500 ml it falls short of the 1.5 litres that defines a massive haemothorax.
Sudden respiratory and circulatory collapse with hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds and distended neck veins indicates tension pneumothorax, needing immediate decompression.
Paradoxical movement of a chest wall segment after major blunt injury indicates a flail segment from ribs broken in two places; the underlying lung contusion drives the morbidity.

Hypotension with distended neck veins after a left chest stab wound, despite a working drain and equal breath sounds, suggests cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad); pericardiocentesis or thoracotomy is needed.
A high-speed deceleration injury with sternal tenderness and a widened mediastinum suggests a contained traumatic aortic rupture, requiring urgent CT angiography.
Unstable blunt abdominal trauma needs a full-length midline laparotomy for rapid access to every quadrant.
Open cholecystectomy uses a right subcostal (Kocher) incision; repeated adhesional obstruction makes a laparoscopic approach hazardous.
An emergency Caesarean is usually done through a low transverse suprapubic (Pfannenstiel) incision, which gives access to the lower uterine segment.
A bilateral subcostal (rooftop) incision gives wide exposure of the upper abdomen for liver transplantation.
Sigmoid and rectal resections are performed through a lower midline incision, which can be extended upwards if the splenic flexure must be mobilised.
GnRH analogues such as goserelin, given by injection or implant, first stimulate then desensitise pituitary receptors, switching off ovarian activity before IVF and causing menopausal symptoms.
Mefenamic acid, an NSAID, reduces menstrual loss and pain by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, but can provoke bronchospasm in asthma.
Long-term use of the combined pill substantially lowers the risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer by suppressing ovulation and endometrial proliferation.
Cyproterone acetate is an anti-androgen that improves acne and hirsutism; it is combined with oestrogen because it could feminise a male fetus.
After hysterectomy there is no endometrium to protect, so oestrogen alone is enough to treat vasomotor symptoms.
Hyper-resonance with absent breath sounds and reduced fremitus but a central trachea and normal saturation indicates a simple pneumothorax.
A patient in extremis with the trachea pushed away from a silent hemithorax has a tension pneumothorax.
Tracheal deviation towards the affected side with upper-zone dullness and reduced breath sounds in a cachectic patient indicates right upper lobe collapse, often from an obstructing carcinoma.
In a septic patient, axillary dullness with bronchial breathing and coarse crackles on the right indicate right middle lobe pneumonia.
Bronchial breathing and fine crackles confined to the apices, with a central trachea, suggest apical fibrosis, for example after tuberculosis.
Hepatitis C, an RNA flavivirus spread by blood, becomes chronic in most people and can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
SARS, first recognised in 2003, is caused by a coronavirus, an RNA virus with a crown-like fringe on electron microscopy.
Shingles is reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus from a sensory ganglion, causing a painful dermatomal vesicular rash.
Common warts are benign squamous papillomas caused by human papillomavirus.
Infectious mononucleosis is caused by Epstein-Barr virus, diagnosed by heterophile antibodies or specific IgM.
The cricopharyngeal part of the inferior constrictor arises from the side of the cricoid cartilage; the weak area above it (Killian's dehiscence) is where a pharyngeal pouch forms.
The anterior pillar of the fauces (palatoglossal arch) is formed by palatoglossus; palatopharyngeus forms the posterior pillar.
The middle constrictor arises from the greater horn of the hyoid and the stylohyoid ligament.
Above the superior constrictor, the pharyngobasilar fascia completes the pharyngeal wall, and the eustachian tube opens into the nasopharynx through this region.
Tensor veli palatini is the one palatal muscle innervated by the trigeminal (mandibular) nerve; the others receive the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus.

where.title: Muscle attachments in the upper limb

items.explanation: The lateral head of triceps arises from the posterior humerus above the radial groove.
Brachialis arises from the anterior lower half of the humerus and inserts into the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna.
Extensor carpi radialis longus arises from the lower part of the lateral supracondylar ridge, just below brachioradialis.
Pronator teres inserts into the roughened area in the middle of the lateral surface of the radius.
Flexor digitorum profundus tendons insert into the bases of the distal phalanges, whereas superficialis inserts on the middle phalanges.

Biventricular failure in a diabetic man with ECG evidence of old anterior damage (poor R-wave progression, conduction delay) and normal enzymes indicates chronic ischaemic cardiomyopathy rather than an acute event.

Fever, splinter haemorrhages and a new early diastolic murmur after a contaminated cannula indicate acute staphylococcal endocarditis destroying the aortic valve; the acute regurgitation precipitates left ventricular failure and may need urgent surgery.

Atrial fibrillation with a low-volume pulse and a soft apical mid-diastolic murmur indicate mitral stenosis; the loud parasternal pansystolic murmur is secondary tricuspid regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension.
