Faint heart sounds, low-voltage complexes and a JVP that rises on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign) in suspected tuberculosis suggest a tuberculous pericardial effusion compromising filling; drain it and give antituberculous therapy.
Clubbing, fixed basal crackles and severe hypoxaemia indicate pulmonary fibrosis; chronic hypoxic pulmonary hypertension then causes right heart failure (cor pulmonale).
Prostatism with a smoothly enlarged gland is usually benign hyperplasia, but a PSA is the test that helps exclude carcinoma before treatment is chosen.
Malar rash, heavy proteinuria, casts and renal failure in a young woman indicate lupus nephritis; anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are specific for SLE and track renal activity.

Haemoptysis with diffuse alveolar shadowing and rapidly progressive renal failure is a pulmonary-renal syndrome; antibodies against glomerular basement membrane (type IV collagen) confirm Goodpasture's disease.

Haematuria, renal failure and polycythaemia with a family history of kidney disease and fatal brain haemorrhage suggest autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, readily shown on renal ultrasound.
Back pain, pancytopenia, hypercalcaemia, renal failure and a very high ESR suggest myeloma; serum protein electrophoresis showing a monoclonal band, with urinary light chains, confirms it.
Oropharyngeal dysphagia with nasal regurgitation, dysarthria and limb weakness suggests bulbar involvement in motor neurone disease, a diagnosis made after excluding structural causes.
Painful dysphagia with white plaques at endoscopy after repeated antibiotics and steroids indicates oesophageal candidiasis, which responds to oral fluconazole.
A 'corkscrew' oesophagus with no structural lesion in a very elderly patient reflects age-related dysmotility (presbyoesophagus), a diagnosis of exclusion.
Progressive dysphagia for solids then liquids with a long, irregular stricture on barium study indicates oesophageal carcinoma; squamous cancer is especially common in parts of China.

Long-standing dysphagia with regurgitation of undigested food, eased by washing food down, and a smooth 'bird's beak' taper at the lower oesophagus indicate achalasia, from failure of the lower sphincter to relax.
Mixed bulbar and limb weakness with normal routine tests and imaging suggests motor neurone disease, which affects upper and lower motor neurones while sparing sensation.
Combining a loop diuretic with metolazone causes profound potassium loss, and severe hypokalaemia produces generalised muscle weakness.
Proximal weakness in a thin, tremulous, tachycardic young woman suggests thyrotoxic myopathy, which improves once thyroid function is controlled.
Ascending weakness with distal sensory symptoms after an infection, progressing to respiratory failure, is Guillain-Barre syndrome; monitor vital capacity rather than peak flow.

Painful wasting and weakness of the thigh muscles in diabetes is diabetic amyotrophy (lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy), which often improves with tighter glycaemic control, sometimes using insulin.
A stroke soon after a long flight suggests a venous clot crossing to the arterial side through a septal defect (paradoxical embolism); bubble-contrast echocardiography shows the shunt.
The 13C urea breath test detects H. pylori urease without endoscopy or blood sampling, which suits a needle-phobic patient.
Sensory symptoms and episodes of visual loss in a young woman suggest multiple sclerosis; delayed visual-evoked responses reveal optic nerve demyelination, complementing MRI.
Recurrent melaena with normal gastroscopy and colonoscopy points to a small-bowel source; a technetium-labelled red cell scan can detect intermittent bleeding.
Nephrotic syndrome in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis suggests AA amyloidosis; a rectal (or fat pad) biopsy showing apple-green birefringence with Congo red confirms it.
Beta-interferon, a disease-modifying injection, reduces relapse frequency in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; flu-like symptoms and low mood are common side-effects.
Infliximab, an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, is used for severe Crohn's disease and refractory fistulae; screen for latent tuberculosis first.
Ongoing ischaemia in an NSTEMI awaiting angiography can be treated with abciximab, a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor blocker that stops platelets binding fibrinogen.

Alpha-interferon was the backbone of hepatitis C treatment, but it can cause severe depression and suicidality, so a recent suicide attempt contraindicates it. Direct-acting antivirals have since replaced it.
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor shortens chemotherapy-induced neutropenia and reduces infections, particularly after a previous neutropenic episode.
Painless progressive jaundice with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law) indicates malignant distal bile duct obstruction, most often pancreatic carcinoma.
Previous biliary pain followed by obstructive jaundice without a palpable gallbladder suggests a stone in the common bile duct; a chronically scarred gallbladder cannot distend.
Ulcerative colitis is the classic association of primary sclerosing cholangitis, a fibrosing, stricturing disease of the bile ducts causing cholestatic jaundice.
Acute jaundice with fever, tender hepatomegaly and transaminases far higher than the alkaline phosphatase indicates acute viral hepatitis; confirm with serology.
Months of itching and dark urine in a middle-aged woman with cholestatic liver tests and antimitochondrial antibodies indicate primary biliary cholangitis, the book's 'primary biliary cirrhosis'.
Small-bowel obstruction in an elderly woman with a tender, inflamed groin lump and no previous surgery points to a strangulated femoral hernia.

Recurrent obstructive episodes after previous abdominal and pelvic operations are typical of adhesions, the commonest cause of small-bowel obstruction in the West; conservative management comes first if there is no strangulation.
Episodic screaming with drawing up of the legs, vomiting and blood and mucus per rectum in an infant indicate intussusception, often reduced by an air or contrast enema.
Large-bowel obstruction preceded by months of altered bowel habit and weight loss in an older man suggests an obstructing colorectal cancer.
A single hugely dilated colonic loop in an immobile, institutionalised elderly man suggests sigmoid volvulus; endoscopic decompression is often tried first.
Low-grade fever on the first day after abdominal surgery, especially when pain limits breathing and coughing, is most often due to basal atelectasis.
A long-term catheter in an elderly patient is a strong risk factor for urinary infection, the likeliest cause of fever without other localising features.
Swinging fever with lower abdominal tenderness several days after appendicectomy for gangrenous appendicitis suggests a pelvic abscess.
A swinging fever with right upper quadrant tenderness, basal crackles and a small effusion after upper abdominal surgery suggests a subphrenic collection irritating the diaphragm.
Peritonitis and sepsis a few days after an anterior resection indicate a leak from the colorectal anastomosis, which needs urgent resuscitation and surgery.
A large renal mass, here a renal-cell carcinoma, can push the pelvicalyceal system downwards on an intravenous urogram (image F).
Bilateral renal enlargement on a plain film (image A) is typical of adult polycystic kidney disease.
Images E and H show dilated, obstructed pelvicalyceal systems on each side, and G shows a dilated system within a duplex kidney; all three are credited.
A horseshoe kidney (C), with both collecting systems rotated, and a duplex system (H) are congenital anomalies of the renal tract; both are credited.
Abnormal calcification includes a bladder stone (D), medullary nephrocalcinosis (I) and a staghorn calculus (J); all three are credited.
Urgency and frequency with leakage that improves on an antimuscarinic such as tolterodine point to detrusor overactivity.
Continuous leakage beginning soon after a difficult hysterectomy indicates a vesicovaginal fistula from unrecognised bladder injury.
A vaginal bulge with voiding difficulty relieved by digitally reducing the anterior wall indicates a cystocele kinking the urethra.
Sudden frequency, urgency and dysuria after a recent procedure, probably with catheterisation, indicate a urinary tract infection.
Stress leakage in a peri-menopausal woman with no rise in detrusor pressure during leakage on urodynamics confirms urodynamic (genuine) stress incontinence.
A small, pedunculated, lobulated rectal polyp is most likely a tubular adenoma, a benign but premalignant lesion that should be removed.
Diarrhoea days after antibiotic prophylaxis with Clostridium difficile in the stool indicates pseudomembranous colitis.
Flask-shaped colonic ulcers with PAS-positive trophozoites containing ingested red cells are diagnostic of Entamoeba histolytica infection.
Sigmoid narrowing with multiple outpouchings and no mass, plus fever and left iliac fossa tenderness, indicates diverticular disease complicated by diverticulitis.
Continuous inflammation from the rectum upwards, crypt abscesses and distortion, no granulomas and negative stool cultures indicate ulcerative colitis.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles, including lateral cricoarytenoid, except cricothyroid.
The conus elasticus (cricovocal membrane) arises from the upper border of the cricoid arch; its free upper edge forms the vocal ligament.
Each vocal fold runs from the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage near the midline back to the vocal process of the arytenoid.
The quadrangular membrane stretches from the side of the epiglottis back to the arytenoid cartilage; its lower free border forms the vestibular fold.
The epiglottis lies behind the root of the tongue, separated from it by the valleculae, and tips over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

where.title: Nerve supply of the muscles of the lower limb

items.explanation: Gluteus medius, with minimus and tensor fasciae latae, is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve; weakness produces a Trendelenburg gait.
The hamstrings, including semimembranosus, are supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.
Tibialis anterior and the other anterior compartment muscles are supplied by the deep peroneal nerve; injury causes foot drop.
Peroneus longus and brevis in the lateral compartment are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve.
Soleus and the other calf muscles are supplied by the tibial nerve.
An alpha-blocker such as doxazosin lowers blood pressure and also relaxes prostatic smooth muscle, easing urinary symptoms once cancer has been reasonably excluded.
With diabetes, dyslipidaemia and LVH, an ACE inhibitor such as ramipril is preferred: it protects the kidneys and helps left ventricular hypertrophy regress.
Methyldopa has the longest safety record in pregnancy and remains a standard choice, alongside labetalol and nifedipine; ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated.
In a hypertensive patient with exertional angina, a beta-blocker treats both problems by slowing the heart and cutting myocardial oxygen demand.
ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough through bradykinin accumulation; an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan blocks the same pathway without this effect.
Foot drop is managed with an ankle-foot orthosis from the orthotist and gait and strengthening work with the physiotherapist; both are needed.

A partially sighted, neuropathic woman newly on insulin needs broad support: chiropody for her feet, dietary advice, district nursing, occupational therapy, social care and a diabetes specialist nurse.

Keeping a person with dementia at home with a struggling carer relies on community support: a social worker for services, occupational therapy and physiotherapy for function and safety, plus dietary and foot care.
After a first presentation with ketoacidosis, the diabetes specialist nurse teaches insulin technique and self-management, with district nurse follow-up at home.

A man with schizophrenia who is neglecting himself needs community psychiatric nurse follow-up and social work support to live independently; the book's key does not add the chiropodist despite the nail problem.
Diabetes, skin pigmentation, signs of chronic liver disease and a ferritin in the thousands indicate hereditary haemochromatosis, an autosomal recessive iron-overload disorder.
Positive smooth-muscle and LKM-1 autoantibodies with a prompt response to corticosteroids indicate autoimmune hepatitis.
Chronic haemolysis in sickle-cell disease produces pigment gallstones, here causing cholecystitis with an obstructive pattern; the infection may also trigger a crisis.
An acute hepatitic illness after travel to India with an IgM response to an RNA virus fits hepatitis A, spread faeco-orally and never chronic.
A raised alkaline phosphatase with itching in ulcerative colitis, and beaded bile ducts on cholangiography, indicate primary sclerosing cholangitis.
Early-onset dementia with involuntary movements and an affected parent indicates Huntington's disease, an autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disorder on chromosome 4.
Gradual memory loss and getting lost, with normal screening bloods and generalised atrophy, fits Alzheimer's disease; cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil give modest benefit.
Cognitive decline with gait apraxia and urinary incontinence, and ventricles enlarged out of proportion to atrophy, is normal-pressure hydrocephalus, which may improve with CSF shunting.
Positive treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA) in both serum and CSF of a patient with dementia indicate neurosyphilis; penicillin halts progression but rarely reverses it.
Progressive language difficulty with relatively preserved memory and focal temporal lobe atrophy suggests frontotemporal (Pick's) dementia.
Cellulitis is usually streptococcal or staphylococcal, so benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin covers both; the book credits the combination.
Offensive watery diarrhoea with sulphurous belching after travel to Russia suggests giardiasis, treated with metronidazole (or tinidazole).
Chlamydial urethritis responds to doxycycline or a macrolide; the book credits clarithromycin and doxycycline, though azithromycin is the usual macrolide choice.
Diarrhoea after repeated antibiotic courses suggests Clostridium difficile infection, treated with oral metronidazole or oral vancomycin, which act within the gut lumen; either is accepted.
Gram-positive diplococci in CSF indicate pneumococcal meningitis; cefotaxime penetrates CSF well as empirical cover and benzylpenicillin suits sensitive strains. Either is accepted.
Proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules is dermatomyositis, which in older adults may signal an underlying cancer; anti-Jo-1 is a myositis-specific antibody.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's) is closely associated with c-ANCA directed against proteinase-3.
A paraneoplastic cerebellar syndrome with lung cancer is linked to anti-Hu (small-cell carcinoma) and anti-Ri antibodies; both are credited.
Steatorrhoea, weight loss and anaemia in a young woman suggest coeliac disease, screened for with IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies.
Fatigable weakness that improves with edrophonium is myasthenia gravis, caused by antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor.
Alternating bowel habit with left iliac fossa pain, a previous barium enema and advice to eat more fibre point to diverticular disease.
Back pain with urinary retention, lax anal tone and saddle anaesthesia indicate cauda equina compression, a surgical emergency.
A new change in bowel habit with iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man must be assumed to be colorectal cancer until colonoscopy proves otherwise.
Severe constipation from infancy with soiling and a huge faecal mass in a teenager suggests idiopathic megacolon, with Hirschsprung's disease as the main differential.
New constipation after a change of medication, most likely an opioid analgesic replacing an NSAID, is drug-induced.
Cyclical bilateral breast pain with nodularity and a cyst that yields clear fluid and then disappears is fibrocystic change (fibroadenosis).
A hard, irregular lump causing asymmetry on arm-raising (tethering) in a woman over 50 is breast carcinoma until triple assessment proves otherwise.
A very tender swelling in a breastfeeding woman a few weeks after delivery is a lactational abscess, usually staphylococcal, needing antibiotics and aspiration or drainage.
Bloodstained single-duct discharge without a lump in a woman in her forties most often comes from a duct papilloma.
A small, firm, highly mobile lump with benign cytology in a teenager is a fibroadenoma.
Image C shows a horseshoe kidney: the lower poles are fused across the midline and both collecting systems are malrotated.
Image B shows contrast in the bladder with a single functioning kidney in the right iliac fossa, the usual site for a renal transplant.
Image J shows a large branching stone filling the right renal pelvis and calyces (staghorn calculus), typically struvite formed with urease-producing organisms such as Proteus.
Image D shows large calculi within the bladder, usually linked with outflow obstruction and urinary stasis.
Image G shows duplicated collecting systems and ureters (duplex kidneys), which predispose to reflux and infection.
Acute back pain with sciatica and reduced straight-leg raising after lifting indicates a prolapsed lumbar disc irritating a nerve root.
Relentless back pain that is worse at night and at rest in an older patient is a red flag for spinal metastases.
A fixed, smooth thoracic kyphosis in an adolescent is Scheuermann's disease, from vertebral wedging during the growth spurt.
Chronic mechanical low back pain with reduced movement and no neurological signs in later life is spondylosis (degenerative disc and facet disease).
Calf pain on walking that settles slowly with rest and leaning forward, with normal pulses, is neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis.
Heavy bleeding straight after delivery with a complete third stage, after a uterus overdistended by polyhydramnios, indicates uterine atony, the commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage.
Sudden bleeding, fetal bradycardia and loss of the presenting part from the pelvis in obstructed labour after a previous Caesarean indicate uterine rupture.
Ongoing bleeding with an empty uterus plus oozing from cannula sites after severe pre-eclampsia and major haemorrhage indicates disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Painful antepartum bleeding with a tender, contracting uterus suggests placental abruption; placenta praevia typically bleeds painlessly.
Brisk bleeding immediately after artificial membrane rupture with an engaged head suggests a torn fetal vessel crossing the os (vasa praevia), which endangers the fetus.

where.title: Diseases of the lung and pleura

items.explanation: Consolidation of an entire lobe with fever and productive cough in a debilitated man is lobar pneumonia, usually pneumococcal.
Bilateral hilar nodes with non-caseating granulomas and no acid-fast bacilli in a young black woman indicate sarcoidosis.
An apical (Pancoast) tumour invading the lower brachial plexus causes shoulder and arm pain; keratinised malignant cells indicate squamous-cell carcinoma.
Foamy alveolar exudate with silver-staining cyst forms in an HIV patient is Pneumocystis pneumonia, an AIDS-defining infection.
A central lung mass with Cushingoid features and hypokalaemia in a smoker suggests ectopic ACTH from small-cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine tumour.
The duodenojejunal flexure lies just left of the L2 vertebra, where the root of the small-bowel mesentery begins.
The first part of the duodenum is closely related to the gallbladder, which can fistulate into it (the usual route for gallstone ileus).
Tall, numerous villi and prominent circular folds characterise the jejunal mucosa, maximising absorption.
The hepatic flexure of the colon rests against the right kidney's lower pole before turning medially as the transverse colon.
The apex of the inverted-V root of the sigmoid mesocolon lies over the left ureter where the left common iliac artery divides.

where.title: Openings in the base of the skull

items.explanation: Stylopharyngeus is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which leaves the skull through the jugular foramen with the vagus and accessory nerves.
The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue's intrinsic muscles and exits through the hypoglossal (anterior condylar) canal.
The upper incisors are supplied by the anterior superior alveolar branch of the infraorbital nerve, the maxillary nerve's continuation, which enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure.
The trochlear nerve, which supplies superior oblique, enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the tendinous ring.
Medial pterygoid is supplied by the mandibular nerve, which leaves the skull through the foramen ovale.
Severe hypertension with hypokalaemia, suppressed renin and high aldosterone indicates primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), caused by an adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.

Frontal bossing, a bitemporal field defect and hyperglycaemia with hypertension point to a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma; confirm with IGF-1 and failure of GH suppression after oral glucose.
Hypertension with large palpable kidneys, renal impairment and secondary polycythaemia in a young adult suggests autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
Widespread atherosclerosis plus a sharp fall in renal function after starting an ACE inhibitor suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis, where filtration depends on angiotensin II.

Paroxysms of sweating, palpitations and headache with severe hypertension and raised catecholamine metabolites indicate phaeochromocytoma, here bilateral; alpha-blockade must come before any beta-blocker.
Ptosis, facial weakness and wasting with an inability to release a grip (myotonia) are classic of myotonic dystrophy, a trinucleotide-repeat disorder.

Myocardial infarction in a young adult with first-degree relatives affected in early adulthood suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia, an LDL-receptor defect treated with high-dose statins and family screening.
Cafe-au-lait patches and cutaneous neurofibromas, with a relative disabled by a spinal tumour, indicate neurofibromatosis type 1.
A long QT interval with torsade de pointes, normal electrolytes and no culprit drugs suggests congenital long QT syndrome; Romano-Ward is the autosomal dominant form without deafness.
A mild, isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia during an acute illness, with otherwise normal liver tests, is Gilbert's syndrome, a benign conjugation defect.
Frequent small-volume bloody, mucoid stools in a child back from South Asia are typical of bacillary dysentery from Shigella.
Fever and cramping diarrhoea after undercooked chicken, with curved, motile Gram-negative rods, indicate Campylobacter jejuni.
Rapid-onset vomiting and diarrhoea after rice kept warm or reheated, settling within a day, is Bacillus cereus toxin-mediated food poisoning.
Profuse diarrhoea after a long hospital stay and repeated antibiotics, responding to oral vancomycin and confirmed by toxin testing, is Clostridium difficile infection.
Diarrhoea followed by renal failure and DIC in an outbreak linked to beef points to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (such as O157) causing haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Corneal microdeposits, photosensitivity and peripheral neuropathy in a patient with heart disease are recognised adverse effects of amiodarone.
Sensory symptoms with episodes of visual blurring, delayed visual-evoked responses and MRI lesions in a young adult indicate multiple sclerosis (central demyelination).
Nephrotic syndrome with a sensory neuropathy and apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining of the biopsy indicates amyloidosis.
Weight gain, lethargy, macrocytosis and hyponatraemia in a woman with vitiligo suggest autoimmune hypothyroidism, which can cause carpal tunnel syndrome and neuropathy.
A strict vegan diet can cause B12 deficiency, giving severe macrocytic anaemia, pancytopenia and a sensory neuropathy; replace with intramuscular hydroxocobalamin.
Fever, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia and cannonball lung deposits suggest renal-cell carcinoma, a classic malignant cause of pyrexia of unknown origin.
Fever with tender nodes and atypical mononuclear cells on the film in a teenager is infectious mononucleosis from Epstein-Barr virus.
A flu-like illness with dry cough after caving suggests histoplasmosis, acquired by inhaling fungal spores from bat or bird droppings.
Fever and cough with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in a young Afro-Caribbean woman, confirmed by bronchoscopy and lavage, indicate sarcoidosis.
Fever, arthralgia, headache and an expanding red rash after walking in deer-rich woodland indicate early Lyme disease (erythema migrans), treated with doxycycline or amoxicillin.

where.title: Common causes of right iliac fossa pain

items.explanation: Years of pain with bloating and variable bowel habit, normal investigations and no alarm features suggest irritable bowel syndrome.
Mild right iliac fossa pain without fever or peritonism, normal tests and spontaneous resolution is non-specific abdominal pain, the commonest final diagnosis.
Right iliac fossa pain following a viral sore throat, with high fever, enlarged neck nodes and a normal white count in a child, suggests mesenteric adenitis.
Lower abdominal pain with fever, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia and cervical excitation indicates pelvic inflammatory disease rather than appendicitis.
Sudden severe one-sided lower abdominal pain in a young woman suggests torsion of an ovarian cyst; pelvic ultrasound and urgent surgery are needed.
High pH with a low CO2, normal bicarbonate and normal oxygen indicate acute respiratory alkalosis from anxiety-driven hyperventilation.
Raised CO2 with a near-normal pH and high bicarbonate indicate chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation, as in stable COPD with type II failure.
Acidaemia with low bicarbonate, low CO2 and hypoxaemia in a breathless pregnant woman suggests pulmonary embolism: lactic acidosis, hyperventilation and type I respiratory failure.
Salicylate poisoning stimulates the respiratory centre (respiratory alkalosis) and adds an acid load (metabolic acidosis); by this stage the acidosis dominates, with normal oxygenation.
Prolonged vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction loses hydrochloric acid, causing severe metabolic alkalosis with a very high bicarbonate and normal oxygenation.
Recurrent Proteus infections promote struvite stones, so a staghorn calculus (J) fits; a duplex system (G) also predisposes to recurrent infection and is credited.
Urinary schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium) damages the bladder wall and predisposes to bladder stones and squamous cancer; image D shows vesical calculi.
Weight loss, night sweats, anaemia and a ballotable loin mass suggest renal-cell carcinoma, which displaces the collecting system (image F).
Bilaterally enlarged kidneys with haematuria, infections, resistant hypertension and polycythaemia indicate adult polycystic kidney disease (image A).
Loin pain provoked by alcohol (a diuresis) in a young man with normal urinalysis suggests pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction; image H shows a dilated left system, cured by pyeloplasty.
Anterior knee pain on stairs in a teenage girl suggests chondromalacia patellae (patellofemoral pain), linked to patellar mal-tracking.
Chronic pain and swelling with a valgus deformity suggests long-standing rheumatoid arthritis; osteoarthritis more often produces a varus knee.
A twisting injury followed by locking, an effusion and a positive McMurray's test indicate a meniscal tear.
Anterior knee swelling in someone who kneels for work is prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee).
A tender lump over the tibial tuberosity in an active adolescent is Osgood-Schlatter disease, a traction apophysitis.
Facial swelling with stridor and no allergen, fever or other cause suggests angio-oedema; protect the airway and give adrenaline if severe.
Hoarseness and surgical emphysema after a direct blow to the front of the neck indicate a laryngeal fracture, which can rapidly obstruct the airway.
A hard, fixed thyroid mass with tracheal compression and stridor in an elderly woman suggests anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, which has a very poor prognosis.
Rapid-onset fever, sore throat and stridor in a child is acute epiglottitis; never examine the throat, and secure the airway in theatre.
Facial burns with hoarseness, stridor and carbonaceous sputum indicate thermal and smoke injury to the upper airway; intubate early.
A smear showing moderate dyskaryosis is a high-grade result requiring colposcopy, with biopsy or treatment as indicated.
Urodynamically proven stress incontinence that fails conservative measures can be treated surgically, for example by colposuspension (now often a mid-urethral tape).
Persistent abnormal bleeding after 40 with a thickened endometrium needs hysteroscopy and biopsy to exclude endometrial pathology; a serosal fibroid does not distort the cavity.
Suspected endometriosis that does not respond to empirical treatment needs diagnostic laparoscopy, which can also treat lesions.
An isolated symptomatic cystocele is corrected by anterior vaginal repair.
A prolonged APTT with normal PT and bleeding time and low factor VIII indicates haemophilia A, an X-linked defect of the intrinsic pathway.
Prolonged PT and APTT with normal platelets and bleeding time indicate deficiency of the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X.
A prolonged bleeding time plus a prolonged APTT with low factor VIII indicates von Willebrand disease, since vWF both anchors platelets and protects factor VIII.
Prolonged bleeding time, PT and APTT with low platelets and clotting factors indicate consumption in disseminated intravascular coagulation.
A prolonged APTT with normal factor VIII but low factor IX indicates haemophilia B (Christmas disease).
The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery, outside the femoral sheath.
The medial boundary of the femoral ring is the lacunar ligament, the part of the inguinal ligament reflected back onto the pubic ramus.
Behind the femoral canal lies the pectineal (Cooper's) ligament on the superior pubic ramus, used to anchor femoral hernia repairs.
A femoral hernia reaches the subcutaneous tissue through the saphenous opening, then turns upwards over the inguinal ligament.
The femoral canal opens below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, a key landmark for telling femoral from inguinal hernias.

where.title: Muscle attachments of the lower limb

items.explanation: Psoas major and iliacus converge into the iliopsoas tendon, which inserts into the lesser trochanter.
The linea aspera gives attachment to the adductors, including longus and magnus, and to vastus lateralis; all three are credited.
The lateral head of gastrocnemius arises from just above and behind the lateral femoral condyle.
Peroneus longus arises from the upper two-thirds of the lateral fibula; brevis comes from the lower part.
Tibialis posterior inserts chiefly into the tuberosity of the navicular, with slips to other tarsal bones.

Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (eruptive xanthomata, pancreatitis) enlarges the non-water fraction of plasma, so indirect methods report a falsely low sodium while osmolality is normal: pseudohyponatraemia.
Encephalitis confirmed by herpes simplex PCR on CSF, with raised intracranial pressure, commonly causes SIADH and hyponatraemia.
Confusion, hypoxaemia and severe hyponatraemia with lymphopenia suggest Legionella pneumonia, which characteristically causes SIADH.
Hypotension, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia during an infection after long-term steroids indicate adrenal insufficiency from a suppressed axis, which responds to hydrocortisone.
Hypothermia, bradycardia with J waves, macrocytosis and hyponatraemia in an older woman with vitiligo suggest severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema).
Progressive breathlessness with fine basal crackles in rheumatoid arthritis suggests rheumatoid-associated interstitial lung disease, which resembles idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Acute breathlessness with confusion, marked hypoxaemia and a relatively clear film in a previously well man fits an atypical pneumonia.
A reduced peak flow that improves well beyond 20% after inhalers and steroids confirms reversible airflow obstruction (asthma), here triggered by exercise.
Sudden breathlessness, tachycardia and hypoxaemia with a normal chest film in a patient with active cancer strongly suggests pulmonary embolism; confirm with CT pulmonary angiography.
Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and lung infiltrates in a young Afro-Caribbean woman indicates sarcoidosis (radiographic stage 2).
Polycystic kidney disease often brings liver cysts and hepatomegaly; ballotable kidneys, renal failure, hypertension and a relative's sudden fatal stroke (probably a berry aneurysm) fit.
Acute hepatitis with transaminases above 1000 after travel to South-East Asia, and serology confirming an RNA virus, indicates hepatitis A.
Skin pigmentation, diabetes and chronic liver disease indicate haemochromatosis; alcohol may coexist and accelerate the liver damage.
Cachexia, a change in bowel habit and multiple echogenic liver lesions with an enlarged liver suggest colorectal cancer with liver metastases.
Long-standing itch progressing to jaundice in a middle-aged woman suggests primary biliary cholangitis. The book prints J, but its answer names primary biliary cirrhosis, which is option I.
Accidental double-dosing of morphine causes opioid toxicity with pinpoint pupils and reduced consciousness, partly reversed by naloxone.
A unilateral dilated pupil with a sluggish light reaction and absent tendon reflexes in a young adult is a Holmes-Adie pupil, a benign condition.
A small, irregular pupil that constricts to accommodation but poorly to light, with positive treponemal tests, is an Argyll Robertson pupil of neurosyphilis.
A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses the third nerve, causing ptosis and a fixed, dilated pupil with the eye turned down and out.
Ptosis and a small pupil on the same side as an apical lung tumour indicate Horner's syndrome from invasion of the sympathetic chain (Pancoast tumour).

Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils in a woman with autoimmune thyroid disease suggests pernicious anaemia, marked by intrinsic factor antibodies. The book prints D, but its answer names intrinsic factor antibody, which is option E.
Steatorrhoea, weight loss and anaemia in a young woman suggest coeliac disease, supported by IgA anti-endomysial antibodies.
Antimitochondrial antibodies are present in over 90% of patients with primary biliary cholangitis.
Proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and a very high creatine kinase is dermatomyositis; anti-Jo-1 is a myositis-specific antibody, and the apical mass raises an associated lung cancer.

Fatigable weakness with lung cancer suggests Lambert-Eaton syndrome, in which strength improves with repeated effort. Its antibodies actually target presynaptic calcium channels; the book keys the closest listed option, acetylcholine-receptor antibody.
Epigastric pain through to the back with vomiting, jaundice and peritonism suggests severe gallstone pancreatitis with a stone obstructing the ampulla.
Sudden epigastric pain spreading across a rigid abdomen in a patient likely taking NSAIDs for rheumatoid arthritis indicates a perforated peptic ulcer.
Long-standing diverticular symptoms with worsening left iliac fossa pain and then generalised peritonism suggest perforated sigmoid diverticulitis.
In large-bowel obstruction the caecum distends most and can become ischaemic and perforate, causing sudden faecal peritonitis.
Sudden abdominal and back pain with collapse and shock in an elderly man is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm until proved otherwise.
Sudden severe scrotal pain with a high-riding testis in a boy is testicular torsion; explore surgically without delay.
Scrotal pain and swelling with fever, preceding urinary symptoms and pyuria indicate bacterial epididymo-orchitis.
A soft 'bag of worms' in the left hemiscrotum that appears on standing is a varicocele (dilated pampiniform plexus).
Painful swelling that does not transilluminate after scrotal surgery in an anticoagulated man indicates a haematocele.
A hard, irregular testicular mass in a man in his thirties with raised beta-hCG but normal AFP suggests seminoma; a raised AFP would point to a non-seminomatous tumour.
Ectopic calcification is seen in image A (a calcified dorsalis pedis artery, typical of diabetes) and image D (a calcified goitre in the neck); both are credited.
Image J shows a fracture of the skull vault after blunt trauma.
Joint space narrowing appears in both cervical spondylosis (C) and knee osteoarthritis (E), along with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis; both are credited.
Cortical thickening with coarse trabeculae around the pelvis (image B) is characteristic of Paget's disease of bone.
Image A, a diabetic foot with osteomyelitis, shows bone destruction with erosion of the cortex around a toe joint.
The same diabetic foot (image A) also shows gas in the soft tissues, a sign of severe infection.
Prolonged vomiting of gastric acid causes a marked metabolic alkalosis with a very high bicarbonate and normal oxygenation.
Diabetic ketoacidosis produces a severe metabolic acidosis with a very low bicarbonate and low CO2 from compensatory Kussmaul breathing.
Acute pulmonary embolism causes hypoxaemia with hyperventilation, giving a respiratory alkalosis with low CO2 (type I respiratory failure).
Stable COPD with chronic CO2 retention shows hypoxaemia and hypercapnia with a normal pH maintained by raised bicarbonate (compensated type II failure).
Life-threatening asthma with exhaustion causes rising CO2 and hypoxaemia plus lactic acidosis, a mixed acidosis that signals impending arrest.
A painless, indurated ulcer with rubbery groin nodes weeks after unprotected sex is the chancre of primary syphilis.
A slow-growing ulcer with a rolled, pearly edge near the inner canthus is a basal-cell carcinoma (rodent ulcer).
Squamous carcinoma arising in an old burn scar or chronic ulcer is a Marjolin's ulcer; nodes are often absent because scar tissue lacks lymphatics.
A large shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus with pigmentation and induration (lipodermatosclerosis) is a venous ulcer, treated with compression once arterial disease is excluded.
A papule evolving into a painless black eschar with toxaemia and regional nodes in a farmer exposed to animals is cutaneous anthrax.
Heavy bleeding with retained tissue in the uterus and a closed os is an incomplete miscarriage.
An empty uterus with free fluid in the pouch of Douglas and a slowly rising beta-hCG above the level where an intrauterine sac should be visible suggests ectopic pregnancy.
Heavy bleeding, an empty uterus without free fluid and a pregnancy test that turns negative indicate a complete miscarriage.
An intrauterine embryo with no heartbeat and growth lagging behind dates is a missed (delayed) miscarriage.
A uterus large for dates with multiple cystic spaces and no fetal pole on ultrasound indicates a complete hydatidiform mole.
Pleuritic pain with a friction rub a few days after a transmural infarct is early post-infarction (fibrinous) pericarditis over the dead muscle.
Right heart failure with right ventricular hypertrophy in long-standing COPD is cor pulmonale from hypoxic pulmonary hypertension.
Sudden death during exertion in a young athlete with massive, asymmetric septal hypertrophy indicates hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Fever after a dental extraction in a patient with rheumatic valve disease, with viridans streptococci in blood cultures, indicates infective endocarditis.
A segment that bulges outwards in systole months after a large anterior infarct is a left ventricular aneurysm, which can cause failure, arrhythmia and mural thrombus.
At the medial end of the canal, the floor is formed by the lacunar ligament, the part of the inguinal ligament reflected back onto the pubic ramus.
A direct hernia pushes through weakened transversalis fascia in the posterior wall of the canal (Hesselbach's triangle).
An indirect hernia enters through the deep ring and may track along the cord down to the scrotum.
The arching fibres of internal oblique, joined by transversus abdominis, form the roof of the inguinal canal.
The inferior epigastric vessels lie medial to the deep ring and so to the neck of an indirect hernia; direct hernias emerge medial to these vessels.
The vertebral artery runs up in front of the C7 transverse process before entering the foramen transversarium of C6.
The internal jugular vein lies deep to the triangular gap separating the two heads of sternocleidomastoid, a landmark for central venous access.
The subclavian artery crosses the first rib in a groove behind scalenus anterior; the vein passes in front of the muscle.
The hypoglossal nerve passes forwards across the internal and external carotid arteries on its way to the tongue.
The superficial temporal artery can be felt just above the zygomatic arch in front of the ear and is the vessel biopsied in giant-cell arteritis.

Pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy shows dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates and cotton-wool spots; exudates around the macula with falling acuity mean maculopathy, which needs urgent ophthalmology referral. All five are credited.
Background diabetic retinopathy consists of microaneurysms (dots), blot haemorrhages and hard exudates, with vision preserved; all three are credited.
Grade II hypertensive retinopathy adds arteriovenous nipping to the arteriolar 'silver wiring' of grade I; both are credited.
A large space-occupying lesion with oedema raises intracranial pressure, causing swollen optic discs with blurred margins (papilloedema).
Haemorrhagic, necrotic retinal patches in advanced AIDS are cytomegalovirus retinitis, which threatens sight and needs ganciclovir.
Chronic heart failure enlarges the cardiac silhouette (cardiothoracic ratio over 0.5) and causes pleural effusions; both are credited.
A collapsed left lower lobe lies behind the heart, giving a 'double' left cardiac contour and effacing the medial left hemidiaphragm; both are credited.
The book credits a raised horizontal fissure, an effusion and a trachea displaced leftwards: a mass pushes the trachea away, although an upper lobe collapse would pull it towards the lesion.
Middle lobe consolidation blurs the right heart border, and a parapneumonic effusion may accompany it; both are credited.
Right lower lobe collapse pulls the horizontal fissure down and obscures the right hemidiaphragm; both are credited.
Stage 1 sarcoidosis is defined by bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal shadowing.
A right tension pneumothorax pushes the mediastinum and trachea over to the left.
Low-grade fever weeks after dental extraction with a regurgitant mitral murmur, anaemia, haematuria and a just-palpable spleen indicates subacute infective endocarditis.
Fever, pneumonitis, hepatosplenomegaly and haemorrhagic retinitis after transplantation indicate disseminated cytomegalovirus infection, treated with ganciclovir.
A high white count made mostly of blasts, with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly, indicates acute myeloid leukaemia; confirm on bone marrow.
Night sweats, painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, eosinophilia and Reed-Sternberg cells on node biopsy indicate Hodgkin lymphoma.
Massive splenomegaly with a white count around 250 x 10^9/l indicates chronic myeloid (granulocytic) leukaemia, driven by BCR-ABL.
A facial port-wine stain in the trigeminal territory with seizures indicates Sturge-Weber syndrome, with leptomeningeal angiomatosis on the same side.
Fever, headache and focal signs with a ring-enhancing lesion in an HIV-positive patient suggest a cerebral abscess, toxoplasmosis being a common cause.
An SSRI plus a thiazide is a classic combination for severe hyponatraemia in older people, causing confusion and seizures.
Sudden severe headache with reduced consciousness, seizures and blood in the ventricles and around the brainstem on CT indicates subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Very little sunlight exposure causes vitamin D deficiency; positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs with seizures indicate hypocalcaemia.
Confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and renal impairment with a positive urinary antigen indicate Legionella pneumonia with multi-organ involvement.
Renal failure developing days after starting a penicillin suggests drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (an immune-mediated glomerular lesion is also possible).
Renal impairment within days of a sore throat suggests IgA nephropathy; post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically follows after about two weeks.
Pulmonary haemorrhage with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis indicates anti-GBM (Goodpasture's) disease.
Nasal symptoms, haemoptysis and rapidly progressive renal failure indicate granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's), supported by c-ANCA.
Image A shows soft-tissue gas, swelling and bone destruction around a toe joint, consistent with osteomyelitis complicating a diabetic foot.
Osteoarthritis appears in the cervical spine (spondylosis, C) and the knee (E), with joint-space loss, osteophytes and sclerosis; both are credited.
Secondary deposits are shown by the ring-enhancing brain lesion (H) and the multiple cannonball lung metastases (I); both are credited.
Image B shows cortical thickening and coarse trabeculae around the hip and pelvis, typical of Paget's disease of bone.
Image F, a lateral skull film, shows a protruding mandible and an enlarged pituitary fossa, consistent with acromegaly.
Long-standing heartburn with circumferential erosions, a stricture and pathological acid exposure on 24-hour pH monitoring indicates severe gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
Rapidly progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids with weight loss in an older man indicates oesophageal carcinoma until endoscopy proves otherwise.
Dysphagia with regurgitation and cardiomyopathy in a man from rural South America suggests Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), which destroys the myenteric plexus to mimic achalasia.
Food sticking high in the throat, with regurgitation helped by pressing on the neck, in an elderly woman indicates a pharyngeal pouch through Killian's dehiscence.
A gas bubble behind the heart on an erect film, with acute pain and vomiting, indicates a para-oesophageal (rolling) hiatus hernia that may strangulate.

where.title: Genetic risk factors for colorectal cancer

items.explanation: Germline APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis, with hundreds of adenomas from adolescence and near-certain cancer without prophylactic colectomy.
Germline mismatch repair gene mutations causing microsatellite instability underlie hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome).
Perioral pigmentation with hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps and a raised cancer risk is Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
Extensive colitis from ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease raises colorectal cancer risk with disease duration, so surveillance colonoscopy begins about 8-10 years after onset.
The Amsterdam criteria identify families likely to have Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) from the number of affected relatives, generations involved and age at diagnosis.
Hypokalaemia and renal impairment potentiate digoxin, causing nausea, vomiting and bradycardia; the strip shows slow atrial fibrillation with reverse-tick ST depression.
Inferior infarction can damage the AV node, causing complete heart block, with cannon waves as the atria contract against closed tricuspid valves.
A fast, regular narrow-complex tachycardia in a young woman that stops with adenosine is a supraventricular (AV nodal re-entry) tachycardia.
A hard lump below the left clavicle is a pacemaker generator, and the strip shows pacing spikes before each complex.
Atrial fibrillation or flutter in hypertension predisposes to atrial thrombus, which can embolise to the mesenteric arteries; both strips are credited.
A firm, painless supraclavicular node with weight loss, itch and night sweats in a young man suggests lymphoma.
A hard node deep to sternomastoid with hoarseness in an older man suggests metastatic laryngeal carcinoma in the deep cervical chain.
A sternomastoid 'tumour' in an infant is a fibrotic swelling of the muscle after birth trauma, causing torticollis.
A firm node just below the angle of the jaw with enlarged tonsils indicates reactive jugulodigastric lymphadenopathy from recurrent tonsillitis.
A smooth lump near the midline that moves on swallowing arises from the thyroid; a solitary nodule needs ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration.
Bacteriuria in pregnancy is often asymptomatic and easily treated, but untreated it can progress to pyelonephritis, sepsis and preterm labour.
HIV in pregnancy is managed with maternal antiretrovirals, planned delivery (Caesarean if the viral load is not suppressed), infant prophylaxis and avoidance of breastfeeding.
Syphilis can harm the fetus and cause late neurological disease in the mother, yet is easily cured with penicillin, hence routine antenatal screening.
Rubella in the first 20 weeks can cause congenital deafness, cardiac defects and learning disability.
Group B streptococcus colonises up to a fifth of pregnant women without symptoms but can cause severe neonatal sepsis; intrapartum penicillin reduces transmission.
A severe macrocytic anaemia with low B12 and normal folate in an older woman is most often pernicious anaemia, from autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells.
Symmetrical small-joint pain, a malar rash, low complement, high-titre ANA and proteinuria with hypertension indicate SLE with renal involvement.
Low T4 with high TSH, weight gain, constipation and a mild myopathy with raised CK indicate primary hypothyroidism, most often Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
Dry eyes and mouth with parotid enlargement, reduced tear production and anti-Ro antibodies indicate Sjogren's syndrome.
Symmetrical proximal weakness with raised CK, anti-Jo-1 antibodies and inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy, without a rash, indicates polymyositis.
The left ureter descends on psoas behind the left colic vessels before crossing the pelvic brim.
The second part of the duodenum lies in front of the hilum and pelvis of the right kidney.
The right ureter crosses in front of the right common iliac artery as it enters the pelvis.
The prostate sits on the deep perineal pouch, directly above the membranous urethra.
The ovary lies in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall, behind the obliterated umbilical artery and in front of the ureter and internal iliac vessels.
The tricuspid valve lies behind the sternum at about the level of the fourth intercostal space; it is heard best at the lower left sternal edge.
Mitral sounds are heard best at the apex, at the apex, fifth left interspace, mid-clavicular line.
The right border of the heart, formed by the right atrium, runs just beyond the right sternal edge from the third to the sixth costal cartilage.
The aortic area is the second right intercostal space beside the sternum.
Near the medial end of the left sixth intercostal space the pleura swings away (cardiac notch), so a needle can reach the ventricle without crossing lung.
Erratic thyroxine use, often catching up just before a blood test, gives a high TSH (reflecting weeks of under-replacement) with normal free hormone levels.
Primary thyrotoxicosis, probably Graves' disease here, suppresses TSH completely with high free T4 and T3; carbimazole and a beta-blocker control it.
In T3 toxicosis TSH is suppressed and free T3 high while free T4 stays normal, so both hormones should be measured when hyperthyroidism is suspected.
Low free T4 and T3 with an inappropriately normal TSH indicates secondary hypothyroidism from pituitary failure; hypotension, hypoglycaemia and amenorrhoea point to wider hypopituitarism.
Acute illness distorts thyroid tests (sick euthyroid syndrome): T3 falls as T4 is diverted to reverse T3, and TSH may be mildly abnormal; repeat after recovery.
Vomiting accompanies small-bowel obstruction (dilated loops, G) and raised intracranial pressure from a ring-enhancing brain lesion (H); both are credited.
Osteomyelitis (A) and obstructed bowel (G) can both seed bacteria into the blood and cause septic shock; both are credited.
Hypercalcaemia can accompany immobilised Paget's disease (B) and malignancy with brain or lung metastases (H, I), through bone destruction or PTH-related peptide; all three are credited.
Headache can arise from cervical spondylosis (C), a ring-enhancing intracranial lesion (H) or a skull fracture (J); all three are credited.
The book counts the diabetic foot (A), Paget's disease (B), a calcified goitre (D) and acromegaly (F) as endocrine or metabolic abnormalities; all four are credited.

Ascites and bilateral effusions with stigmata of chronic liver disease and a liver mass suggest cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B complicated by hepatocellular carcinoma; the effusions are transudates.
Peripheral oedema and an effusion with ECG signs of old anterior infarction indicate heart failure from ischaemic cardiomyopathy.
Several large round lung deposits with an effusion and anaemia suggest cannonball metastases, classically from renal-cell carcinoma.
Progressive breathlessness with right ventricular strain on the ECG (dominant R in V1, right axis deviation) and effusions suggests recurrent pulmonary emboli.
Muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, Kussmaul's sign and low voltages with bloodstained pericardial fluid in a young man with weight loss suggest tuberculous pericarditis with tamponade.
Erythromycin inhibits hepatic enzymes and raises phenytoin levels; toxicity produces a cerebellar syndrome of ataxia, slurred speech, dysdiadochokinesia and nystagmus, all of which are credited.
Bradykinesia and a mask-like face that respond to levodopa indicate Parkinson's disease, with a characteristic resting tremor.

A dominant-hemisphere stroke with preserved comprehension but no coherent speech is expressive dysphasia; failure to identify objects by touch is astereognosis from parietal involvement. Both are credited.
Diabetic glove-and-stocking neuropathy removes proprioception, producing a sensory ataxia that worsens in the dark.
Gait dyspraxia, confusion and incontinence with ventricular dilatation that improve after shunting indicate normal-pressure hydrocephalus.
Atrioventricular dissociation with a slow escape rhythm and cannon waves indicates complete heart block, which needs a permanent pacemaker when symptomatic.
Profound bradycardia and hypotension provoked by head-up tilt and carotid sinus massage indicate neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope with a carotid sinus component.
Collapse on looking upwards suggests vertebrobasilar insufficiency, where neck extension compromises flow in the posterior circulation.
Exertional syncope with a narrow pulse pressure, a slow-rising carotid pulse and LVH on the ECG indicates severe aortic stenosis; arrange echocardiography.
Several vasodilating and antihypertensive drugs in an elderly man with a normal 24-hour tape make drug-induced postural hypotension the likely cause of his fall.
Pancytopenia, massive splenomegaly and B cells with hair-like cytoplasmic projections in a middle-aged man indicate hairy-cell leukaemia.
An IgM paraprotein with immunoparesis but normal calcium and renal function and no bone lesions points to Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia rather than myeloma.
Rapid-onset painful lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, mouth ulcers and circulating blasts indicate acute leukaemia; in an adult this is most likely AML.
A very high count of mature lymphocytes without blasts in an elderly man is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, traditionally treated with chlorambucil when symptomatic.
Neck lymphadenopathy with night sweats, weight loss and Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy indicates Hodgkin lymphoma.
A change to looser stools with rectal bleeding, mucus, weight loss and anaemia in an older man indicates colorectal, probably left-sided, carcinoma.
Outbreaks of vomiting, diarrhoea and fever among young children are typically viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus or norovirus); rehydration is the key treatment.
Severe diarrhoea with fever and leucocytosis after a cephalosporin in an elderly in-patient suggests Clostridium difficile pseudomembranous colitis.
Liquid stool leaking around impacted faeces in a chronically constipated, immobile patient is overflow diarrhoea; rectal examination confirms it.
Lower abdominal pain with diarrhoea, low-grade fever, left iliac fossa guarding and leucocytosis in an older woman indicates acute diverticulitis.
Randomised controlled trials prospectively compare interventions with random allocation, minimising bias, and are the gold standard for testing treatments.
A systematic review gathers and appraises primary studies using a predefined, reproducible search and selection method.
Meta-analysis statistically pools the numerical results of several trials addressing the same question to give a more precise estimate.
Cohort studies select groups by exposure and follow them forward to compare outcomes, as in the British doctors' smoking study.
A case series describes several patients with the same condition to highlight a feature; it ranks low in the evidence hierarchy but can raise early alerts.
A pigmented lesion on the palm or sole, or under a nail, in a dark-skinned patient is acral lentiginous melanoma.
A slowly enlarging irregular brown patch on sun-damaged facial skin in an elderly person is lentigo maligna (Hutchinson's freckle), an in-situ lesion curable by excision.
A benign naevus whose melanocytes proliferate only at the dermo-epidermal junction is a junctional naevus.
An undifferentiated anal tumour without visible pigment that stains positive for S100 is an amelanotic (mucosal) melanoma.
A large irregular, variably pigmented lesion still confined to the epidermis in a young adult with heavy sun exposure is superficial spreading melanoma, the commonest type.
Complications of prematurity, such as respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and infection, are the largest contributors to perinatal mortality.
Indirect maternal deaths arise from pre-existing disease aggravated by pregnancy, such as cardiac disease or epilepsy; maternal medical conditions are the leading group.
Thromboembolism, especially pulmonary embolism, has long been the leading direct cause of maternal death in UK confidential enquiries.
In severe pre-eclampsia leaky capillaries and impaired renal excretion mean modest fluid overload can cause fatal pulmonary oedema, so fluids must be tightly restricted.
Birth asphyxia causes relatively few perinatal deaths but generates the most complaints that reach litigation.

where.title: Diseases of the upper gastrointestinal tract

items.explanation: Red, velvety columnar mucosa extending up the oesophagus with intestinal metaplasia on biopsy is Barrett's oesophagus, a premalignant complication of reflux.
An ileal stricture with cobblestoning plus non-caseating granulomas in gastric and duodenal biopsies indicates Crohn's disease affecting several gut segments.
A punched-out antral ulcer with benign biopsies and active chronic gastritis (probably H. pylori) is a chronic peptic ulcer, here complicated by bleeding.
Steatorrhoea with folate deficiency, anti-endomysial antibodies and villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes on duodenal biopsy indicate coeliac disease.
An antral mass in an older man with weight loss and iron deficiency, showing infiltrating atypical glands and signet-ring cells, is gastric adenocarcinoma.
Pain eased by leaning forward with widespread concave ST elevation (ECG H) indicates pericarditis; with night sweats and tender nodes, tuberculosis must be considered.
Inferolateral ST elevation with posterior changes indicates a large inferoposterolateral infarct, which can damage the AV node and cause complete heart block (ECG I).
The book matches this to ECG E, an evolving infarct with established Q waves and T-wave inversion across several territories; whatever the exact pattern, he needs urgent hospital transfer.
Left bundle branch block distorts the ST segments and can mimic an anterior STEMI; with fast AF this is ECG D, and comparison with old ECGs helps.
Fast AF in ischaemic heart disease can cause widespread rate-related ST depression, as in ECG C; slowing the rate relieves the ischaemia.
The gallbladder lies in its fossa along the lateral side of the quadrate lobe; the ligamentum teres runs along the medial side.
The caudate process forms the upper boundary of the epiploic foramen (entrance to the lesser sac), with the duodenum below and the IVC behind.
The hepatic artery, portal vein and bile duct enter or leave the liver at the porta hepatis.
The right adrenal and the top of the right kidney sit against the bare area of the liver, bounded by the coronary ligament.
The superior recess of the lesser sac extends upwards behind the caudate lobe.
The right coronary artery arises from the anterior (right) aortic sinus and runs in the right atrioventricular groove.
Diagonal branches arise from the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery to supply the anterolateral left ventricle.
The anterior interventricular artery runs down to, and usually around, the apex, which it supplies.
The book keys the circumflex artery; in practice the sinoatrial nodal artery comes from the right coronary artery in about 60% of people and from the circumflex in about 40%.
The left main coronary artery passes between the left auricle and the pulmonary trunk before dividing into the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries.
